10004-the-warriors:
Anna Robertson Brown Lindsay, writing from Philadelphia in November 1902, called her book The Warriors and framed it as a call to a higher conquest. It opens with chords of awakening, a prelude on the call of Jesus, and a processional of the church of God.

The world-march that follows summons kings, prelates and evangelists, sages, traders, and workers to the same high purpose. Lindsay, author of What Is Worth While, writes earnest, uplifting prose for readers of faith. The book offers encouragement to live bravely and serve, in language meant to stir rather than merely inform.
10046-salute-to-adventurers:
John Buchan's novel, illustrated with a view of 1798 Edinburgh, tells of old Virginian ways in the voice of a Scot who crossed the Atlantic. Its early chapters introduce sweet-singers, a high-handed lady, the Canongate Tolbooth, a stairhead, and a sea-captain.

The hero's first coming to Virginia, his education, his unpopularity, Red Ringan, doings in the Savannah, and an old song follow, with a wild wager and a great folly. Buchan writes adventure with historical color. Readers get the colonial frontier as a young Scot found it: rough, generous, and full of risk.
10122-fairies-and-fusiliers:
Robert Graves, then a young officer in the Royal Welch Fusiliers, published this poetry book in 1918, near the end of the First World War. The title joins two worlds he knew at once: fairy lore from childhood and the hard life of soldiers at the front. Many poems first reached readers in magazines or small books.

Some pieces mourn dead friends, face fear, or joke grimly about army life, while others turn to fauns, fairies, and strange dreams. Graves shifts between pity, anger, and playful fantasy without losing plain speech. Readers get an early, vivid record of a war poet finding his voice between battle and myth.
10132-the-sowers:
Henry Seton Merriman published this political adventure novel in 1895, setting much of it in Russia and western Europe. A young Englishman is drawn into Russian intrigue, where diplomats, princes, and secret agents play for high stakes. The steppe, the Volga, Moscow, and Paris form the shifting stage.

Plots, unmaskings, and sudden flights carry the hero from a waif on the steppe toward a dangerous offer of friendship. Love, charity, and loyalty cut across the schemes of wire-pullers and clubs. Readers get a tense, old-style tale of empire, conspiracy, and honor, written with brisk, clear prose.
10474-the-lost-naval-papers:
Bennet Copplestone published this naval mystery in 1917, in three parts: William Dawson, Madame Gilbert, and Seeing is Believing. The plot opens with a story and a visit, close quarters, an inquisition, and sabotage, as lost naval papers threaten wartime secrets. Copplestone writes with brisk, patriotic suspense, in the manner of First World War thrillers.

A marine sentry, Trehayne's letter, a woman and a man, and a progressive friendship at Brighton carry the middle tale. Guessing, bafflement, and proof close the case, as the papers are traced and the guilty unmasked. Readers get a lively thriller of spies, sailors, and stolen documents.
10516-bits-about-home-matters:
H. H., author of Verses and Bits of Travel, published this essay collection in 1873 on home matters, from parenting to lodging houses. H. H. writes with warmth, wit, and moral care about the small tyrannies and kindnesses of family life. The pieces are short, plain, and meant for ordinary readers.

Essays treat corporal punishment, needless denials, rudeness, breaking the will, the awkward age, a day with a courteous mother, and the republic of the family. Rainy days, children's parties, and a simple Christmas bill of fare add domestic detail. Readers get a lively, Victorian-era book on making homes kinder and happier.
10537-the-governors:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published this novel in 1909, with pictures by Will Grefe and Howard Somerville. Oppenheim, author of A Maker of History and The Missioner, builds the tale in books, opening with Mr. Phineas Duke, cousin Stella, storm clouds, and a meeting of giants. Treachery, firearms, and conspirators soon follow.

Mr. Weiss in a hurry, a professional burglar, Mr. Norris Vine, and Stella's obstinate stand carry the first book toward a truce. A second book will deepen the plot of power and intrigue. Readers get a stylish, Edwardian thriller of society, politics, and hidden control.
10545-the-sea-lions-or-the-lost-sealers:
James Fenimore Cooper published this sea novel in the 1840s, in an edition dated 1860, on lost sealers in southern seas. Its preface warns that men, engrossed by worldly aims, rarely pause to contemplate divine majesty, mercy, and justice amid nature's marvels. Cooper joins adventure to moral reflection.

Two ships, rival sealers, and a harsh polar world test crews through ice, storms, and greed. Faith, doubt, and the specter of the tomb haunt the tale, as Campbell's motto warns. Readers get a serious, atmospheric Cooper novel of sealing, shipwreck, and the human heart at sea.
10575-the-profiteers:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published this novel in 1921, opening at a Kensington garden party given by the Marchioness of Amesbury. Two stockbrokers, Roger Kendrick and Maurice White, escape the City crush for iced drinks and talk of B. and I. shares, which White finds sickening and hard to advise on. The scene sets a world of money, gossip, and post-war profiteering.

Kendrick, well-to-do and well-preserved, notes talk of Rockefeller backing, while White insists on judging the board on its merits. Finance, society, and ambition will drive the plot. Readers get a stylish, post-war novel of London money, parties, and the men who profit from them.
10627-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-08:
John Lord's Beacon Lights of History turns to great rulers in this eighth volume, opening with Alfred the Great and the Saxons in England. The lectures trace the Saxon conquest, the division of England into small kingdoms, the conversion of the Saxons, and the Danish invasions that nearly broke Wessex. Alfred's laws, forts, ships, and schools take center stage.

Lord tells Alfred's life as a story of defeat, recovery, and wise rule, with attention to learning and justice. Further lectures in the volume treat other rulers in the same narrative style. Readers get a vivid, popular history of kingship, written for audiences who liked their history as biography.
10641-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-10:
John Lord's tenth volume of Beacon Lights of History treats European leaders of the reform age, opening with William IV and the English reforms. Lectures follow Lord Grey's ministry, the Reform Bill, Lord John Russell, Henry Brougham, and the troubles of Ireland under O'Connell. Sir Robert Peel, the abolition of West Indian slavery, and the repeal of the Corn Laws complete the picture.

Lord writes for popular audiences, turning politics into lives and turning points. His accounts stress character, speech, and moral choice over dry policy. Readers get an engaging survey of Britain's move toward wider voting rights and freer trade in the early nineteenth century.
10644-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-11:
John Lord's Beacon Lights of History reached American founders in this eleventh volume, which gathers lectures on the men who built the United States. Alexander Hamilton stands at its center, placed here among his fellow founders after earlier editions had grouped him elsewhere. Daniel Webster appears in a companion volume on later American leaders.

Lord writes each life as a story of character and crisis, explaining what each founder believed and did at turning points of the young republic. The lectures were first spoken to popular audiences, and they keep a speaker's pace and warmth. Readers get an accessible, old-style introduction to the founders and their quarrels.
10647-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-12:
John Lord's twelfth volume of Beacon Lights of History gathers American leaders of the generation after the founders. Daniel Webster's lecture, moved here from an earlier grouping, now sits beside papers on Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun. The preface notes that, with the Civil War era past, North and South can weigh these controversies more calmly.

Lord presents each leader through life and speech, showing how Webster, Clay, and Calhoun argued over union, slavery, and the Constitution. His style is popular and biographical, built for lecture halls. Readers get a clear introduction to the great Senate debates that shaped America before the Civil War.
10718-the-house-of-whispers:
William Le Queux published The House of Whispers in 1910, a mystery of Scotland, spies, and family secrets. The laird of Glencardine, James Flockart, the Muries of Connachan, and Gabrielle with her secret drive the early chapters. Later chapters add seals of destiny, the curse of the cardinal, a Frenchman's visit, and a spy revealed.

Le Queux, a master of the invasion and spy tale, keeps the plot moving through whispers, confidences, and sudden turns. The story travels from Scottish mists to the Mediterranean. Readers who like Edwardian thrillers will find here intrigue, romance, and a villain worth hissing.
10928-bengal-dacoits-and-tigers:
Maharanee Sunity Devee of Cooch Behar collected true stories from Bengal into two groups: dacoit tales and tiger tales. The first part follows robbers, disguises, and narrow escapes, including a jewelled traveller in a palanquin, a girl who poses as the goddess Kali, and a child caught up in a raid. The second part turns to tigers met on roofs, in palkis, and on forest roads.

Told in plain, lively prose, the stories mix danger with local custom, from marriage visits to village courts. They were written for readers far from India, and they keep the flavour of tales told aloud. Together they give a vivid picture of rural Bengal life, where bandits and wild animals were real, everyday threats.
10948-the-stories-of-the-three-burglars:
Frank R. Stockton wrote this 1889 comic tale about a country householder plagued by burglars. Living about twenty miles from New York with his wife, small son, servants, and Aunt Martha, the narrator finds his neighbourhood robbed again and again. Each household must guard itself.

Three burglars take turns telling their stories, including a dispute over dividing loot that ends in a beating and a kick out the front door. Stockton plays the crimes for laughs, letting thieves argue, boast, and blunder. The book charms readers who enjoy gentle crime comedy, where the criminals are more foolish than frightening.
1095-the-light-of-the-western-stars:
Madeline Hammond, a rich young woman from the East, travels to her brother's Arizona ranch and finds a wild country of rustlers, gunmen, and open sky. Zane Grey sets her among cowboys who court her and outlaws who threaten her, while she learns to ride, shoot, and judge men by their deeds.

A proud cowboy named Gene Stewart wins her trust through danger and hard work, and the ranch wars test them both. Grey writes the desert in glowing color and the action at full gallop. The novel is a sturdy western romance, and it helped make Grey the best-loved writer of the range.
10962-concerning-animals-and-other-matte:
E. H. Aitken, writing as Eha, collected natural history essays first printed in the Strand, the Pall Mall Magazine, and the Times of India. A memoir by Surgeon-General Bannerman opens the 1914 volume, and illustrations by J. A. Shepherd picture the animals described. Chapters take body parts as their theme: feet, bills, tails, noses, and ears, each compared across species.

Later essays cover barn owls, domestic animals, snakes and snake-charmers, the cobra bungalow, and a panther Aitken did not shoot. Indian subjects follow, from the coconut tree and betel nut to a Hindu festival, Indian poverty, and words borrowed from Indian languages. The book mixes close observation with humour, and it rewards readers who enjoy animals watched carefully and described with wit.
11019-van-bibber-and-others:
Richard Harding Davis collected short stories about Van Bibber, a young New York man-about-town, in this 1892 volume. Van Bibber passes stage-door keepers with calm politeness on the first night of a comic opera, The Sultana, stepping into paint, gaslight, and backstage panic. Other stories follow his man-servant, a hungry man fed, races, an experiment in economy, and a first hunt.

Eleanore Cuyler, a recruit at Christmas, a patron of art, and a chorus girl named Andy McGee complete the set, with an unfinished story at the end. Davis writes with light, confident humour about society, theatre, and sport. The stories capture Gilded Age New York leisure, and Van Bibber remains one of Davis's most likeable creations.
11025-phaethon-loose-thoughts-for-loose-:
Charles Kingsley, writing in dialogue form in 1852, sets this philosophical talk beside a limestone stream, where Templeton and his friend fish and dream instead of catching anything. The keeper scolds them for missing rises, but their minds run on deeper questions. A young man from Rhodes, who left wealth and a merchant's heiress to seek truth at Athens, argues with older thinkers.

Through sophists such as Hippias, Polus, Gorgias, and Protagoras, the dialogue tests what truth is and how it should be lived. The title Phaethon hints at a rash drive toward the sun, and the talk warns loose thinkers against chasing bright ideas without discipline. Readers get Victorian philosophy in story form, with fishing, scenery, and debate woven together.
1104-the-comedy-of-errors:
Two sets of identical twins, separated at birth by a shipwreck, wander the same streets of Ephesus on the same day. Mix-ups pile up: wrong wives, wrong debts, wrong beatings, and a gold chain that fits no one. William Shakespeare's early farce runs on mistaken identity at full tilt.

The play borrows its plot from Plautus and doubles it, so every error lands twice as hard. A merchant father faces death at dusk unless his sons appear, which gives the farce a sharp edge. The comedy is short, fast, and very funny, and it still works on any stage.
11191-captains-all-and-others:
This 1911 volume gathers W. W. Jacobs's Captains All stories in one place, from the title tale of Sam Small to The Boatswain's Mate. The Nest Egg, The Constable's Move, Bob's Redemption, The Four Pigeons, and The Madness of Mr. Lister. A night-watchman narrates most of them, spinning yarns about sailors, poachers, and village tricksters in Thames dialect. The White Cat closes the set.

Read together, the stories show Jacobs's range within a narrow form: the same voices, new schemes, and endings that punish greed or vanity. The collection is the easiest way into his work, since it holds his best-known short sea comedy together. Its humor has dated in dialect but not in structure.
11394-fighting-in-flanders:
E. Alexander Powell's Fighting in Flanders, written as special correspondent of the New York World with Belgian forces, reports the war's opening months in 1914. Chapters cover war correspondents, the city of gloom, death in the air, life under the German eagle and spiked helmets. the Belgian battle line, the coming of the British, and the fall of Antwerp, with photographs by Donald Thompson. Powell dedicates the book to his friends the Belgians, quoting Kipling.

Powell opens by comparing correspondents to doctors: they do not wish men killed, but while men are killed they want to witness and report it. His account is vivid and partisan, sympathetic to Belgium. The book remains a firsthand record of the German invasion as American readers first learned it.
11418-the-grafters:
Francis Lynde's Grafters follows the rise of Gaston, a lusty infant city on the brown plain when the boom broke and a junto was born. Its beginnings run back to Mormon migrations, Zophar Smith's ox-train wells at Dry Creek, and Jethro Simsby, a Mormon deserter turned Dry Creek cattle king. Western Pacific locating engineers bring the railroad, and chapters move through ashes of empire, Bostonians, law-making, haymakers, gerrymanders, junketers, conspirators, and the relentless wheels.

Lynde, a railroad novelist, writes political fiction about western corruption, with a woman intervening and a borrowed conscience among late chapters. The novel's plain is both setting and metaphor for speculation. Readers of western political novels will find it a vigorous, now neglected example.
11482-deep-waters:
W. W. Jacobs's 1919 collection Deep Waters gathers his night-watchman stories in one volume, from Shareholders and Paying Off through Made to Measure. Sam's Ghost, Bedridden, the Convert, Husbandry, Family Cares, the Winter Offensive, the Substitute, Striking Hard, and Dirty Work. The opening story compares a sailorman to a fish, safest at sea and in trouble ashore, where money, marriage, and magistrates await. One sailor hid sixteen pounds so well he never found it again.

The watchman's Thames-side dialect unifies the set, with each yarn turning on greed, vanity, or bad luck. Deep Waters is the fullest collection of Jacobs's later short fiction. Readers who enjoyed Captains All will find the same humor here, darker and more domestic.
1153-the-chessmen-of-mars:
Edgar Rice Burroughs sends Gahan of Gathol across the dead sea bottoms of Mars to rescue Tara, princess of Helium. She is held in the city of Manator, where prisoners play jetan, a giant living chess game, to the death. John Carter's Mars, with its green men, thoats, and thin air, frames the quest.

The novel explains jetan move by move, and the final game decides Tara's fate. Burroughs writes the pulp Mars at full color, with duels, escapes, and monsters. The book, fifth in the Barsoom series, still draws readers who love old planetary romance.
11615-the-grammar-of-english-grammars:
Goold Brown's massive Grammar of English Grammars sets out, with a historical and critical introduction, the whole of English grammar methodically arranged and amply illustrated. Forms of correcting and parsing, improprieties for correction, examples for parsing, and questions for examination fill its pages.

Parts cover orthography, etymology, and syntax, with chapters on letters, syllables, spelling, and the parts of speech. The present tense, Brown explains, is the root form of the verb, as be, act, rule, love, and defend. The book is a reference work for teachers, built for drill and dispute.
11718-the-camp-fire-girls-at-school-or-t:
Hildegard G Frey's 1916 Camp Fire Girls book opens with Gladys Evans and a bead band. The band is a yard long, worked in colours to tell a summer camping trip. Shadow River and a canoe upside down appear in beads. A Fourth of July pageant appears as well.

The Winnebagos meet on a crisp October evening for a work meeting. They recall each event as don't you remembers fall thick and fast. Later a Washington guard throws a ball to a massed group. Sahwah leaps high to catch it and scores from the field. The book follows school, work, and games, with Wohelo as its watchword: work, health, and love.
11737-barks-and-purrs:
Colette Willy's Barks and Purrs, translated by Maire Kelly, gathers animal pieces around a lady's country house, described by Madame Millet Robinet. Orchard, kitchen garden, stable, poultry yard, bee-hive, and hot-house, the introduction says, hold no mysteries for Colette.

Dialogue follows between Toby-Dog and Kiki-the-Demure, a cat who teases a sad dog about his hanging lip and froggy eyes. Toby sniffs that next year might do, while Kiki promises pleasures and friends again, with a farmer's dog crunching bones in the kitchen. The book is a French writer's affectionate, comic portrait of household animals.
11874-hodge-and-his-masters:
Richard Jefferies's Hodge and His Masters examines English country life in the late nineteenth century through twenty-eight linked chapters. The table of contents moves from a farmers' parliament at the Jason Inn to chapters on leaving a farm, borrowing and gambling, haymaking, and the squire's round robin.

Jefferies writes about laborers, farmers, parsons, solicitors, and landlords as people shaped by wages, rents, and seasons, not as pastoral types. Passages on milk sent to London, on fieldfares and blackberries. On cottage children give the social argument its ground, making the book both a survey of rural change and a piece of close natural observation.
11876-the-three-sisters:
May Sinclair's 1914 novel opens in Garthdale, a handful of grey stone houses huddled by a beck beneath the high moor. Three sisters live at the lonely vicarage with their father, cut off from the world by landscape, poverty, and the strict habits of their household.

Alice, Mary, and Gwenda each reach for a different kind of freedom, through marriage, work, and love, and each choice costs something. Sinclair follows their rivalries and loyalties with close psychological attention, making the remote Yorkshire dale feel less like a backdrop than a force pressing on every decision.
12044-the-grimke-sisters:
Catherine H. Birney's 1885 biography The Grimké Sisters presents Sarah and Angelina Grimké as the first American women advocates of abolition and woman's rights. Birney, writing with diffidence from inexperience in literary work of such length, drew on diaries and letters placed in her hands.

The sisters, born into a South Carolina slaveholding family, left the South, spoke against slavery. Argued for women's rights, paying a high social price for public speech. Birney quotes their glory of self-sacrifice as an epigraph. The biography remains an early, sympathetic life of two women whose conversion from privilege to protest shaped both movements they joined.
12059-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Volume 9 of The World's Greatest Books, jointly edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton and published in 1910, covers lives and letters. Its table of contents runs from Abélard and Héloïse's love letters and Amiel's fragments of an intimate diary to Saint Augustine's Confessions and Boswell's Life of Samuel Johnson.

Further lives include Sir David Brewster's Life of Sir Isaac Newton, among others, in the series' condensed form, which retells great books in short, readable summaries. The volume serves readers who want an introduction to biography and letter-writing at their most famous, before turning, if they wish, to the full works themselves.
1214-the-street-of-seven-stars:
Mary Roberts Rinehart tells of a young American girl who goes to Vienna to study music. She lodges in a house on the Street of Seven Stars, where artists, students, and lovers cross her path. Her voice, her hopes, and her first taste of freedom tangle with a romance and a mystery.

Rinehart writes Vienna with color and writes her heroine with warmth and humor. The novel mixes romance with a light suspense plot, and it moves at a brisk clip. It suits readers who like Rinehart's blend of feeling, fun, and a touch of danger.
12170-the-wolf-hunters:
James Oliver Curwood published this wilderness adventure novel in 1908. Set in the Canadian north in winter, it follows two young men and their Native guide on a trapping expedition that turns into a fight for survival.

Roderick and Wabigoon, with the guide Mukoki, track wolves for bounty, cross frozen lakes, and take shelter from storms. They find a dead trapper, a hidden cache, and a wolf cub they raise, while a hostile band known as the Woongas closes in. The novel mixes outdoor detail with a simple code of loyalty. Its lasting draw is the snow country itself, rendered as both beautiful and merciless.
12176-the-gate-of-the-giant-scissors:
The Gate of the Giant Scissors is a children fantasy about Joyce, a girl who cries up in Monsieur Greville tallest pear tree. She is miserable and tired of being managed, and she hides in the farthest corner of the garden, out of sight of the house.

Chapters follow a new fairy tale, a great gate, and a letter and a meeting. Later come a Thanksgiving barbecue, Joyce playing ghost, and old Number Thirty-One. Christmas plans bring an accident and a great discovery. The giant scissors of the title belong to a world of magic just beyond the garden wall. The book mixes everyday childish sorrow with fairy adventure, in the manner of late Victorian stories for girls.
1233-the-origin-and-nature-of-the-emotio:
George W. Crile, a surgeon and pioneer of shock research, gathers papers on the origin and nature of the emotions. He argues that emotions grew from bodily responses to danger, pain, and action in animal life. Crile, a Cleveland surgeon, studied shock in wounded soldiers and in animals.

Crile links fear, anger, and love to glands, nerves, and muscles, in a theory that joined surgery to psychology. The papers show early twentieth-century medicine reaching toward a biology of feeling. His emotion theory, linking glands to feeling, influenced later work on stress.
12456-the-troubadours:
The Reverend H. J. Chaytor's 1912 Cambridge study traces the troubadours of Provence and their influence. Chapters cover courtly love, technique, the early troubadours, the classical period, the Albigensian Crusade, and troubadours in Italy and Spain, closing with Provençal influence in Germany, France and England.

Chaytor argues that few literatures shaped other peoples so deeply as this poetry did. Songs of love, service and craft travelled with courts and crusades, changing lyric writing across Europe. The book, with bibliography, notes and index, remains a clear introduction to medieval lyric, written for students who want history with their poetry.
12480-clairvoyance-and-occult-powers:
Swami Panchadasi's 1916 lessons teach clairvoyance and kindred powers as a system, from astral senses to crystal-gazing. The synopsis lists clairaudience, premonition, psychometry, distant, past and future clairvoyance, second sight, astral travel, psychic influence, healing, telepathy and thought transference.

Opening lessons argue that the five ordinary senses are not infallible, and that subtler senses lie behind them. Later lessons give methods for development, with cautions and exercises for the student. The book belongs to early twentieth-century occult publishing, earnest and instructional, and it records what its readers hoped mind and sight might do beyond the body.
12572-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Volume ten of The World's Greatest Books, edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton, covers lives and letters in summary form. Contents include Hugo's Deeds and Words, Hume on Elizabeth and Mary Queen of Scots, and Irving on Columbus and Washington. Josephus, Lockhart on Scott and Burns, Luther's Table Talk, Mirabeau, Moore on Byron, Pepys's Diary and Pliny's Letters follow.

Rousseau's Confessions, Sévigné's letters, Southey on Nelson and Richelieu's Political Testament complete the range. Each entry retells a classic life or letter collection in brief, readable form. The volume served readers who wanted the great biographies at a glance, and it remains a handy guide to lives that shaped European letters.
12594-creative-impulse-in-industry-a-pro:
Helen Marot's 1918 proposition for educators, issued by the Bureau of Educational Experiments in New York, argues for creative impulse in industry. Dedicated to Caroline Pratt, whose work on children's play deepened Marot's sense of growth in industrial and adult life, the book asks what schooling should do for workers.

Chapters cover production and creative effort, adapting people to industry the American way and the German way, and educational industry with associated enterprise. Marot doubts German industrial education would suit America, even if it worked. She wants efficiency joined to human growth, not drilled obedience. The tract is a progressive-era plea for work that uses mind and hand together.
12600-old-and-new-masters:
Robert Lynd's 1919 essays, Old and New Masters, dedicated to Sylvia Lynd, survey writers from Dostoevsky the sensationalist and Jane Austen the natural historian. Chesterton, Belloc, Wordsworth, Keats, Henry James, Browning, Synge, Villon, Pope, Flecker and Turgenev follow.

Later essays treat Strindberg's madness, Rossetti and ritual, Bernard Shaw, Masefield's secret, Yeats, Chekhov the perfect story-teller and Lady Gregory. Lynd writes as a humane, witty critic, judging books by life and feeling as much as by form. The collection remains a charming guide to early twentieth-century taste, opinionated, readable and fond of its subjects.
12605-parish-papers:
Norman Macleod, chaplain to the Queen for Scotland, published Parish Papers in 1863. It is dedicated to parishioners of Loudoun, Dalkeith and the Barony, to whom he ministered as pastor. Contents ask what Christianity is, who Jesus Christ was, what we can believe if we do not believe in him, and what if Christianity is not true.

Further papers treat the final judgment, future life in its physical, intellectual, devotional, social and active forms, and future punishment. What after death, moments in life, labourers together with God, revivals, the Christian congregation and the cure for schism follow. Macleod writes as a parish preacher, plain and pastoral. The book offers Victorian parish theology in sermon form, earnest and humane.
12632-yesterdays-with-authors:
James T. Fields's Yesterdays with Authors, seventeenth edition 1879, recalls a Boston publisher's friendships with great American writers. Fields, clerk at fourteen in a Boston bookstore and later partner in Ticknor, Reed and Fields, published most of the great American writers of the century. A Shakespeare motto fronts the book: was it not yesterday we spoke together?

Fields tells how he persuaded a jobless, despondent Hawthorne to let him print The Scarlet Letter, and recalls other authors in the Saturday Club circle. The book, inscribed to fellow club members, mixes publishing history with personal memoir. It remains a delightful source for Hawthorne, Longfellow and their world, told by the man who printed them.
1267-kai-lung-s-golden-hours:
Ernest Bramah returns to Kai Lung, his Chinese storyteller, who must spin tales to save his skin in this book of linked stories. Each golden hour brings a new fable of mandarins, merchants, and rogues, told in Bramah's grave, ornate English.

The frame tale gives the stories their stakes: Kai Lung's wit is his only weapon against power. The fables turn on fate, greed, and clever words. The book charms readers who loved The Wallet of Kai Lung, and it keeps Bramah's imagined China glowing. Bramah's fables keep his imagined China glowing for new readers.
12778-the-young-engineers-in-mexico-or-f:
Tom Reade and Harry Hazelton, Hancock's young engineers, take work in Mexico for mine owner Don Luis Montez. What looks like a fair engineering job soon turns crooked: the mine shows signs of salting, a trick that makes poor rock seem rich. Don Luis wants the pair to sign a report that would cheat his buyers.

Tom and Harry refuse to lend their names to a lie, and must outwit armed men, false friends, and a tempting offer. Their stand turns on a simple point: an engineer's signature must mean true work. The story pairs mine craft with a clean moral, in the brisk adventure style Hancock used across the series.
12799-quiet-talks-with-world-winners:
S. D. Gordon's Quiet Talks with World Winners sets out a missionary call in gentle, earnest chapters. Part one covers the master passion, the plan, the need, the opportunity, and the coming victory. Part two names the winning forces: church, each believer, Jesus, the Holy Spirit, prayer, money, and sacrifice. The theme is God's longing to win the world home.

Gordon uses home pictures, like a broken family circle and a sickroom crisis, to make urgency vivid. His style is warm and plain, meant for church readers rather than scholars. The book captures early twentieth-century evangelical hope in world missions.
12818-heathen-slaves-and-christian-ruler:
Elizabeth Andrew and Katharine Bushnell published Heathen Slaves and Christian Rulers in 1907 as an attack on the traffic in Chinese slave girls in California and abroad. Dedicated to Margaret Culbertson, who fought for rescued girls at peril of life, it argues that Christian rulers failed to stop a trade carried on in their own ports. Court cases and testimony fill the pages.

One case tells of a woman jailed for stealing a child. The buyer who paid fifty-three dollars and confined the girl went unpunished, a fact the judge called an opprobrium to justice. The book is a fierce reform tract, meant to shame readers into action.
12835-lena-rivers:
Mrs. Mary J. Holmes wrote 'Lena Rivers in 1897 as a domestic novel of hidden kinship and second chances. Young Lena, raised in hardship, comes to live among richer relations, where scheming, pride, and old letters shape her fate. Maple Grove, Woodlawn, and Frankfort mark stages of her rise.

A key scene finds Mr. Graham overhearing cruel talk about Lena and offering to adopt her as his daughter. Love, marriage, loss, and reunion follow across many chapters. Holmes's sentimental style, hugely popular in its day, still appeals to readers who like family secrets resolved with warmth.
12948-the-boy-scouts-with-the-motion-pic:
Robert Shaler's Boy Scouts with the Motion Picture Players brings Hugh Hardin and the Oakvale troop to a haunted make-believe castle on a fall Friday afternoon. Five lads in faded khaki rest by a cold spring, and their path soon crosses film people shooting chivalry scenes, with swords clashing and a castle assault. Tramps, panic, and midnight scouting add fun.

A camp scene finds Monkey Stallings hearing talk in the bushes, Billy fearing tramps have returned like a bad penny, and Alec grabbing a stout club. Hugh spots figures making straight for their place. The book blends scout life with early movie magic.
13000-the-rough-riders:
Theodore Roosevelt wrote The Rough Riders in 1899 about raising and leading his volunteer cavalry in the Spanish-American War. As Assistant Secretary of the Navy, Roosevelt had preached intervention in Cuba, and when war came he determined to reach the front himself. The book, dedicated to the five regular regiments beside his own at Santiago, follows the regiment from camp to battle.

A Santiago passage shows Roosevelt in command: canteens filled, wounded and heat-exhausted men sheltered in ranch buildings, and the Ninth Cavalry hurrying up too late for the fight. Roosevelt writes with energy and pride. The book remains a classic American war memoir.
13057-the-philanderers:
The Philanderers, by A. E. W. Mason in 1897, opens in mid-Africa, where five Englishmen watch a camp fire in a forest clearing. Rifles and sleeping troops ring the camp, and one man points east as dawn fades the purple sky. The prologue sets a tale of empire, risk, and tangled hearts.

Back in England, Clarice Le Mesurier grows vexed as Sidney Mallinson, Mrs. Willoughby, and her father all hint the same thing about Drake. She means to ask her question that afternoon and have done with him for good. Mason's novel blends African adventure with a drawing-room plot of pride and love.
13135-pardners:
Rex E. Beach's 1904 stories, titled Pardners, celebrate friendship on the northern frontier. Contents run from the title tale to the mule driver, the colonel and the horse thief, the thaw at Slisco's, and tales north of fifty-three where northern lights come down at night. Beach, author of The Spoilers, writes in rough, spoken prose.

Joyce opens by fixing old quotations: marriages may be made in heaven, but pardnerships are the sanctified relation. One partner crawls snow-blind and starving from Sheeps-Horn to Miller's, losing fingers and toes in twelve-foot drifts, to save his mate. Wild Pierre, reckless and tireless, scoffs at peril yet scorns a weak companion. The stories praise loyalty tested by cold, hunger, and risk.
13191-the-cross-of-berny-or-irene-s-love:
The Cross of Berny, or Irene's Lovers, is a joint novel by Madame Emile de Girardin, Théophile Gautier, Jules Sandeau, and Méry. Its American preface notes that literary partnerships rarely succeed in imaginative work, and that four-way partnerships almost always fail, even among bright minds. This novel, the preface claims, stands almost alone as a harmonious joint work.

Irene, with changeable gray eyes and chestnut braids, walks to Pont de l'Arche in mud and puddles, her little boot unsoiled. A lover calls himself Don Quixote, ready to jump into fire to save a Lady Penock for a reward like hers. The novel is a French romance of letters, lovers, and honor, written by four hands in one voice.
13265-a-book-of-fruits-and-flowers:
A Book of Fruits and Flowers, an early modern receipt book, shows the nature and use of fruits and flowers for meat or medicine. It teaches preserving, conserving, candying, drying, and pickling, and gives recipes for pies, marchpanes, caudels, cakes, broths, fritters, puddings, tarts, syrups, and salads. For medicine it offers poultices, ointments, and waters for wounds, agues, coughs, and stones.

One receipt beats Jordan almonds with small ale, strains them, boils the caudle with mace, and sweetens it with sugar. Another steeps dragons, angelica, rue, and wormwood in white wine for a day, distills the water, and gives six or seven spoonfuls fasting against infection. The book is a rich window on seventeenth-century kitchens and stillrooms.
13314-barford-abbey-a-novel-in-a-series-:
Barford Abbey is a novel in letters in two volumes, printed in London in 1768 for Cadell and Payne. It opens with Lady Mary Sutton at the German Spaw writing to Miss Warley in England. Mary weeps over Fanny's mournful detail, not for a departed saint, but for all who knew her god-like virtues. The novel is told wholly through letters, in the fashion of its age.

Later, a narrator rushes from a chamber to a crowd of fifty or sixty well-dressed people, women crying and laughing, men swearing and stamping over a dispute below. Another letter tells of a lord who drops a gift respectfully, while the writer, struck dumb, cannot answer and speaks instead to Mr. Jenkings about horseback. The novel is an eighteenth-century romance of manners, sentiment, and social comedy.
13397-history-of-the-comstock-patent-med:
Robert B. Shaw, a Clarkson College historian, traces the W. H. Comstock firm of Morristown, New York, and its famous Dr. Morse's Indian Root Pills. For more than ninety years the small riverside factory, with only a few dozen workers, stood at the centre of village economic life while its pills travelled far beyond it.

Shaw follows rival partners, travelling agents, disputed accounts, court raids, and arrests, then the almanacs, jokes, and bold cure claims that sold the pills. Packaging changed from oval veneer boxes to glass bottles and tins, and the old claims faded after the 1906 food and drug law. The study ends as a clear case of how a modest firm sold hope in a box.
1345-the-vicar-of-tours:
Honoré de Balzac tells of Abbé Birotteau, the gentle vicar of Tours, whose comfortable rooms and quiet life are stolen by a scheming priest and a spiteful landlady. The tale follows Birotteau's fall from his lodgings to a garret, and his meek endurance of the plot against him.

Balzac writes provincial church politics with irony and compassion, and the vicar's innocence against cunning gives the tale its pathos. The novel is short and sharp. It suits readers who like Balzac's tales of small lives crushed by small malice. Balzac's short novel shows small malice crushing a gentle life.
1351-the-chignecto-isthmus-and-its-first:
Howard Trueman writes the history of the Chignecto Isthmus, the narrow neck joining Nova Scotia to New Brunswick, and of its first settlers. Acadians, New England planters, and Yorkshire folk all left marks on the marshland. Trueman, a local historian of the Maritimes, gathered family records for the isthmus.

Trueman follows families, farms, and dykes across the isthmus, using local records and memory. The book serves genealogists and local historians, and it preserves the story of a border country often overlooked. The dyked marshes, reclaimed from the Bay of Fundy, made Chignecto rich farmland.
13570-sketches-of-the-covenanters:
J. C. McFeeters, minister of the Second Church of the Covenanters in Philadelphia, sketches the unconquerable Covenanters who bound themselves to defend worship. Natural, civil, and divine rights, till they overcame or were sent down under debate. His motto promises to tell it to generations following, for God is our God for ever.

Civil rulers, McFeeters argues, are God's ministers who should conserve true religion, seek union of churches in doctrine, worship, discipline, and government, and suppress openly criminal features of society. Troops break a promise and capture eighteen stragglers, then attack a conventicle at Lillies-leaf moor where John Blackader preaches through an alarm shot. The sketches honour Scottish faith under persecution.
13708-walking-stick-papers:
Robert Cortes Holliday's 1918 collection of light essays, dedicated to three critics he admired, takes its title from the cane he carried about town. The pieces range over book reviewing, art shows, London literary life, Henry James, lodgings, policemen, and the small humiliations of being a writer.

Holliday writes as a cheerful observer, sorting piles of review copies at Christmas, watching strangers on the street, and trading jokes with fellow journalists. The essays are short, urbane, and full of names and anecdotes from the New York and London book world. They read as a genial record of literary life just after the First World War, when the old magazine world was still intact.
13764-the-art-of-letters:
Robert Lynd gathered literary essays in The Art of Letters, published in New York in 1921. Many first appeared in the London Mercury, the New Statesman, and the Daily News. Lynd dedicates the book to J. C. Squire, godfather to many chapters. Essays treat Pepys, Bunyan, Campion, Donne, Walpole, and Cowper, plus Elizabethan plays and poetry.

Lynd writes as a humane critic, fond of diaries, letters, and odd detail. He notes Pepys writing in French when conscience troubled him. Other pieces weigh the office of poetry and the craft of prose. The tone stays conversational and witty throughout. Readers who enjoy criticism as talk will find Lynd an easy companion.
1380-the-two-brothers:
Balzac's sombre novel follows two brothers divided by their mother's favour and by money. Philippe, a soldier of dash and waste, and Joseph, a steady painter, grow up in a household where love is uneven and debts pile high. Their rivalry shapes the family's slow ruin and partial repair.

Through Paris salons, army camps, and artists' studios, the book traces how a mother's blind love can spoil one son and starve the other. Balzac's eye for domestic greed and pride is at its keenest here. It is a powerful study of family, favouritism, and the long cost of bad choices.
13860-men-of-the-bible-some-lesser-known:
Several scholars contributed studies of lesser-known Bible figures to this 1904 volume. George Milligan, Alfred Rowland, W. J. Townsend, and others take turns. Enoch, Eldad and Medad, Barzillai, Adonijah, Hiram, and Jeroboam open the list. Later studies cover Asa, Ahaziah, Gehazi, Hazael, Manasseh, and Amaziah.

Each essay retells a life from Scripture and draws a moral lesson. Writers stress faith, loyalty, pride, and repentance in small compass. The book avoids famous heroes to show how minor figures shape larger stories. Its tone is devotional and scholarly at once. Sunday readers and students of the Bible will find it accessible and thoughtful.
1392-the-seven-poor-travellers:
This Christmas story counts six poor travellers in Rochester, plus the narrator himself to make seven. Gathered at an old inn on Christmas Eve, they share supper and, in turn, tell tales of their lives, while the narrator listens and adds his own reflections on charity and chance.

Told in three short chapters, the book moves from the ancient city streets to the inn parlour and back to the road. Its mood is kindly and its humour is gentle. It is a small seasonal piece about strangers made into company for one night by food, fire, and story.
1404-the-federalist-papers:
Written in 1787 and 1788 to persuade New York to ratify the new United States Constitution, these eighty-five essays argue the case for a strong federal union. Hamilton, Jay, and Madison take turns, with Hamilton writing most, to explain each part of the plan: the presidency, the courts, taxation, and the balance of powers.

The papers answer fears of tyranny, of faction, and of a distant capital, and they set out the theory of checks that still shapes American debate. Read together, they form both a campaign document and a classic of political thought. They remain the first guide to what the Constitution was meant to do.
1406-the-perils-of-certain-english-priso:
Set in 1744 on the Island of Silver-Store, this Christmas story follows Gill Davis, a private in the Royal Marines, and a small English garrison taken by pirates. Cut off from help, the prisoners must use wit, courage, and local knowledge to survive, escape, or turn the tables on their captors.

Told in Davis's bluff voice, the tale moves from the island stockade to jungle paths and a desperate fight for freedom. Its humour is rough and its action is brisk. It is a compact adventure of the old navy, written for a fireside audience that liked peril with its Christmas pudding.
14255-hints-for-lovers:
Arnold Haultain's Hints for Lovers, published in 1909 in a limited edition of five hundred and forty numbered copies, collects aphorisms on courtship and marriage. Chapters run from girls, men, and women through love, lovers, making love, beauty, courtship, jealousy, kisses, engagements, marriage, and the human heart. A Greek motto from Euripides' Phaedra opens the book.

Tenderness forms the central test. Haultain writes that tenderness is the worship of soul by soul, and that lovers think the world was made for them, while onlookers watch with amusement, pity, and compassion. Jealousy, self-deception, and the purblind masculine heart recur as themes: a reserved, virtuous woman may fail where a bold rival wins openly. Witty, worldly, and Edwardian in tone, the book offers lovers sentences to argue over rather than rules to obey.
14275-the-necromancers:
Robert Hugh Benson wrote The Necromancers as a novel of faith tested by spiritualism. Laurie Baxter, a man drawn to séances and talk, stands at its center. His mother Maggie watches him with worry, fearing the teaching will pull him from his church. The novel sets London drawing rooms against a world of mediums and unseen powers. Benson writes as a Catholic novelist who holds the spirit world real and perilous.

Laurie tells his mother he has left spiritualism alone for two months, and says it so well that Maggie believes him. Yet a lady of his circle feels a faint distaste creep into her love of the teaching, like the sour note in cut flowers kept in water. The novel follows that turn from charm to dread. It warns that curiosity about the dead can open a door no one can shut.
14334-the-range-dwellers:
B. M. Bower wrote this 1906 Western novel, with pictures by Charles M. Russell. Its narrator is an Eastern man who aches to ride a real range horse under a range saddle. He joins a round-up crew and learns the work, the jokes, and the risks of cow country. A quarrel with a neighbor rancher drives much of the plot. The tale is told in the first person, with a light, teasing voice.

A wild ride opens the action, as the narrator spurs his horse Shylock at a padlocked gate. His pursuer swings a rope just behind him, so there is no time to pull wires loose. He puts Shylock at a low stretch of fence and clears it. Later scenes pair him with Frosty, a dry hand who doubts Eastern notions of the range. The novel charms through horse sense, hard riding, and the slow thaw between rivals.
1435-miscellaneous-papers:
Drawn from Charles Dickens's journalism and occasional writing, this volume gathers short pieces first printed in papers and magazines. Early items take up the agricultural interest, a mock threatening letter to Thomas Hood, and a host of social subjects, from railways to street life and public shows.

The pieces show Dickens off the novelist's stage: brisk, funny, and often indignant, with an eye for odd characters and unfair customs. Some are slight, some are sharp, but all carry his voice. The book is a useful shelf for readers who know the novels and want Dickens in shorter form.
14374-john-redmond-s-last-years:
Stephen Gwynn wrote this 1919 study of John Redmond's last years as leader of the Irish Parliamentary Party. Gwynn holds that a life cannot be written, since the party's story is not closed. The book follows Redmond from the Home Rule Bill of 1912 through war, rebellion, and the Convention. It shows a chairman guiding his party with authority. Gwynn writes as a friend of the man.

A Volunteer committee of twenty-five split between soldiers and parliament men, and only Willie Redmond of them bore arms. Redmond knew no Irish army could stand without the consent of the Imperial Parliament. At the Convention, northern Nationalists refused to deny the rest of Ireland self-rule, and a vote for temporary exclusion passed by a margin. Gwynn credits Devlin's gifts for the win, won at cost to Devlin. The book gives a fair view of a leader near the end.
14406-the-intriguers:
Harold Bindloss wrote The Intriguers in 1914, a novel of the Canadian North. Blake, a hard man of the prairie, holds a restless companion named Benson close. The tale moves from river boats and prairie bluffs to muskeg, frozen trails, and caribou country. Kidnapping, fever, and a startling find drive the plot. Bindloss writes of men who endure cold, hunger, and each other's tempers.

Blake picks his horses close beside him at night, warning Benson that a foot escape means a ride down after daybreak. Benson, tormented by craving, sits mute by the fire and wraps his blanket round him. Later the pair divide their last meat by a log, unsure if they will reach the factory that night. A trapper's word guides them across a wide treeless stretch toward wooded bluffs. The novel charms through grit, cold, and stubborn loyalty.
1462-some-roundabout-papers:
William Makepeace Thackeray's Roundabout Papers, gathered from the Cornhill Magazine, are familiar essays on whatever catches the author's eye: carp at Sans Souci, old ladies, young artists. The small vanities of London life. Thackeray wanders by design, and the digression is often the point.

The tone is that of a genial clubman talking to friends, with satire softened by sympathy. Readers meet a novelist at ease, remembering, grumbling, and laughing at himself. The papers are a pleasant shelf of Victorian essay writing, best dipped into rather than read straight through.
1477-the-toys-of-peace-and-other-papers:
Saki's posthumous collection opens with a memoir of H. H. Munro and then offers his last short stories. The title tale gives children war toys in place of peace toys, with results their elders did not foresee. Other pieces, from The Wolves of Cernogratz to The Interlopers, mix wit, malice, and sudden violence.

Through tea parties, country houses, and railway carriages, Saki's cool, elegant voice turns polite society inside out. The stories are short, sharp, and often end with a sting. The book is a fine late sample of an author whose humour never quite forgave the world it mocked.
14888-the-inheritors:
Joseph Conrad and Ford M. Hueffer call their 1901 novel an extravagant story, dedicated to Borys and Christina. Its narrator meets a woman who speaks of ideas with contempt. Their talk by an old gateway sets a strange tone, with saints' effigies, fretted canopies and bird droppings in noon sun.

She asks what associations and historical ideas the gateway suggests, and he stutters an answer she dismisses. From that meeting grows a tale of a new kind of person, inheriting a world the old order cannot hold. Conrad and Ford write in a modern, unsettling mode: dialogue, impression and a future that arrives without asking permission.
1491-letters-to-dead-authors:
Andrew Lang's playful letters address dead writers as if they were alive and could answer back. Sixteen letters, later more, go to figures from Homer to Thackeray, teasing, praising, and quarrelling with their books in a familiar, witty voice that assumes the reader already loves them.

Lang defends old favourites, scolds new fashions, and drops literary gossip along the way. The form lets him mix criticism with fantasy, and the best letters read like talk with a brilliant friend. The book is a charming piece of Victorian bookish fun, and a window on Lang's wide reading.
14967-a-gentleman-vagabond-and-some-othe:
F. Hopkinson Smith notes that there are gentlemen vagabonds and vagabond gentlemen, and that once in a lifetime one meets a gentleman simple and pure. Without premeditated intent, he has selected types from each kind and entangled them in the threads of stories between these covers, leaving readers to group them by experience.

A gentleman vagabond, a knight of the Legion of Honor, John Sanders the labourer, Baader, the lady of Lucerne, Jonathan, along the Bronx, another dog and Brockway's hulk follow. The opening finds a major before Delmonico's interviewing a large bare-headed personage. Smith writes New York and travel sketches with an artist's eye for character, manners and the road.
1504-the-comedy-of-errors:
Shakespeare's shortest comedy, set in Ephesus, doubles everything: twin masters and twin servants, separated at birth, meet by chance in one city. Mistaken identity piles on mistaken identity, as wives, merchants, and a duke all take one twin for the other, and beatings, debts, and arrests follow.

The tangle unwinds in a final scene of recognition, where parents, wives, and twins sort themselves out at last. The play is pure farce, built on speed and symmetry. It is an early, joyful showpiece of Shakespeare's comic craft, best enjoyed for its clockwork confusion.
15117-sea-and-shore-a-sequel-to-miriam-s:
Catharine Warfield's 1876 novel continues Miriam's Memoirs, opening with a verse on a proud ship that sails forever, until its last hour strikes. Sea and shore set the scene for a Southern romance of family, love, and storm, in the author's well-known melodramatic style. The book was sold in morocco cloth at a dollar seventy-five.

Warfield, author of Monfort Hall and The Household of Bouverie, writes for readers who loved long, emotional domestic tales. Ships, ports, and stately bearing mix with household feeling. Fans of nineteenth-century Southern fiction will find the sequel lush, earnest, and full of period color.
15179-the-inner-sisterhood-a-social-stud:
Douglass Sherley's 1884 social study in high colors sketches Louisville young women just after the ball and through the season. Each sketch pairs a girl with a type: Kate Meadows after the ball, Belle Mason as a lover's choice, Alice Wing as the buzz-saw girl, and Rose Clendennin flirting for revenue only. Other sisters follow.

Sherley writes in the first person at times, with a storm door banging and a dull escort driving off in a rattletrap coupe. The tone is satiric, affectionate, and very much of its place and year. Readers interested in Southern society, courtship, and period wit will find the sketches sharp and entertaining.
15276-bears-i-have-met-and-others:
Allen Kelly's 1903 bear book gathers firsthand tales of California grizzlies, with pictures by Ernest Thompson Seton and others. Chapters tell of Monarch, Clubfoot, Mountain Charley, and a valley of shadow, plus Boston's big bear fight and Yosemite days. A letter from Seton fronts the set.

Kelly writes as a hunter and naturalist who knew bears at close range, with humor and respect for the animals. Stories of smoky dens, campfire talks, and brainy bears of the Pecos fill the book. Animal lovers will enjoy its rugged tales, even where hunting views now feel dated.
15416-the-spinners:
Eden Phillpotts published this long novel in 1918, set among the people of a spinning mill. Its two books follow Sabina, Raymond, Abel, and their neighbors through work, courtship, quarrels, and loss. Chapters move from a funeral and a tavern to the mill floor, the warping room, and the foreman's garden, giving the whole life of a working town.

The story spans years, so early choices ripen into later trouble: debts, offers refused, ambitions nursed, and marriages weighed. Phillpotts keeps the mill itself at the center, with its noise, skill, and strain shaping who prospers and who breaks. Readers who like broad, patient novels of English working life will find here a full community drawn over time, not a single hero's tale.
15489-dream-psychology-psychoanalysis-fo:
Sigmund Freud's Dream Psychology, subtitled Psychoanalysis for Beginners, appeared in an authorized English translation by M. D. Eder in New York in 1920, with an introduction by André Tridon. Freud argues that dreams have a meaning, and that the dream is the dreamer's own psychical act, not a message from gods or demons as prescientific ages held.

Nine chapters lay out the case: the dream mechanism, why dreams disguise desires, dream analysis, sex in dreams, the wish in dreams, and the function of the dream. Later chapters treat primary and secondary process, regression, and the unconscious against consciousness and reality. Written for beginners, the book gives Freud's theory in compact form, and it remains a starting point for readers curious about psychoanalysis.
15511-mr-pat-s-little-girl-a-story-of-th:
Mary F. Leonard published this children's story in Boston and Chicago in 1902, with pictures by Chase Emerson. It is subtitled a story of the Arden Foresters. Its chapter titles borrow Shakespeare: things begin to happen, friendship, and puzzles. The magician makes tea, Rosalind is met, and a lost ring turns up. A dedication to a beloved aunt opens the book.

The tale follows a little girl among forest folk who play at the world of As You Like It, with hedges, magic, and a ring to lose and find. Maurice, puzzles, and an unquiet morning add small mysteries to the woodland play. Leonard writes for young readers who know, or will soon meet, Shakespeare's comedy, turning its forest into a place where a child can wander, make friends, and learn kindness.
15525-miriam-s-schooling-and-other-paper:
Mark Rutherford's papers, edited by his friend Reuben Shapcott, were published in London in 1890 by Kegan Paul. Shapcott dedicates the result of his editorial labors to Stephen Willsher, dear to the dead friend. He explains a frontispiece seal, once an ancestor's, engraved with a device from Lilly. The seal itself cannot now be found, but Walter Crane reproduced it from description.

Contents include Gideon, Samuel, Saul, Miriam's Schooling, and Michael Trevanion. Gideon opens with Jotham, an old man telling his children the achievements of his father Gideon. He speaks on the day before his death, when the children of the East had oppressed Israel for seven years. Rutherford writes biblical and domestic tales with a Nonconformist gravity, and the volume shows his quiet, reflective prose at its most personal.
15535-violin-mastery-talks-with-master-v:
Frederick H. Martens gathered these talks with master violinists and teachers, published by Frederick A. Stokes in New York in 1919, with sixteen portraits. A frontispiece shows Eugène Ysaÿe with a handwritten note. Each interview pairs a player with a working theme, from tools and method to temperament and teaching.

Ysaÿe speaks on the tools of mastery, Leopold Auer on a method without secrets, and Mischa Elman on life and color in interpretation. Jascha Heifetz warns of practicing too much, Fritz Kreisler of personality in art, and Franz Kneisel of the perfect string ensemble. Students get counsel from the great players of the day, direct and practical. The volume preserves a golden age of violin playing in its own voices.
15577-a-history-of-the-mcguffey-readers:
Henry H. Vail published this history of the McGuffey Readers in Cleveland in 1911, with the Burrows Brothers Company, as the fourth of the Bookish Books, with three portraits. Vail opens before four small books, roughly bound in boards, with paper-covered sides. Two bear copyright entries from 1836, the others from 1837, the earliest editions found after a search lasting forty years.

The first and second readers appeared in 1836, the third and fourth in 1837. They were improved and enlarged in 1838, remodeled in 1843 and 1844 as newly revised, and remade as six books in 1853. Vail traces an enterprise that called for the best exertions of many skilled men, and took a conspicuous part in the education of millions of citizens. The book is a history of America's most famous schoolbooks.
15590-rough-stone-monuments-and-their-bu:
T. Eric Peet, formerly scholar of Queen's College, Oxford, published this study of rough stone monuments in London and New York in 1912, with Harper and Brothers. A frontispiece shows Stonehenge from the south-east, and plans, plates, and figures support the text. The book asks who raised the great stones, and why.

Ten chapters survey the field: Stonehenge and other English and Welsh monuments, Scotland and Ireland, Scandinavia, France, Spain, Portugal, Italy and its islands, Africa, Malta, and the dolmens of Asia. Closing chapters treat the builders' habits, customs, and religion, and ask who they were and whence they came. Peet writes as an early archaeologist, careful with plans and measures, and the book remains a clear introduction to megalithic monuments.
15604-piano-mastery-talks-with-master-pi:
Harriette Brower, author of The Art of the Pianist, published this book of piano talks in 1915, with Frederick A. Stokes and the Musical Observer Company, illustrated with sixteen portraits. A frontispiece shows Ignace Jan Paderewski. The volume adds an account of a Von Bülow class, hints on interpretation by two American teachers, and a summary by the author.

Talks pair players with themes: Ernest Schelling on the hand of a pianist, Ernesto Consolo on making the piano a musical instrument, and Sigismond Stojowski on mind in piano study. Rudolph Ganz treats conserving energy, Tina Lerner an audience as teacher, and Ethel Leginska relaxation as keynote. Harold Bauer, Raoul Pugno, and Tobias Matthay close the set. The book preserves great pianists' working advice in plain talk.
15648-american-merchant-ships-and-sailor:
Willis J. Abbot, author of Naval History of the United States and Bluejackets of 1898, published this history in New York in 1902, with Dodd, Mead, illustrated by Ray Brown. The book traces American merchant ships and the men who sailed them, from early colonial craft to the age of steam. A frontispiece declares that New England early took the lead in building ships.

Illustrations follow the shallop and the ketch, the broad arrow on white pines, and the farmer-builder at the helm. Schooner-rigged craft, ocean traders, and later merchantmen fill later pages. Abbot writes a popular history of commerce under sail: shipbuilding towns, hard voyages, and sailors' lives. The book honors the merchant marine as the quiet arm of American trade, carrying goods and building fortunes long before steam.
15854-initial-studies-in-american-letter:
A survey of American literature by Henry A. Beers, issued by the Chautauqua Press in New York in 1891. Beers wrote it as a companion to his sketch of English literature, From Chaucer to Tennyson, for the Chautauqua Circle. He follows the same plan: a continuous essay, not a primer or a list. The Council of Six recommended the book, without approving every doctrine in it.

Beers traces American letters from colonial beginnings through the national age, weighing poets, novelists, and essayists. His judgements stay clear and readable, aimed at home students. The volume shows a young nation's literature finding its voice. It still serves as a friendly first history of American writing.
15861-the-things-which-remain-an-address:
An address to young ministers by Daniel A. Goodsell, a bishop of the Methodist Episcopal Church. Jennings and Pye in Cincinnati and Eaton and Mains in New York issued it in 1904. Goodsell speaks to men starting in ministry, on what lasts when fashions pass. His text is short, earnest, and practical.

Followers of Him who said I am the Truth, Goodsell warns, can never hold or spread what is false. Teaching force depends on faith, and power in preaching needs strong belief. Doing and knowing, and the divine call with its conditions, frame his counsel. The address still challenges young preachers: preach only what you believe, and live what you preach.
15941-an-englishwoman-s-love-letters:
A book of love letters by an unnamed Englishwoman, issued in New York by the Mershon Company. An explanation fronts the letters, insisting the writer never thought they would be read by anyone but their addressee. A request, conveyed under circumstances the writer would call all-commanding, urges their publication. Little has been omitted, and the letters stand in complete form and sequence.

The letters trace a love affair in the writer's own words, from hope to longing to parting. Privacy gives them force: no editor smooths the feeling away. Readers meet a woman of wit, pride, and tender honesty. The book fascinates as a document of Edwardian love: private words, made public, with their fire intact.
16000-the-ship-of-stars:
A West Country novel by Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, known as Q, issued in 1899. Q dedicates the book to Leonard Henry Courtney, Member of Parliament, with pride in the West Country that claims him. Places in the tale appear on no map: a visitor may find Nannizabuloe, but not its lighthouse, or seek Tredinnis along the sand-hills. Much of the tale is true in a fashion, even to fact.

Sir Harry Vyell, who lived and hunted foxes near the model borough of Liskeard, lends his deeds to the hero. Coast, church, and country folk fill the chapters. Q writes with Cornish warmth and a storyteller's grace. The novel charms as a regional romance: a ship of stars, a wild coast, and a hero shaped by his home.
16026-de-quincey-s-revolt-of-the-tartars:
Thomas De Quincey's Revolt of the Tartars, edited with introduction and notes by William Edward Simonds of Knox College. Ginn and Company issued it in Boston in 1899, printed at the Athenaeum Press. A portrait after Archer fronts the book. David Masson describes De Quincey as small and fragile, with a head and forehead rising high over a wrinkled visage and gentle deep-set eyes.

De Quincey tells of the Kalmuck Tartars' flight from Russia to China, a vast migration through desert and war. Simonds's notes guide students through the ornate prose. The tale mixes history with romance, in De Quincey's dreamlike manner. The edition still serves classrooms: a strange, true flight, told by a master of English prose.
16171-our-boys-entertaining-stories-by-p:
Saalfield of Akron, Ohio, published Our Boys in 1904, a profusely illustrated gift volume of stories by popular authors. George Cary Eggleston, Mary E. Wilkins, Frances A. Humphrey, Margaret Eytinge, Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney, and Mary D. Brine head the list, with more names behind them. The book opens with Clara Doty Bates's poem The Cat-Tail Arrow, in which little Sammie whittles a bow and sighs for an arrow.

Stories of boyish adventure, mischief, and kindness follow in the same warm vein, made for family reading aloud. The volume captures the Edwardian ideal of wholesome fun for boys, with pictures on nearly every turn. Modern readers can enjoy it as a nostalgic sampler of children's writing from a century ago.
1621-miss-or-mrs:
Wilkie Collins's novella about a miss or a mrs turns on a question of title and of marriage. Sir Joseph Graybrooke's household, a Levant merchant named Richard Turlington, and a young surgeon, Launcelot Linzie, all appear in the tale. They are drawn into a plot where a woman's status, a will, and a secret marriage decide fortunes and reputations.

Collins builds his puzzle from documents and testimonies, with a superannuated seaman adding comic relief. The novella is short and tightly wound. It is a neat Collins mystery for readers who like a domestic riddle solved by law and by love. The riddle turns on a secret marriage and a will.
16324-the-women-of-the-caesars:
Guglielmo Ferrero looks at Rome's imperial house through its women in this 1911 study. Livia, wife of Augustus, leads the cast, followed by Julia, the daughters of Agrippa, Agrippina, the sisters of Caligula, and Messalina. Marriage law and custom in old Rome open the book and frame all that follows.

Ferrero mixes political history with domestic detail, showing how marriages, births, and court intrigue shaped the empire. Plates of coins, busts, and villas add visual depth. The result is a readable history that puts wives, mothers, and sisters at the center of Rome's first imperial century.
16494-the-transvaal-from-within-a-privat:
J. P. Fitzpatrick, author of The Outspan, gives a private record of Transvaal politics in this 1899 book, written in 1896 and privately circulated before publication. Part one runs from earlier days and the reform movement through the invasion, Doornkop, and the arrest and trial of the reformers, with life in gaol. Part two covers three years' grace and the beginning of the end.

Appendices print the Pretoria and London Conventions, Kruger's affairs, and Volksraad debates. Fitzpatrick writes as an insider, careful to note that national labels are political, not racial. The book is a key source on the crisis that led to the Boer War.
1650-the-light-of-egypt-or-the-science-o:
This second volume of The Light of Egypt, linked to the names of Wagner and Burgoyne, sets out an occult science of the soul and the stars. Astrology, spiritual law, and the hidden order of life fill its pages. The Light of Egypt, in two volumes, belongs to the Hermetic Brotherhood of Luxor circle.

The work belongs to nineteenth-century esoteric writing, where Egypt stood for ancient wisdom. Modern readers will find it as a document of occult belief, not as science, and as a window on its movement. Its astrology, with planets and soul growth, drew readers who sought hidden wisdom.
16529-lost-leaders:
Andrew Lang reprints his Daily News leaders in this 1889 volume, chosen and arranged by Pett Ridge. The opening piece, Scotch Rivers, praises September on Scottish waters, when bracken turns gold and hardy trout rise to the fly despite snow-dusted anglers. Later leaders range across books, places, and the passing scene.

Lang writes with grace and a light, learned touch, never heavy even when the topic is serious. The pieces were meant for a newspaper day, but they read well together as short essays. Readers who enjoy Lang's criticism will find here his journalism at its most charming and varied.
16542-imperialism-and-the-tracks-of-our-:
Charles Francis Adams read these two papers before the Lexington Historical Society on December 20, 1898, and printed them in Boston in 1899. Imperialism takes up America's new empire after the Spanish war. The Tracks of Our Forefathers looks back to the founders' path, in Burke's phrase, where a man can neither wander nor stumble.

Adams writes as a New Englander uneasy with empire, measuring the present against the past. The Yuletide season frames his opening, linking Passover and New England's December days. The papers give a sharp, early voice against imperialism, from inside the American establishment itself.
16630-empire-builders:
Francis Lynde's 1907 novel follows Charles Edward and a railroad empire in the making. Chapters run from A Master of Men and a spiked switch through cold storage and wanted thirty-five millions. The awakening of Charles Edward, hammer and tongs, the race to the slow, and the sinews of war follow. Hurry orders, the entering wedge, and the mills of the gods follow.

Lynde writes with inside knowledge of railroads, finance, and the men who built them. The tale mixes business intrigue with romance and danger. Readers of industrial fiction will find a brisk, knowing novel of ambition, steel, and the price of empire.
16635-the-climbers:
Clyde Fitch's play in four acts, printed in 1905 by Samuel French, follows social climbers in New York. Act one opens in late winter at the Hunters', with later acts carrying the action through drawing rooms and seasons. The printed text is for reading only: no performance, professional or amateur, may be given without written permission from the acting-rights owner.

Fitch writes with sharp comedy and a keen eye for ambition, money, and manners. The play was a stage hit of its day, and the text keeps its brisk dialogue. Readers of American theater will find a witty, still-pointed satire of society on the make.
16675-tommy-atkins-at-war-as-told-in-his:
James A. Kilpatrick put together this 1914 book of a British soldier's own letters from the Great War, issued by McBride, Nast in New York. It opens with a German officer's praise for English fire, then lets Tommy Atkins speak of grim fights, chivalry, kindness, and the lift of battle. The note calls it the soldier's story, vivid and close.

Kilpatrick lets letters carry the tale, so the reader hears fear, jokes, mud, and mates in a private voice. The book shows war as men lived it, not as generals planned it. It remains a moving, short first-hand record of 1914 fighting, valued for its plain speech and its human warmth amid horror.
16714-under-sealed-orders:
H. A. Cody wrote this 1917 tale of the Canadian woods, where a young man works near falling water, a mill, and a power scheme. The plot turns on sealed papers, a bid for work, a cabin, and a girl caught between rival claims. Chapters move from spring floods to a wild storm, a rescue, and a late clearing of doubt.

Cody blends work life, love, and a slow unmasking of who can be trusted. Falls, dams, and timber camps give the story its hard edge, while the sealed orders hold the key to who gains and who loses. Readers who like old north-woods tales will find brisk action, plain heroics, and a neat close.
16722-americans-and-others:
Agnes Repplier gathered these essays in Boston in 1912, five of them new in print and the rest first seen in magazines such as the Atlantic Monthly. She writes on manners, humor, goodness, nerves, girl graduates, the sea, travel tales, zeal, Eve, charity, letters, gifts, borrowers, and even a grocer's cat. Each piece is short and self-standing.

Repplier argues with wit and a sharp eye, praising plain kindness while poking at fashion, cant, and self-pity. Her tone is bright and sure, and she likes a clean point made in a few pages. The book gives a lively view of American life a century back, and it still reads well for anyone who likes essays that judge people with humor.
16836-mark-hurdlestone-or-the-two-brothe:
Mrs. Moodie wrote this novel of Mark Hurdlestone, or the two brothers. She was sister of Agnes Strickland and author of Roughing It in the Bush. The third edition was issued by De Witt and Davenport in New York. A verse at the front speaks of winter nights, duty, and fancy calling visions to life. The first chapter opens on a lean, haggard wretch who made a god of sordid gold and offered up his soul.

Moodie tells of two brothers divided by greed and gold, with moral weight on every choice. The tale moves in the earnest, sermon-like style of its day. Readers who like long Victorian moral novels will find a story of wealth, waste, and brotherhood, told with feeling and a firm sense of right and wrong.
16903-the-gold-stealers:
Edward Dyson wrote this Australian tale of Waddy, a mining town school, and gold theft. It opens at the Waddy schoolhouse, built by local labor and gifts after Joel Ham, a graduate, came to town and stayed. Townsfolk at the Drovers' Arms resolved to raise a sound building and make Ham its headmaster, though no one quite knew what else to make of him.

Dyson mixes school life, mining camps, and crime, as gold goes missing and suspicion falls round the town. His tone is dry and local, with humor in committee talk and schoolroom pride. Readers who like Australian yarns will find a lively, talky tale of a small town, its school, and the gold that tempts its folk.
16931-four-american-leaders:
Charles W. Eliot wrote these four essays on American leaders, issued by the American Unitarian Association in Boston in 1906. A note warns each essay is only a partial portrait, written for a celebration, showing the man in some aspects and qualities, not in full proportion. Contents take up Franklin, in an address for his two hundredth birthday in Philadelphia in 1906. Washington follows, in a Chicago address in 1903. Channing appears at a statue unveiling in Boston in 1903, plus a fourth leader.

Eliot praises Franklin, Washington, and Channing as types of American character: ingenuity, duty, and conscience. His tone is earnest, civic, and Unitarian. The book gives a clear, period view of American heroes, useful for readers of biography and of how 1906 honored its founders.
16949-flowers-from-a-persian-garden-and-:
W. A. Clouston wrote this 1890 book of papers on Persian literature, issued by David Nutt in London and dedicated to E. Sidney Hartland of the Folk-Lore Society. An epigraph from Sir W. Ouseley calls Persian letters a smiling garden, where nature strews fragrant flowers, fruits abound, and the nightingale tunes her love-labored song while wisdom speaks moral sentences.

Clouston gathers tales, lore, and notes from Persian books, with other papers on eastern story. He writes for English readers who want the East in translation and tale. The book gives a fragrant, old-style sampler of Persian wit and wisdom, best dipped into for a tale or a proverb at a time.
16951-richard-lovell-edgeworth-a-selecti:
Beatrix L. Tollemache edited this 1896 selection from Richard Lovell Edgeworth's memoirs, issued by Rivington, Percival in London. Tollemache found the memoirs in a second-hand bookshop and, struck by their interest and amusement, drew other readers' attention to them. A verse at the front likens life to an inn where guests tarry, rest, and depart carrying sweet thoughts and hopes.

Edgeworth's memoirs mix invention, travel, family, and Irish life in the 1700s, told with wit and candor. Tollemache's selection keeps the best tales and scenes. Readers who love Georgian memoirs will find a lively, well-chosen volume, full of a restless, inventive man and the world he moved through.
16971-a-prince-of-sinners:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this novel of politics, wealth, and sin, in three parts. Part one follows Mr. Kingston Brooks, political agent, the Bullsom family at home, the Marquis of Arranmore, a man who went to hell, a thousand pounds, and charity called a crime. Later parts bring Mary Scott, a marquis on matrimony, Brooks as philanthropist, ghosts, and a new Don Quixote.

Oppenheim mixes high society, political intrigue, and moral fall, as Brooks tests whether a sinner can turn prince. The tale moves through dinners, suppers, and awkward questions with brisk, popular pace. Readers who like Edwardian society thrillers will find a long, plot-rich novel of money, power, and redemption.
1702-little-masterpieces-of-autobiograph:
