An odd little old man with a borrowed title and a stairway to sell gives Shaw his premise. What Ray offers, and what it costs, unfolds from that first inexplicable detail. Shaw wrote brisk, idea-driven science fiction for the magazines he also edited. The tale keeps its mystery social, a strange man at the door of the space age, asking to be believed.
23268-the-scalp-hunters:
The Scalp Hunters opens on an empty plain, seen with a poet's eye. The narrator stands in open country and turns his face north, south, east, and west. On all sides, the blue circle of the heavens rings him round, unbroken by rock or tree.

What covers that broad expanse, as far as his eye can range? Only flowers, beautiful flowers, in every direction. The calm of that prairie sea sets the stage for a frontier tale of hunters and danger. Readers get the western plains at full stretch, where beauty and risk share the same horizon.
23322-the-three-bears:
This verse retelling of the three bears tells of Bruin, his wife Mammy Muff, and their son Tiny-cub, who live in a wood with thick porridge, good chairs, and good beds. Bruin, the biggest bear, is surly and rough, with a great granite bowl and a cast-iron chair.

The tale follows the familiar visit of a little girl who tries porridge, chairs, and beds in turn. Told in rhyming couplets with pictures, it is the nursery classic in its early Victorian picture-book form. Mammy Muff's bowl and chair are made of brick-bats, yet both suit her, while Tiny-cub's set is the best of all.
23378-tales-of-the-sea-and-of-our-jack-t:
W. H. G. Kingston gathered nine sea stories in this volume, short and long, drawn from the lives of sailors and coastal folk. The longest, Happy Jack, takes a third of the book, following a youth who defies his lawyer father, runs to sea, and is at last presumed lost.

Other tales include two episodes of Uncle Boz, who rescues a wrecked crew and its passengers on a stormy Christmas Day near his house. Homecomings, wrecks, rescues, and hard work at sea fill the pages, with Jack's return, unrecognized by his sisters but known at once by the girl raised with them, as a high point. Kingston writes with warmth and pace, making this a fine set for readers who love the sea in story form.
23454-sweets-for-leisure-hours-amusing-t:
Dean and Munday printed this sixpenny book of sweets for leisure hours in London, adorned with sixteen neat coloured engravings. Short amusing tales and verses for little readers fill the pages, each with a picture to linger over.

The frozen bird opens the set. A child finds a robin half numb on the ground and longs to cage it for song. The child then asks if wings made to soar should sit in prison, and sets the bird free. Other tales follow in the same kind, gentle vein, praising mercy and good sense. Small children will enjoy the rhymes and pictures, while parents will value the mild morals, taught through pity rather than through fear.
23493-under-the-waves-diving-in-deep-wat:
R. M. Ballantyne wrote this diving tale after trying diving gear himself, once surfacing fast and upside down when too much air was sent down, an episode echoed in the book. Rooney Machowl, an Irishman, leaves his ship's carpenter trade to become a diver, and two or three stories run side by side in Ballantyne's familiar way.

Deep water work, wrecks, salvage, and the strange world below the waves fill the pages, with plain detail of suits, air pumps, and the risks of pressure. Ballantyne's first hand feel gives the diving scenes a vivid, believable edge. Young readers who love the sea will enjoy a tale that goes beneath it, showing both the wonder and the danger of work under water in the age before modern gear.
23535-the-invaders:
Benjamin Ferris wrote this weird tale, first printed in Weird Tales in March nineteen fifty one, of Wide Bend, a county seat over three valleys where the Sallinook River forks. Big Joe Merklos appears first, cash in hand at the Wide Bend National Bank, his flashing smile and easy strength winning trust at once.

Joe is the first buyer in fifteen years for Dark Valley, a bone yard of lonely dreams, once the richest valley, with solid houses, barns, and orchards laden with fruit. Then one spring the middle fork failed and the crops began, as the caption warns, to grow backwards. Ferris builds dread from that reversal, as magic, denied in words, works in fields. Horror readers will enjoy the slow invasion of a valley by forces no bank, smile, or strong body can bargain with.
2359-stories-by-english-authors-france-s:
Scribner's Stories by English Authors: France gathers tales set in France by writers including Robert Louis Stevenson, Ouida, and Wilkie Collins. The anthology opens with Stevenson's Lodging for the Night, in which the poet Villon spends a snowy Paris night among thieves, and continues through storms, strange beds, and perilous amours. France serves as a stage for English imagination.

The collection shows how Victorian writers used French settings for romance, horror, and adventure. Its variety is its charm. Readers of short fiction will enjoy a well-chosen sampler. Stevenson's Villon tale is the anthology's most anthologized piece.
23601-the-u-boat-hunters:
James B. Connolly wrote this sea book of U boat hunters, printed by Charles Scribner's Sons with pictures. It is one of a long shelf of his sea tales from Running Free to The Seiners and Out of Gloucester. The hunters of the title chase German submarines in the Great War, with small craft, keen eyes, and nerve.

Connolly, a master of sea detail, writes chases, patrols, and close calls with the salt and grit of a man who knew ships and men. An opening scene, with a hail of where you all going, sets the plain spoken, working tone. Readers who love naval adventure will enjoy the hunters' war, fought not in great fleet actions but in small boats, hard weather, and sudden danger beneath the waves.
23674-swept-out-to-sea-or-clint-webb-amo:
W. Bert Foster published this boys' sea adventure in 1913, another volume in the Clint Webb series after his tales among the sealers and on a windjammer. Clint narrates his own story, beginning with a serious falling out with his cousin and a mystery fourteen years old that his family has kept from him.

Clues pile up through talks with Ham Mayberry and an old coachman, until Clint sleeps aboard the Wavecrest and wakes to a deserted ocean. From there the story carries him south among whalers, with a remarkable haven, a strange natural wonder, and a voyage to southern seas. It is brisk, first-person adventure in the classic boys'-book manner.
2368-the-angel-and-the-author-and-others:
Jerome K. Jerome's Angel and the Author, and Others collects essays and sketches in which the author argues with his guardian angel, reflects on writing, and pokes fun at modern life. The title piece lets Jerome's angel point out the gap between his books and his behavior, to comic effect. Other pieces range from holiday mishaps to literary gossip.

The volume shows Jerome's familiar voice: genial, digressive, and fond of a paradox. It is best read as a companion to his novels, a glimpse of the man behind them. Fans will enjoy its easy charm.
2369-one-of-ours:
Willa Cather's Pulitzer Prize novel One of Ours follows Claude Wheeler, a Nebraska farm boy who feels trapped by prairie life and finds purpose, and death, in the First World War. Cather writes Claude's youth with sympathy and his war service with stark realism, from training camps to the trenches of France. The novel's second half shifts from farm to front with startling force.

The book divided critics: some found its war chapters glorious, others naive. Its portrait of a young man seeking meaning still moves readers. Cather fans will find it essential, if uneven.
2372-the-woman-haters:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Woman-Haters follows two Cape Cod bachelors who swear off women, only to have their resolve tested by the arrival of a capable, charming newcomer. The novel's humor comes from the men's bluster, their small-town routines, and the inevitable softening of their vows. Lincoln's dialect and seaside detail carry the comedy.

The story is gentle and good-natured, with romance arriving in spite of every precaution. Readers who like Cape Cod fiction will find a cozy, funny tale. It pairs well with Lincoln's other town chronicles.
23757-men-of-affairs:
Roland Pertwee published Men of Affairs in 1922, a novel that opens at a pawnshop in the Gray's Inn Road. There Richard Frencham Altar disposes of the last of his worldly goods: Savile Row suits, Jermyn Street shoes, hosiery, dressing-table brushes, and the gold cigarette case Doreen gave him at their engagement.

For all this he leaves with twenty-seven pounds sixteen shillings, and settling with his landlady takes nineteen pounds more. With eight pounds sixteen left, Altar must live by his wits. Chapters named Dissolution, Eight Closed Doors, and A Little Housebreaking show the road ahead: a comedy of money, nerve, and reinvention.
23946-lalage-s-lovers:
George A. Birmingham published Lalage's Lovers in 1911, narrated by a churchwarden whose office is hereditary in his family. He calls on Canon Beresford, the rector, on parish business, but the canon has gone out to fish. Miss Battersby, Lalage's governess, explains her agreeable solitude by saying Lalage is with her father.

She is misinformed, and the comedy that follows turns on Lalage, her lovers, and the parish world around them. Graveyard walls crumble, sextons need appointing, and a mother keeps the narrator up to his duties. Birmingham, a master of Irish clerical comedy, writes the churchwarden's boredom and duty with a straight face and a sly wit.
24088-lincoln-s-last-hours:
Charles A. Leale, a young army surgeon, was the first doctor to reach Abraham Lincoln after the president was shot at Ford's Theatre. In February 1909, Leale gave this address in New York before the Military Order of the Loyal Legion. He recalled that night and the funeral days that followed, on the hundredth anniversary of Lincoln's birth.

Leale describes riding in the funeral procession in Washington, deep in thought as crowds lined the route, and tells what he saw and did beside the dying president. His account is short, plain, and firsthand, which is why it endures: it comes from a man who was in the box, not from later retelling. It remains a key witness record of Lincoln's last hours.
24089-the-five-jars:
M. R. James, known for ghost stories, wrote this fantasy tale for younger readers, published in New York and London in 1922. The narrator writes to his friend Jane about a hot September day by a woodland stream, when a dream of a plant led him to a real discovery in the wood. What follows is told across chapters on the first jar, the second jar, and the small people.

Later chapters bring danger to the jars, a cat, a bat-ball game, and a creature called Wag at home. James keeps the tone of a letter from a friend who has stumbled on something strange and half-believed. Readers get a gentle wonder tale of woods, small folk, and jars that must be guarded.
24160-the-basket-of-flowers:
Christoph von Schmid wrote this moral tale for young readers, published in London by John F. Shaw and Company, with pictures by Watson Charlton and W. E. Evans. It opens with Mary, a gardener's daughter, in a foreign country long ago, where manners differ widely from our own. The story teaches two lessons the author says may be learned in all countries, beginning with the sinful heart and its bitter fruit.

Chapters follow the basket of flowers, a missing ring, Mary in prison, and her trial and sentence. Later comes a new home and new friends, her father's last words, and at last how the ring was found, with reparation and forgiveness of an enemy. Readers get a gentle, earnest tale of innocence accused, suffering borne, and wrongs set right.
24166-the-destroyers:
Randall Garrett wrote this science fiction story, with pictures by van Dongen, on war as the death of a way of life. It opens with Anketam, forty-five, stretching at sunset after his crew has set the last green seedlings in the fields. The greenhouses stand empty, ready for the next seeding, and by working a little harder each day the crew has finished four days ahead of schedule.

That gain means four days of fishing, hunting, or plain loafing, since the Chief cares only that the work is done. Anketam still feels strong enough for his day's work, though his shoulders twinge and his back aches. Garrett sets this contented farm life against the ruin war brings. Readers get a pastoral opening to a story of loss.
2425-a-bundle-of-letters:
Henry James's Bundle of Letters tells a story entirely through correspondence, as American travelers in Europe write home about each other. The novella's young heroine, Miranda, becomes the subject of competing letters, with each writer revealing more about themselves than about her. James's irony sparkles in the gaps between accounts.

The form lets James play with point of view, a technique he would deepen for decades. The book is short, witty, and elegantly constructed. Readers new to James will find an accessible entry point. James wrote the novella in 1879, early in his long career.
2432-barchester-towers:
Anthony Trollope's Barchester Towers, the second of his Barsetshire novels, follows the battle for power in a cathedral close after the old bishop's death. The new bishop, his wife Mrs. Proudie, and the oily chaplain Mr. Slope clash with Archdeacon Grantly and the gentle Mr. Harding over doctrine, patronage, and the fate of the hospital. Trollope's comedy of church politics is unmatched.

The novel's large cast, from the signora Neroni to the Thornes of Ullathorne, gives it a rich social world. Trollope's narrator guides readers with wit and warmth. Fans of Victorian fiction will find a masterpiece of clerical comedy.
24388-squirrels-and-other-fur-bearers:
John Burroughs wrote this book of squirrels and other fur-bearers, with fifteen pictures in colors after Audubon and a frontispiece from life. It was published by Houghton, Mifflin and Company in Boston and New York. Its copyrights run from 1875 to 1900. Its frontispiece shows a red fox, photographed by Wm. Lyman Underwood of Belmont, Massachusetts. Chapters run from squirrels, the chipmunk, and the woodchuck to the rabbit and the hare, the muskrat, and the skunk.

The fox, the weasel, and the mink follow, with the raccoon, the porcupine, the opossum, wild mice, glimpses of wild life, and a life of fear. The squirrel chapter opens in October woods, where the ground lies thick with large unopened chestnut burrs, every one cut off with an inch of stem adhering. Not accident, but design: some wise squirrel marked the finest fruit Burroughs had seen. Readers get neighbors, watched with delight.
24540-country-neighbors:
Alice Brown published this story collection at Boston and New York in 1910, with the Riverside Press imprint. Its sixteen stories include The Play House, His First Wife, A Flower of April, The Auction, Saturday Night, A Grief Deferred, and The Challenge. They are set among country neighbours in New England.

Brown's people are plain, proud, and tender: a woman watching from a front-chamber window, a gardener, a poetess in spring, and a silver tea-set with a history. Her stories are quiet and keenly observed, full of the talk and feeling of village life. Readers who love New England fiction will find this collection among her best.
24543-the-circuit-riders:
R. C. FitzPatrick wrote this short science-fiction story, illustrated by Schoenherr. Its title comes from a watch room board, where little lights glow for people out in the night of the city-jungle. Each light stands for human passions, strong emotions, and crimes yet to happen.

Watchmen take turns at the board, and one light bothers an experienced watcher. Its dial has stood high all night and keeps climbing, slow and steady. FitzPatrick's story turns on what the watchers should do about a crime they can see coming. Readers get a tense, compact tale of prediction, duty, and fate.
24566-faithfully-yours:
Lou Tabakow wrote this short science-fiction story, first printed in Astounding Science Fiction in December 1955 and illustrated by Emsh. It opens on 18 July 1949, with a fugitive lying face down in a foul place, on the run from the law. Tracking down and recapturing an escaped criminal, the story hints, is not the worst thing one might do.

Later scenes turn stranger, with a grove full of chirpings and whistles, a small creature at a transparent wall, and a chubby, contented man tending a patient. Tabakow's tale blends pursuit with alien wonder. Readers get a short, odd, and memorable story about escape, capture, and what faithfulness might mean.
2457-stories-by-english-authors-italy-se:
Scribner's Stories by English Authors: Italy gathers tales set in Italy, from a faithful retainer's devotion to a brigand's bride and a general's widow. The anthology includes work by James Payn, W. E. Norris, Mary Robinson, Laurence Oliphant, and Anthony Trollope, each using Italy as a stage for English passions. The settings range from country houses to bandit country.

The collection's variety shows how Italy fired the Victorian imagination. Readers of short fiction will enjoy a well-chosen tour. It pairs with the France volume in the same series. Trollope's contribution shows his talent for the short tale as well as the long novel.
24622-the-pianolist-a-guide-for-pianola-:
Gustav Kobbe, author of How to Appreciate Music, wrote this guide for pianola players, published at New York in 1907. The pianola, a mechanical piano-player, let a novice play great music by working pedals and stops, and Kobbe argues that it popularised music and sharpened musical taste.

Chapters cover the charm of playing an instrument yourself, first steps for the novice, the thrill of the great masters, an open sesame to Chopin, and notes on other masters. Kobbe ends with educational factors and a few don'ts for pianolists. Readers curious about home music-making a century ago will find this guide delightful.
24678-the-three-commanders:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote this sea tale, the third in a tetralogy running from The Three Midshipmen to The Three Admirals. Its three heroes will be familiar to Kingston's young readers, and the book serves as a fine way into mid-nineteenth-century naval life. Action soon moves to East Africa.

There the story shows the anti-slave trade patrols at work, as Britain opposed slavery while Portuguese, Americans, Arabs, and East African states carried it on behind her back. Then the tale moves to the Crimea. Young readers get a stirring naval adventure, with history and seamanship woven through it.
24790-early-english-meals-and-manners:
Early English Meals and Manners gathers medieval English texts on how to behave at table, issued for the Early English Text Society. Its core pieces are John Russell's Boke of Nurture, the Boke of Keruynge on carving, the Boke of Curtasye, and the Babees Book, with notes, recipes, and side notes through the volume.

Readers meet the rules of a great household: where each guest sits by rank, how meat is carved, and how a young servant should speak and serve. The old spelling and sidenotes make the book a rich source for food, rank, and daily life in late medieval England. It suits readers of social history and early English writing.
24832-labrador-days-tales-of-the-sea-toi:
Wilfred Thomason Grenfell, a doctor in Labrador, published these tales in Boston and New York in 1919. Eleven stories follow the sea toilers of Newfoundland and Labrador: fishermen, dog teams, and families on the ice. Titles include There's Trouble on the Sea, Nancy, Sally's Turns, and The Red Island Shoals.

Grenfell keeps the local speech, with its odd spellings, and his scenes run on ice, boats, and winter shores. One tale tells of hauling a lost old man through dark and fast-forming ice, saved by a girl who roused the boys. The book gives a warm, firsthand portrait of hard lives on a hard coast, told by the doctor who served them.
24870-the-stars-my-brothers:
Edmond Hamilton wrote The Stars, My Brothers, a space tale set in the year 1981. Reed Kieran, a physics teacher driven from Ohio by a sniffling pupil, joins the United Nations Reconnaissance Corps and serves on Wheel Five, a lab that circles the Moon. A ferry crash kills Kieran, and his blind, voiceless body is left wheeling in slow orbit.

Kieran wakes far in the future, among a people called the Sakae, who are not human, and humans who are not free. The tale turns on rights: if the Sakae are wise and the humans are not, who owns the world? Hamilton mixes space adventure with a sharp question about what makes a people count.
24965-the-deadly-daughters:
Winston K. Marks's science-fiction story, illustrated by Novick, opens with Dr. Hubert Long, forty, assistant professor of political science at Mentioch University, denouncing the Humanist Party before eight hundred students. The party, he shouts, is no party at all but an oligarchy, with elections rigged to keep a select group of feminists in absolute power. The lecture may cost him his position, but he insists citizens must face a government become little better than dictatorship.

Long argues the numbers deceive. Only thirty percent of legislatures are women, yet three-fourths of key committee posts are held by women. The balance are held by men whose wives sit at the Humanist Party's top level. A reporter from the Mentioch Bugle presses him, and later a woman rages at his plan to win his point through headlines and a goon squad. The story mixes campus politics with pulp conspiracy.
25000-english-book-collectors:
William Younger Fletcher's 1902 volume, edited by Alfred Pollard for the English Bookman's Library and published by Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner, surveys the great English book collectors in alphabetical order. The roll runs from Arundel and Ashburnham through Askew, Bagford, Banks, Beauclerk, and Beckford to Burghley, Burney, Burton, Cotton, and Cranmer, with the Earl of Crawford among the later entries. A frontispiece portrait of George John, second Earl Spencer, opens the book.

Each entry traces a collector's library, its treasures, and its fate, giving book lovers a gallery of the collectors who preserved England's printed heritage. Fletcher writes for collectors and librarians alike, valuing provenance and bindings as much as texts. The volume remains a standard reference for the history of English book collecting.
25067-the-planet-strappers:
Raymond Z. Gallun's Planet Strappers, published by Pyramid Books in 1961, is a space adventure about the first colony beyond the Moon. Two young spacers, Nelsen and Ramos, fly a tiny plastic-bubble craft toward Mars, alert to every danger of the void.

Outlaws drift between the worlds, waiting to strike passing ships, and the colonists must defend domes, gardens, and air supplies with little more than courage and quick thinking. A dynamite blast that shatters a dome leaves Nelsen fighting for survival among wrecked equipment. The novel mixes hardscrabble frontier spirit with the perils of early space travel.
25098-the-tree-dwellers:
Katharine Elizabeth Dopp's Tree-Dwellers, the first book of her Industrial and Social History series for primary grades, imagines early human life in the age of fear. Illustrated by Howard V. Brown, it was written to teach young children how people lived before farming, writing, or settled towns.

Through the family of Sharptooth and his kin, children see tree-top homes, berry gathering, fire tending, and the constant watch for danger. Dopp keeps the story simple and concrete, using daily tasks to show how tools, shelter, and cooperation grew out of need. The book is both a school reader and a period piece in early childhood education.
25126-modern-saints-and-seers:
Jean Finot's Modern Saints and Seers examines the revival of occult belief after the First World War. Evan Marrett translated it from the French for a London edition in 1920. Finot argues that four years of desolation made the attraction of the beyond irresistible, as millions of dead seemed to draw the living toward mystery.

Chapters survey seers, saints, spirit mediums, and Russian sects. Their doctrines of spiritual love, multiple Christs, and holy men reached from village churches to the court of Rasputin. Finot writes as an observer rather than a believer, testing the bridge his subjects claim to build between this world and the next.
25267-astronomy-for-amateurs:
Camille Flammarion's Astronomy for Amateurs, in Frances A. Welby's authorized translation, was published by Appleton in 1910. Flammarion, founder of the Astronomical Society of France and director of the Juvisy Observatory, writes for readers with no telescope and little mathematics.

He presents the sun as one star among many, warming worlds that may bear life, and argues that life is the goal of nature. Unknown inhabitants of other worlds, he suggests, may think of Earth as Earth thinks of them. The book's wonder and speculation made Flammarion the most beloved popular astronomer of his day.
2532-the-half-brothers:
Elizabeth Gaskell sets this short tale on a lonely Cumberland farm near the sea, where a widowed mother marries again and bears a second son. The narrator, her younger boy, grows up beside his half brother Gregory, a gentle lad whom others call slow and dull.

Their stepfather treats Gregory harshly, school fails him, and farm work becomes his only place. Yet Gregory stays patient and kind, and his bond with his younger brother deepens through hardship. Gaskell tells the story with quiet power, and its ending turns on loyalty, forgiveness, and the worth of a life others had written off.
25337-genuine-mediumship-or-the-invisibl:
Swami Bhakta Vishita's Genuine Mediumship, or The Invisible Powers, published in Chicago in 1919, teaches occult powers as natural forces, not miracles. Vishita, author of Seership, insists his subject is supernormal, not supernatural and not abnormal.

Part one surveys nature's finer forces, vibrations, unseen worlds, and interpenetrating planes, arguing that humans sense only vibratory motion. Part two treats mental vibrations and transmission, and the higher senses latent in all people. Vishita draws a ring pass-not around nature: all experience, normal or supernormal, stays inside it. Vishita writes for students of psychic phenomena who seek reason rather than wonder.
25429-the-peril-finders:
George Manville Fenn sends failing California fruit-growers after a golden dream. Blights and insects have beaten them, when a dying prospector arrives from the mountains with rich gold samples. He tells of ancient cities where gold lies abundant, then dies after a few lucid moments. Several settlers give up their farms and set out across huge distances to find the gold-mountains.

Their road brings rattlesnake episodes, a rock-carved city sacked centuries before, and an Apache attack beaten off by a clever trick. They travel for years and never find the gold-mountains, though they find much else. A prefatory note calls it a long and excellent book, and it shows Fenn at his best in desert adventure.
25430-the-innocents-a-story-for-lovers:
Sinclair Lewis's Innocents, published by Harper and Brothers in 1917, is a story for lovers, not the ponderous realism Lewis promises elsewhere. His dedicatory introduction admires young British writers such as Mackenzie, Walpole, Onions, Lawrence, and Beresford, and their master H. G. Wells.

Seth Appleby and his wife, almost old, call each other Father and Mother. They visit their daughter Lulu and her husband Hartwig. Neighbors play tennis at the country club and five hundred on Saturday evenings, while Mother begs to dust and make beds and Father offers to rake the lawn. Lewis treats old age with humor and tenderness.
25505-the-merryweathers:
Laura E. Richards, author of Captain January and Melody, writes this 1904 family story for children, illustrated by Julia Ward Richards. An opening verse sets the tone, with sunlight on golden fields, asters at a meadow's edge, goldenrod standing proud, and a wild bird calling its mate at day's end.

The Merryweathers themselves fill the chapters that follow, in a tale of home life told with warmth and gentle humour. Richards keeps scenes short and vivid, letting seasonal country sights and family talk carry a story meant to be read aloud or enjoyed alone.
25514-the-ranger-boys-and-the-border-smu:
Claude A. Labelle writes for boys aged twelve to sixteen in this 1922 Ranger Boys tale. It belongs to a series that also follows the boys to a rescue, a hermit, timber thieves, and a reward. Here the young rangers take on smugglers working a border route. Hidden goods and secret carriers raise the stakes.

An illustration points to the key clue. A man wears a chamois money belt, suspected of hiding jewels inside it. Tracking, watchfulness, and teamwork drive the pursuit, rather than brute force. The boys work step by step to expose the smuggling ring.
25524-the-young-berringtons-the-boy-expl:
W. H. G. Kingston tells of a London family ruined in business who sail to Australia to join cousins running a profitable station there. The book first appeared in parts in a children's magazine, and its short length suits young readers new to tales of settler life.

Life proves harder than the newcomers expect. Local Aboriginal people threaten the station, a storm tears the roof from the house, and a flood higher than any remembered destroys house and much stock. The family must then look farther inland for a fresh start.
25598-citizenship-a-manual-for-voters:
Emma Guy Cromwell writes this 1920 manual for voters. She had served as state librarian of Kentucky and enrolling clerk of the House of Representatives. The manual sold in paper for seventy-five cents and cloth for one dollar twenty-five. She dedicates it to the new voters of America, a great factor in good government.

Cromwell, author of a compendium of parliamentary law, saw a need for a citizenship manual for new voters in Kentucky. She compiles information on government and its workings for all voters, especially those just entering political life, in plain, practical form suited to first-time ballots.
2560-the-three-partners:
Bret Harte opens this novel at sunset on the Black Spur Range, where red light eats along pine crests and night wind wrestles the shadows climbing from the valley. Three mining partners, bound by a claim and old debts, find their pact tested by gold, love, and betrayal.

Harte moves between camp, town, and mountain trail, letting each partner's past catch up with him. The prose mixes landscape painting with sharp talk, and the partnership itself becomes the real subject. The book offers a compact western drama about trust among men who have little left but each other.
25644-the-man-who-hated-mars:
Randall Garrett writes this science fiction tale of Ron Clayton, a big, hairy man who begs to be put in prison. He speaks in a trembling voice to Lieutenant Phoebe Harris of the Terran Rehabilitation Service, seated behind a desk far too big for her.

Clayton, judged big, ugly, cowardly, and dangerous from his dossier, wants escape from Mars itself. Escape means leaving a sealed exile camp, getting aboard an unboardable ship, and breaking a steel wall. Mars, Garrett warns, does evil things to men, until Clayton is no longer even Clayton.
25648-the-peterkin-papers:
Lucretia P. Hale writes the Peterkin Papers, in a seventh edition from Houghton Mifflin in 1893, with a copyright dating to 1880. She dedicates the stories to Meggie, daughter of the lady from Philadelphia, to whom they were first told. Mrs. Peterkin putting salt into her coffee fronts the book.

The lady who put salt in her coffee opens the farces. Elizabeth Eliza's piano follows, with the Peterkins trying to become wise. A late dinner, a summer journey, and being snowed up follow. Keeping a cow, a Christmas tree, and a tea party come next, as the well meaning family solves small problems in the longest possible way.
25728-desert-conquest-or-precious-waters:
A. M. Chisholm writes Desert Conquest, or Precious Waters. He had written The Boss of Wind River. Grosset and Dunlap published the book in 1913. Clarence Rowe supplied pictures. Sheila, snapping that she will make one quiet after a hard pace told on her temper through bruises, fronts the book.

Miss Nita Hess opens the tale flattening a snub nose against a Pullman window. She stares at expressionless plains she knew only from light literature. She read that literature in secret at a select eastern school for young ladies. Her remarks would shock the ultra correct, and desert water, claimed and fought over, drives a western tale of love and rivalry.
25763-murphy-a-message-to-dog-lovers:
Major Gambier-Parry writes Murphy, a message to dog lovers, published in New York by Mitchell Kennerley in 1913 with two drawings by the author. A Tobit epigraph opens the book, telling how Tobit sent his son on a journey with an angel, and the young man's dog went with them.

Murphy, the dog of the title, fronts the book in a drawing by his master. Gambier-Parry writes for readers who love dogs as companions, not as property, praising loyalty, patience, and joy. The short book mixes story, reflection, and pictures in a tribute to one dog and to all dogs.
25836-young-hilda-at-the-wars:
Arthur H. Gleason, author of The Spirit of Christmas and Love, Home and the Inner Life, writes Young Hilda at the Wars, published by Frederick A. Stokes in September 1915. Hilda, in motor ambulance uniform wearing the Order of Leopold II conferred by King Albert in person, fronts the book.

Gleason dedicates the book to Chevalier Helen of Pervyse, and an experience preface opens the chapters. Young Hilda at the wars, with good will as a theme, follows a young woman driving an ambulance in wartime Belgium and France, facing danger, duty, and compassion at the front.
2584-the-first-1000-euler-numbers:
This plain text file lists the first 1000 Euler numbers, issued as number 20 in a series of mathematical constants. Euler numbers, also called secant numbers, appear in the series for the secant function and alternate in sign as they grow.

The values swell quickly, reaching hundreds of digits by the later terms, and hand calculation would be slow and error prone. The file gives students and programmers a clean, exact reference to check work or feed into programs. Like its companion lists, it is a bare table, valued for accuracy and completeness.
25849-the-launch-boys-adventures-in-nort:
Edward S. Ellis follows a crew of boys on a second cruise in their motor launch, this time into northern waters. The boys face scrapes on shore and on the water, and much of the fun comes from quick thinking in tight spots. One long night scene puts them upstairs in a house while burglars work on a safe below, with only a lookout posted and a single useless rifle at hand.

The tale is the second volume of the Launch Boys series, printed in 1912 with pictures by Burton Donnel Hughes. Chapters move from a proposal and a scouting trip to night visitors, narrow escapes, and a race to act in time. The pace stays brisk, and the boys win through by nerve, teamwork, and steady pluck rather than by force.
2585-the-first-1001-fibonacci-numbers:
This plain text file holds the first 1001 numbers of the Fibonacci sequence, issued as number 21 in a series of mathematical constants. Each term after the first two is the sum of the two before it, so the list begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and grows with great speed.

By the thousandth term the figures run to hundreds of digits, far beyond hand reckoning. The file serves as a ready reference for students, programmers, and puzzle solvers who need exact values without computing them. It is a tool, not a treatise, and its value lies in its clean, complete run of terms.
2586-the-first-498-bernoulli-numbers:
This plain text file gives the first 498 Bernoulli numbers, issued as number 22 in a series of mathematical constants. Bernoulli numbers turn up in sums of powers, in the series for the tangent function, and in many corners of number theory.

The fractions grow large and unwieldy, which is why a printed table still helps: exact values can be lifted straight from the list. Students and programmers use such tables to test formulas and code. The file is a spare reference work, plain in form and precise in content. Its plain format suits quick lookup rather than cover to cover reading.
25876-the-house-with-the-green-shutters:
George Douglas sets a Scots town novel around John Gourlay and the new house he has built at the head of the brae. The book opens on a still morning in the Square, with the Red Lion maid flinging wash water from her pail and Gourlay listening to its swash. Townsfolk watch him with awe and dread, and when he must be faced, baker, provost, and deacon vie to be hindmost.

Douglas writes the town in its own Scots voice, dry, sharp, and often comic, as the deacon is coaxed to do the approaching no one else will. The green shutters mark a house of pride and a man set apart, and the tale follows how that pride bears on kin, trade, and town talk. It is a keen, unsparing portrait of a small place and a hard man.
2588-stories-by-english-authors-scotland:
This anthology gathers Scottish stories by English authors, chosen for Scribners, and it reads as a tour of Scotland in fiction. J. M. Barrie courts T'nowhead's Bell, S. R. Crockett sends a Heather Lintie, and Ian Maclaren presents a doctor of the old school.

Sir Walter Scott contributes Wandering Willie's Tale, Professor Aytoun tells of the Glenmutchkin Railway, and R. L. Stevenson closes with Thrawn Janet. The set mixes humor, horror, and homely wisdom, all in Scots voices. It offers a fine single shelf of the short Scottish tale at its best.
25884-found-in-the-philippines-the-story:
Captain Charles King tells a tale of the Philippines through a woman's letters, printed in 1899 and 1901. It opens at division headquarters, where regulars and volunteers line the sentry posts and watch for orders to move. For a month the men have shivered in Pacific fogs on the Presidio Heights or drilled on bleak slopes, envying comrades shipped to Manila and those who stormed Santiago.

The story turns on letters found after the fighting, and on folk like Mrs. Frost, returning stronger yet fragile from a drive as boxes are packed for the transport. A crowd gathers near the Baldwin Hotel round a young soldier of twenty one or two, arrested by a patrol and held by armed guards. King writes of war, waiting, and love with a soldier's plain eye.
25895-a-walk-through-leicester-being-a-g:
Printed at Leicester by T. Combe in 1804, this pocket guide leads strangers through the town and its environs, with notes on history and antiquities. The editor aims to serve travelers and townsfolk alike, hoping the little companion will help hosts point out the most memorable objects of their ancient and honorable town. A Shakespeare motto opens the walk, promising a view of manners, traders, and buildings before dinner.

The stroll takes in churches, halls, and streets, then winds out to wooded walks west of town. Ruding's Walk, left open by its owner, winds through shrubbery to a grove of tall elms, with town roofs broken by trees. The guide praises the town's mails and travel comforts, and it lingers on old stones, markets, and the pride of place that binds a native's mind.
25923-brandon-of-the-engineers:
Harold Bindloss sends Dick Brandon, a promising young engineer, into trouble, punishment, and plotters in this 1916 novel. The frontispiece shows a woman crying that Dick must come away, since she cannot let him live among plotters and gamblers. Clare, the daughter of the charming but failing Kenwardine, watches her father's hold slip as servants stay on despite wages paid late, drawn by his easy charm and his rare fault finding.

Kenwardine's weakness for liquor bars him from a better post, yet his daughter feels his charm as strongly as anyone, even as his failings shock her. Clare knits her brows and gazes up a straight white road through pastures and yellow cornfields where harvesters work. Bindloss ties engineering, finance, and love into a tale of a young man proving his worth.
25969-chimney-pot-papers:
Charles S. Brooks gathers light essays in Chimney Pot Papers, printed by Yale University Press in 1919 with woodcuts by Fritz Endell. Many pieces first ran in the Unpopular Review and the Century Magazine. Contents move from chimney pots and the quest of the lost digamma to rainy mornings, 1917, going afoot, livelihoods, friendly giants, holidays, and runaway studies.

Brooks muses on turning forty, on wit versus humor, on parties, leather suspenders, boots for runaways, and hanging a stocking at Christmas. His windows look across the roofs, and his pages praise red haired, freckled lads as sure guides to adventure, like Crusoe, Kidd, and Raleigh in their youth. The essays are gentle, witty, and fond of small wonders.
25972-two-little-travellers:
Ray Cunningham, pen name of Frances Browne Arthur, tells a girls' story of two small travelers, printed by Nelson in 1903. Dedicated to the author's children, the book opens under a huge cedar tree at Firgrove on a golden Sunday afternoon in September, with apples red overhead and ripe nuts showering down. A Dickens motto on the innocent heart of a child fronts the tale.

Chapters run from left behind and babes in the wood to far, far away, gone amissing, and the cruise of H.M.S. Dreadnought. Hill difficulty, Bambo and Bruno, a sudden flight, and a foe on the trail follow, with a happy land at the end of the road. One scene shows little Joan quizzing Bambo, who is barely bigger than Darby, on whether he calls himself boy or man.
26051-bolshevism-a-curse-danger-to-the-w:
H. W. Lee, editor of Justice, warns workers against Bolshevism in this twopenny pamphlet of February 1919, with a foreword by Will Thorne, member of Parliament. Lee calls Bolshevism a curse and danger to workers, and argues from its own instructions and deeds. The pamphlet, second edition from the Twentieth Century Press, speaks to trade union readers in plain, partisan prose.

Lee quotes instructions showing personal safety guaranteed only to top government and council members. Local party and control committee men might be shot at any time by a small town extraordinary commission on whose ground they stood. Executions, he says, cannot be excused as mere correction of irregular acts. The pamphlet is a socialist's case against revolution by terror.
2608-roundabout-papers:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote these roundabout papers as familiar essays on whatever caught his eye. A lazy idle boy, two children in black, ribbons, screens in dining rooms, and Tunbridge toys each get a short, wandering treatment.

Thackeray moves from jokes heard from Thomas Hood to Christmas trees, chalk marks on doors, and being found out, with the ease of a man talking after dinner. The essays mix satire, sentiment, and gossip about his own age. They show the novelist at his most companionable, thinking aloud for readers he treats as friends.
26093-the-memory-of-mars:
Raymond F. Jones's science-fiction tale follows Mel Hastings, a reporter who should stay objective even about a hospital, but cannot while his wife Alice lies in surgery. Alice had always said they would go to Mars for a vacation again, yet now she is dead, and the surgeons say she was not even human.

Hastings knows two things at once: he loves his wife, and they have never been off Earth. A tourist ship, the Martian Princess, streaks the dawn sky as he waits. Later a steward explains a change of ship from shuttle to liner that Hastings never heard when he bought tickets. Memory, love, and a Martian past that may never have happened drive the story.
26115-a-small-boy-and-others:
Henry James's memoir gathers particulars of his early life and of his brother William James, set in their native and domestic air. Written so that later memorials of William might read more plainly, it appeals first to memory, and lets one consequence of that appeal crowd out others.

School scenes recall Mr. Jenks, a master who kept a ferule in his arms and whacked at times, yet kept a dignity that softened the memory. James does not recall the whacking as ugly or droll; it fails to break the spell of the civilization he contemplates. The book is less a straight life than a meditation on childhood, family, and the air that formed two brothers.
26242-the-bill-toppers:
Andre Castaigne's 1909 novel follows the Clifton family, a troupe chasing stardom across the seas. It opens on a ship in the Bay of Bengal, where Clifton watches his eight-year-old daughter Lily wave a white coral necklace bought in Australia. Lily, a child cyclist billed as a star, has won bouquets by the cartload at Melbourne and Sydney, and her father plans still bolder tricks for Calcutta.

Clifton began as an office clerk, turned amateur cyclist, then professional, and married an Englishwoman at Wellington. He built the act around Lily, whose first memories are of riding on her mother's shoulders, her mother on her father's, her father on his bike. Later, Lily visits a young man named Jimmy at his brain-work, and the novel tracks a family's climb toward the top of the bill.
26358-eastern-tales-by-many-story-teller:
Mrs. Valentine's Eastern Tales, in the Chandos Classics from Frederick Warne in London, gathers stories for youthful readers from ancient and modern French, Italian, and English sources. Its preface says tales from the Tales of the Genii were trimmed by a few words to fit young readers. Pictures run through the volume.

Contents list Jalaladdeen of Bagdad, the story of Haschem, the pantofles, the prince and the lions, and the city of demons. Jussuf the merchant of Balsora, the seven sleepers, and Misnar the sultan of India follow. Later tales bring the four talismans, Bohetzad the lost child, Urad the fair wanderer, and Alischar and Smaragdine. The book offers wonder, morals, and far-off courts.
26536-the-good-neighbors:
Edgar Pangborn's short story, published in Galaxy in June 1960, opens with a spherical ship about twenty-seven miles across, orbiting some 3,400 miles above Earth. Sighted briefly and without a good fix, it excites little wonder in a late twentieth century used to visiting spaceships that come and go discouraged. Three-dimensional television, promising Dora the Doll in every living room, matters more to most people than one more ship.

Then the region of Seattle suffers an eclipse that is not an eclipse, but a near shadow, and not a shadow but a thing drifting from the northern Pacific. It breeds thunder without lightning or rain, then wind, high waves, and fog. Radar goes crazy for an hour, and aircraft rise ready to shoot, as Pangborn's good neighbors make their inconvenient arrival.
26565-the-sheep-eaters:
W. A. Allen, a dentist, published this short history with the Shakespeare Press at New York in 1913. Its subject is the Sheep Eaters, a mountain people Allen calls extinct for about fifty years. Their history survives in rock inscriptions in Wyoming and Montana. Arrows and tepees near Black Canyon and the great shrine wheel on Bald Mountain add more traces. Twenty-eight tribes, he says, worshipped the sun there twice a year.

Chapters tell an old squaw's tale, a gold seeker in the mountains, a trip to the Paint Rocks, a talk with Little Bear, and the story of Aggretta and the Red Arrow. Allen describes asp-bark tepees, mountain sheep as the staple food, and the Shoshones as a branch who married Mountain Crows. It is an amateur, romantic account, best read as a period record of local lore.
26613-ruth-fielding-at-college-or-the-mi:
Alice B. Emerson published this Ruth Fielding book with Cupples and Leon in 1917, sending her heroine from the Red Mill to college. It opens in September woods near the mill, where Aunt Alvirah Boggs awaits Ruth and the twins Helen and Tom Cameron on their last outing together. Tom heads for Harvard, while Ruth looks collegeward to Ardmore, where boys are said to be barred from the lawns.

College chapters bring Miss Cullam's trouble, the Stone Face joke, a tempest in a teapot, and what was found in Rebecca's trunk and heart. A deep, dark plot, a squall, and treasure hunting lead toward the missing examination papers of the subtitle. The book ends with a perfect year, closing a school story about friendship, fame, and fair play.
26658-celebrated-travels-and-travellers-:
Jules Verne wrote this history of nineteenth-century exploration, translated by N. D'Anvers and published at London in 1881 by Sampson Low, Marston, Searle and Rivington. Fifty-one drawings by Léon Benett and fifty-seven facsimiles of early manuscripts and maps illustrate the volume. D'Anvers dedicates her translation to Dr. G. G. Gardiner and thanks Andrew Carter for tracing quotations.

Chapters follow Burckhardt, René Caillié, Denham and Clapperton, and other travellers through Egypt, Arabia, India, Africa, and beyond. Caillié's caravan of seventy persons and thirty-two camels leaves Gandiolle in February 1819 for the desert. Verne strings journals, maps, and portraits into a continuous story of a century that mapped the world's blank spaces.
26843-the-dope-on-mars:
Jack Sharkey wrote this diary of the first trip to Mars, illustrated by Wood. A writer narrator gets the job through his agent Louie, who wants the human slant rather than scientific reports, and advises him to keep a diary. Louie adds that if nothing happens, he should fake it, and the narrator answers that his diary is honest. Five people fly: a pilot, co-pilot Jones, navigator Lloyd Streeter, biochemist Dwight Kroger, and the writer himself.

The diary opens October 1, 1960, with a 260-day one-way trip planned from a date in the March 1959 New York Times. Kroger, old for the rigors of the journey but chosen for his skill over a greener man, tells jokes in the washroom while Streeter bends over his maps. On Mars the air is very cold, the sun burns hot, the sky shows blinding pink, and the sand runs rose-colored and smooth underfoot.
26853-vice-versa-or-a-lesson-to-fathers:
F. Anstey published this comic novel in June 1882, and the present John Murray impression carries it through many reprintings. A preface apologizes, after the fashion of a punctiliously polite Greek at a child's funeral, for offering a tale with the modest, frivolous aim of mere amusement. Anstey dedicates the little book particularly to the British paterfamilias, borrowing the form of words from a popular Anglo-Portuguese phrase-book.

Black Monday opens on a January evening in 1881, with Paul Bultitude, a Mincing Lane colonial produce merchant, sitting alone in his lofty dining-room at Westbourne Terrace. A grand transformation scene follows, and the father finds himself a minnow amongst tritons at his son's school, facing disgrace, learning and accomplishments, and a day of rest. Chapters run through an error of judgment, the Rubicon, hard pressure, a perfidious ally, and the reckoning.
26857-christopher-and-the-clockmakers:
Sara Ware Bassett published this boys' book with Little, Brown and Company of Boston in 1925, with pictures by William F. Stecher. It is dedicated to Richard Parsons, Simon Willard, and John Bailey. They were three conscientious craftsmen whose handiwork still cheers the author's home and testifies daily to their fidelity and skill. Its hero bears a tremendous name: Christopher Mark Antony Burton, the fourth of his line, christened so before he was an hour old.

Christopher's father also put five hundred dollars in the savings bank on the day of his birth, but counted the name the greater gift. Eighteen chapters mix the boy's adventures, from escaping being a hero to an encounter with the police, with the history of timekeeping. Clock giants, clocks on land and at sea, jewels that help tell time, clocks in America, and the romance of the watch all take their turn.
26941-wanted-7-fearless-engineers:
Warner Van Lorne's pulp science-fiction novella opens in a Depression-era park, where unemployed engineer Dick Barrow spots a strange newspaper ad. The ad seeks a brave young engineer willing to leave home for life, face danger, and master huge machines far from his own people.

Barrow answers and joins six other engineers on a journey to Yorpun, a hidden civilization far ahead of Earth in its machines. Each man takes charge of a domed city section, learning to run its systems while cut off from the world he left. The story turns on courage, teamwork, and what a man gives up for a grand task.
26974-prisoners-their-own-warders:
Major J. F. A. McNair's 1899 record describes the convict prison at Singapore, which ran from 1825 to 1873 in the Straits Settlements. McNair, a former colonial engineer and comptroller of Indian convicts, writes with W. D. Bayliss, a former superintendent of the prison.

The book explains its title system: trusted convicts served as their own warders, working as artificers and petty officers under British rule. It adds a shorter history of the convict stations at Bencoolen, Penang, and Malacca from 1797, with maps, muster lists, and firsthand detail on how the system ran.
27095-the-boy-ranchers-at-spur-creek-or-:
Willard F. Baker's The Boy Ranchers at Spur Creek, or Fighting the Sheep Herders, published in 1923, returns Bud and his cousins to the Diamond X country. Shots in the night and missing papers open the story, and the trail leads to Spur Creek and a campfire council.

The range war at the heart of the book pits cattlemen against sheep herders, with the frontispiece showing a snake caught on an animal's horn. Baker keeps the action brisk and the boys' code clear, in a series entry that mixes ranch work with a fight for the valley's future.
27112-children-s-books-and-their-illustr:
Gleeson White's Children's Books and Their Illustrators, a special winter number of The International Studio priced at fifty cents, surveys the art of the children's book. Its opening pages advertise Scribner's new books for the young, including Mrs. Burnett's juveniles with original illustrations by Reginald B. Birch.

Little Lord Fauntleroy, Sara Crewe, and Little Saint Elizabeth sit beside three new volumes by G. A. Henty, with tales of Frederick the Great and Wat Tyler's march on London. The number traces a hundred revivals of the applied arts into children's books worth keeping.
27153-spare-hours:
John Brown's Spare Hours, Horae Subsecivae, published in Boston in 1864, gathers essays by the Edinburgh doctor who wrote Rab and his Friends. Its epigraphs set the tone, including Pierce Egan's tale of a young ass that nibbled Cicero's Orations and ate nearly all the index of a folio Seneca.

Brown writes with humor and humanity on books, gardens, machinery, and the treatment of the illustrious dead by the quick. The volume collects the leisure-hour pieces of a physician essayist, warm, learned, and fond of dogs, friends, and old Edinburgh.
27317-the-cheerful-smugglers:
Ellis Parker Butler, author of Pigs is Pigs, published this comic novel with the Century Company in May 1908, with illustrations by May Wilson Preston. Its humor turns on the tariff: a family saves pennies in a pottery pig for baby Bobberts. The grown-ups scheme over boxes of bon-bons, trunks, and a pink shirt-waist that must somehow cross the customs line.

Chapters titled The Fenelby Tariff, Kitty's Trunks, The Amateur Detective, and Tariff Reform show how far the game goes, up to a small coup d'état. Butler keeps the tone light even as his characters dodge inspectors. The novel still amuses as a satire on taxes, rules, and otherwise respectable people breaking them.
27435-the-faith-of-our-fathers:
James Cardinal Gibbons, Archbishop of Baltimore, wrote this plain exposition and vindication of the Church founded by Jesus Christ. It came in a ninety-third carefully revised and enlarged edition from John Murphy Company in Baltimore in 1917. It is the classic American Catholic apologetic, written to explain the faith to neighbors and inquirers.

Chapters take up the Trinity and Incarnation, the unity, holiness, catholicity, and apostolicity of the Church, and its infallible authority. They also take up the Church and the Bible, the primacy and infallibility of the popes, saints, the Virgin Mary, purgatory, and civil and religious liberty. Gibbons answers charges of persecution, including the Spanish Inquisition, in a calm, direct voice.
27436-brand-blotters:
William MacLeod Raine, author of Wyoming and Bucky O'Connor, published this western novel with Grosset and Dunlap, from a 1909 Lippincott copyright, with illustrations by Clarence Rowe. Raine dedicates it to Frank N. Spindler, in memory of Sunday afternoon tramps on which they solved the problems of the nation.

Part one, Melissy of the Bar Double G, gives a crossed trail, brand blotting, an accusation, a man with a Chihuahua hat, a tenderfoot's claim, and the renewed Boone-Bellamy feud. Part two, Dead Man's Cache, adds a kidnapping, the real Bucky and the false, a photograph, and the taking of the cache. It is a brisk cattle-country tale of fraud, feud, and rescue.
27445-love-of-brothers:
Katharine Tynan, author of The Middle Years and Miss Gascoigne, published this Irish novel with Constable in London in 1919. Its chapters name the O'Garas of Castle Talbot, Patsy remembers, a tea party, Stella, and Brady's bull. They go on to Sir Shawn sees a ghost, mother-love, the old love, and, near the end, the lakh of rupees.

The story opens on a bright moonlit night, when small Patsy Kenny searches for a goat that has broken her tether. He was driven out by a fierce old grandfather with awful threats if he returns without her, his hot-potato meal still on the table. Family feeling, old wrongs, and a story finally told carry the novel. Tynan writes Irish domestic life with warmth and feeling.
27461-the-orchard-of-tears:
Sax Rohmer, author of Dr. Fu-Manchu, published this novel with Methuen in London, first issued in crown octavo in October 1918 and in cheap form in 1921. Rohmer dedicates it, as a loving cup, to the slaves of the pomegranate. They are Adam's sons and Eve's daughters, drinking at life's fountain, and the dedication hints at its mystical color.

The story moves in three parts: At Lower Charleswood, Flamby in London, and The Key. It opens at noon on a flawless summer day, with Paul Mario on a terrace above lawns, rose paths, and a river winding toward a distant town. A lark pours out its music overhead. Rohmer's romance blends English country life with an undercurrent of mystery.
27557-learning-to-fly-a-practical-manual:
Claude Grahame-White and Harry Harper wrote this practical manual for beginners, published by the Macmillan Company in New York and printed in England, fully illustrated. Its photographs come from the Grahame-White Flying School at the London Aerodrome, Hendon.

Chapters treat theories of tuition, temperament and the airman, and first experiences with an aeroplane, as described by Grahame-White himself. They go on to controlling latest-type craft, the stages of tuition, test flights, and perils of the air. Factors that make for safety, cross-country flying, and aviation as a profession close the book. A school machine well aloft fronts the volume.
27650-the-doers:
William John Hopkins wrote this children's book, with illustrations, published by Houghton Mifflin in Boston, New York, Chicago, Dallas, and San Francisco in 1914, as a school edition. Its stories name the workers a child watches: the digging-men, the mason, the carpenter, and the water-men.

Later stories bring the shingle and clapboard men, the plumber, the painter, the tree-men, and the pole-men, with clearing-up, setting-out, and moving-men stories. The book opens with a little boy, almost five, wandering in the garden and road near his house, with his cat, his cart, his shovel, and his hoe, always in overalls. One morning men arrive with a large cart and two horses, and stop in a field.
27718-parables-from-flowers:
Gertrude P. Dyer wrote these nine parables for children, each built around a flower and a virtue: the forget-me-not for fidelity, the snowdrop for faith, the foxgloves for gratitude. The book was published in Edinburgh by W. P. Nimmo, Hay, and Mitchell.

Each flower tells its own short story in the first person, drawing a moral lesson from its own habits and legends. Dedicated to three young friends, Mabel, Elsie, and Ruby Tarr, the collection belongs to the Victorian tradition of nature teaching used to shape children's character.
27785-a-book-about-lawyers:
John Cordy Jeaffreson, barrister-at-law, wrote this book about lawyers, reprinted from the London edition in New York by Carleton in 1875, with two volumes in one. Its contents range across houses and householders, loves of lawyers, money, costume, music, amateur theatricals, legal education, and mirth.

Chapters treat ladies in law colleges, fees to counsel, judicial corruption, wigs, bands and gowns, the piano in chambers, and wit in silk and ermine. Jeaffreson writes as an insider with anecdotes, and the book remains a rich social history of the English legal profession in its age.
27911-the-giraffe-hunters:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote The Giraffe Hunters, returning to Africa with the young hunters Hans and Hendrik von Bloom, Groot Willem, and Arend van Wyk, old friends from The Young Yagers. The party camps on the banks of the Limpopo around a hunter's fire, ringed by horses, dogs, and young men.

Hans hopes to extend his botanical researches between the Limpopo and Zambezi before visiting Europe, while Groot Willem seeks game he has not yet encountered. Reid mixes natural history with boyish adventure, and the book is a classic of Victorian hunting fiction for young readers.
27918-the-mines-and-its-wonders:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote The Mines and Its Wonders, opening on a summer evening in a village, where only women, girls, and children are seen, because every man and lad is below ground. Beyond green fields stands a black region of coal dust, tall chimneys, and steam engines.

Kingston explains the engines, shafts, galleries, ventilation, and wagons that lift coal and pump water, and the dangers miners face daily. The book teaches young readers how coal mining works and what it costs, with the vivid industrial scenery of Victorian England.
27958-in-convent-walls-the-story-of-the-:
Emily Sarah Holt wrote In Convent Walls, the story of the Despensers, continuing a tale begun in her earlier volume In All Time of Our Tribulation. That book closed with Isabelle of France at her most ambitious; this one shows nemesis falling on her and her chief partner in guilt.

Holt presents Isabelle as a woman given grand opportunities who chose self over God, inscribing her name on a black page of English history. The annals open in 1360 with Dame Cicely de Chaucombe, and the novel blends medieval history with Holt's earnest Protestant moral vision.
280-records-of-a-family-of-engineers:
Robert Louis Stevenson traces his family's engineering line from medieval Scotland to the lighthouses. Records of a Family of Engineers, from the 1912 Chatto and Windus edition, opens with the surname's spread from Forth to Clyde. Stevensons swore fealty in 1296 and rode through border wars.

Later chapters follow the engineers who built lights on wild Scottish coasts, Stevenson's own kin. The introduction weighs name, place, and trade with antiquarian care. Stevenson writes family history as adventure and duty. The book delights readers who know him only as a novelist. Stevenson's family pride shines through every chapter of the book.
28116-the-red-watch-with-the-first-canad:
Colonel J. A. Currie wrote The Red Watch in 1916 about the First Canadian Division in Flanders. Currie, a member of Parliament and colonel, served with the division and dedicates the book to Canadians who fell in Flanders. His verse preface praises men who barred the invader and held their trenches or fell.

The narrative follows Canadian soldiers in battle, in camp, and under fire, with Currie's own eye for ground and guns. Published in London and Toronto, the book gave home readers a soldier's report of Ypres and the salient. It remains a valued Canadian account of the First World War.
28198-a-budget-of-christmas-tales-by-cha:
A Budget of Christmas Tales, published in New York in 1895 by Louis Klopsch of the Christian Herald, gathers holiday stories by Charles Dickens and others. Dickens leads with A Christmas Carol and The Chimes, joined by The Christmas Goblin and The Poor Traveler. Margaret E. Sangster, Hezekiah Butterworth, Harriet Beecher Stowe, and Ella Wheeler Wilcox add tales of their own.

Other pieces cover a western Christmas, a Puritan tree, a princess, and a poor man's dinner, with songs and legends of the tree. The collection mixes ghosts, gifts, and family warmth in the style of the day. It offers a broad shelf of Victorian Christmas reading in one volume.
2823-the-fitz-boodle-papers:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote these Fitz Boodle papers, opening with a letter from George Fitz Boodle to Oliver Yorke at the Omnium Club, dated May 20, 1842. Fitz Boodle confesses himself considered a man of a certain sort, and his confessions follow.

Dorothea, Ottilia, and two professions give the papers their shape, mixing romance, satire, and self mockery. Thackeray writes as a young man of the world, amusing himself and his readers. The papers charm as an early showcase of the voice that would write Vanity Fair. Fitz-Boodle's confessions mix vanity with unexpected honesty.
2828-under-the-deodars:
Rudyard Kipling gathered eight stories of Anglo-Indian life in Under the Deodars, named for the Himalayan cedars of the hill stations. The Education of Otis Yeere, At the Pit's Mouth, A Wayside Comedy, The Hill of Illusion, and Only a Subaltern follow officers, wives, and officials through flirtation, failure, and small disasters. Kipling frames one tale as the history of a failure worth printing for younger readers.

The stories cut close, since reputation in a small station can be ruined by a glance or a careless word. Lovers bargain over trust, soldiers learn their limits, and a member of Parliament named Pagett gets his enlightenment. The collection shows Kipling's early mastery of the short, sharp society tale set against imperial India.
28288-vanished-towers-and-chimes-of-flan:
George Wharton Edwards wrote and pictured Vanished Towers and Chimes of Flanders, Philadelphia, 1916, as a record of Belgian towns before and during the First World War. Edwards visits Malines, Dixmude, Ypres, Commines, Bergues, Nieuport, Alost, Courtrai, Termonde, Louvain, Douai, Oudenaarde, and Furnes, noting towers, belfries, and carillons, many since destroyed.

His pictures show the Cloth Hall at Ypres, St. Rombauld at Malines, and belfries across Flanders, with a closing word on the Belgians. Edwards writes as an artist-traveller, fond of old streets and bells. The book preserves, in words and pictures, a Flanders the war was already erasing.
28298-cavalry-in-future-wars:
Lieutenant-General Frederick von Bernhardi wrote Cavalry in Future Wars, first published in 1906 and revised in 1909, on the place of horse soldiers in modern war. Bernhardi, commander of the Seventh Division of the German Army, argues for reforms in training, tactics, and equipment, and for a cavalry able to scout, fight, and pursue. Charles Sydney Goldman translated the book, with an introduction by Sir John French.

Bernhardi notes that none of his demands had yet been met, though his principles had won wide acceptance in the arm. The book shows German military thought just before the First World War, when cavalry still seemed vital. It serves historians of tactics and of 1914.
28389-goat-feathers:
Ellis Parker Butler's Goat-Feathers, published in 1919, is a humorous confession by a writer who keeps getting sidetracked. Butler jokes that he ought to earn as much as Robert W. Chambers and outshine George Ade and Mark Twain as a humorist, if only he did not keep gathering goat-feathers.

Goat-feathers, in his definition, are the side pursuits and stray interests that drag a man away from his work and hold back his success. Each one takes days or weeks to gather and proves about as useful as a stone-bruise. Butler tells his own fifty-year career of stray pursuits with cheerful self-mockery, and the book remains a funny warning against wasted time.
28391-true-to-his-colors:
Harry Castlemon, the pen name behind many boys' adventure series, published True to His Colors in 1889 as part of his War Series. The story opens at a military academy, where cousins quarrel over a flag. One boy refuses to let his family's flag be hauled down, while another demands the Stars and Bars in its place.

As the Civil War breaks, chapters follow a paid spy, a struggle on a tower, a committee at work, a call to arms, and a first company in action. Marcy changes his clothes, is forced into service, and turns privateersman. Castlemon writes brisk schoolboy adventure against a divided nation's loyalties, with the flag itself as the first battleground.
28413-the-student-s-companion-to-latin-a:
George Middleton's Student's Companion to Latin Authors, published by Macmillan in 1896, gives students a compact guide to Roman literature from its beginnings to the later empire. Its introduction promises a trustworthy book that supplies a real want for readers of Latin.

Four chapters cover early poets and prose writers, the Ciceronian age, the Augustan age, and post-Augustan writers. Livius Andronicus, Plautus, Cicero, Caesar, Catullus, Virgil, Horace, Ovid, Livy, Seneca, Tacitus, Juvenal, and Suetonius all receive entries. Appendices and indexes complete a handbook still useful for students finding their way through Latin authors.
28599-australian-writers:
Desmond Byrne's Australian Writers, published by Richard Bentley and Son of London in 1896, asks what marks the literature of a young country. Australia, self-governing in all but name and largely native-born in population, had grown fast in wealth and comfort. Byrne tests whether such a place could already show distinctive national traits in its books.

The essays treat Marcus Clarke, Henry Kingsley, Ada Cambridge, Adam Lindsay Gordon, Rolf Boldrewood, Mrs. Campbell Praed, and Tasma. Byrne weighs each writer against American and English examples, judging how far a new society speaks in its own voice. Readers get a pioneering survey of Australian letters in the 1890s.
28674-babylonian-and-assyrian-laws-contr:
C. H. W. Johns, a lecturer at Cambridge, wrote this 1904 study of ancient Mesopotamian law, published in New York. The book opens with the earliest Babylonian laws and the Code of Hammurabi. It then works through later law, courts and judges, crime, the family, marriage and divorce, inheritance, slavery, land tenure, and trade. A second half prints and explains letters from Hammurabi, Sennacherib, and other rulers and private writers.

Johns draws on clay tablets and inscriptions to show a working legal world, not just famous monuments: loans, leases, wages, pledges, and sales all appear as everyday business. The book suits readers of ancient history who want the substance of Babylonian and Assyrian law in English, with the sources laid out beside the argument.
28699-historic-ghosts-and-ghost-hunters:
H. Addington Bruce wrote this 1908 book about famous hauntings and the people who investigated them. Its chapters take up the devils of Loudun and the drummer of Tedworth. They also cover the haunting of the Wesley family, the visions of Emanuel Swedenborg, and the Cock Lane ghost. Further chapters treat a ghost seen by Lord Brougham, the seeress of Prevorst, and the medium Daniel Dunglas Home. A closing chapter compares ghost hunters of yesterday and today.

Bruce retells each case as history rather than horror, weighing testimony and asking what witnesses really saw. The Loudun chapter opens with a sleepy French town that was once busy with markets, churches, and a convent. Readers interested in psychical research get a fair-minded survey of its classic cases, written before modern debunking but with a reporter's care for evidence.
28713-beside-still-waters:
Arthur Christopher Benson wrote this 1910 memoir of a quiet life, in forty-two chapters that follow one man from childhood to old age. The book moves through family, school, Cambridge, practical work, resignation, and retirement, then through his father's friendship, his sister's death, and a long search for faith. Later chapters treat art, Platonism, sacrifice, and the renewal of youth, ending with a garden of God and the romance of life.

Benson, a fellow of Magdalene College, Cambridge, writes in a reflective, unhurried voice, valuing stillness over action. The memoir suits readers who like introspective writing about ordinary days, friendship, and belief. It is less a tale of events than a record of a mind growing clearer, and it rewards slow reading.
28767-the-defenders:
Philip K. Dick wrote this short story about a future war fought by machines while people live safely underground. Taylor, a technician who helps design the war's nerve center, enjoys his rest period at home, proud of the pounding his side's bombs are giving Moscow. His wife Mary tells him about the leadys, the robot soldiers shown to schoolchildren as proof of what their contributions buy.

The story's turn comes from what the machines are really doing while humans sit out the fighting. Dick uses a small domestic scene to ask a large question: what happens when weapons can think for themselves, and when a war no longer costs its makers anything. Short, tense, and ironic, it is an early sample of the themes that made Dick famous.
28804-oswald-bastable-and-others:
E. Nesbit wrote this collection of stories about Oswald Bastable and other children, reissued in 1960 by Ernest Benn in London and Coward-McCann in New York. The Bastable tales include an object of value and virtue, the runaways, the arsenicators, and the enchanted house. Other stories bring Molly, the measles, and the missing will, Billy and William, a twopenny spell, and the princess and the cat.

Charles E. Brock and H. R. Millar drew the pictures, including Oswald warning against breaking down a door while villains may return. Nesbit writes in the voice of a child narrator, funny, boastful, and warm. Readers who know The Railway Children and Five Children and It will find here more of her best work: clever children, small magic, and everyday adventure.
28853-the-children-s-book-of-stars:
G. E. Mitton wrote this 1907 children's book of stars, published by A. and C. Black in London, with twelve full-page pictures in color by John Williamson. Mitton, author of The Children's Book of London and Animal Autobiographies, tells star stories in a way meant to rivet attention. The frontispiece shows the moon-child who must keep running round her mother earth.

The book teaches the sky through stories rather than tables, giving young readers the moon, the planets, and the constellations as characters in a tale. Its historical sketches, the Scotsman was quoted as saying, leave lasting impressions useful when studies grow more advanced. Readers get a gentle Edwardian introduction to astronomy, written for children who look up and wonder.
28860-the-memoirs-correspondence-and-mis:
David Widger edited this index to the papers of Thomas Jefferson, as collected by Thomas Jefferson Randolph in 1829. The index covers four volumes of memoirs, correspondence, and miscellanies, beginning with Jefferson's handwritten draft of the Declaration of Independence. Volume one lists his memoir with appendices on coinage, crimes and punishment, and his 1774 instructions to Virginia's delegation.

The correspondence runs from a 1775 letter to Dr. William Small through letters to John Randolph, Benjamin Franklin, Patrick Henry, and George Washington. The index lets a reader trace Jefferson's thought letter by letter across the Revolution and the early republic. It is a finding aid for one of America's great documentary collections, useful to anyone studying Jefferson in his own words.
28903-all-that-matters:
Edgar A. Guest wrote this 1922 book of poems, All That Matters, published by Reilly and Lee in Chicago, with pictures by W. T. Benda, F. X. Leyendecker, and others. The index lists poems on home and family life: All That Matters, A Boy and His Dad, The Boy's Ideal, Bread and Gravy, The Common Touch, and The Family Doctor. Other pieces treat mothers and babies, old-fashioned letters, and the grate fire.

Guest, America's most popular newspaper poet, writes in plain, rhyming verse about work, kindness, and the home. His poems speak of dads and lads, neighbors and mothers, in language any reader can follow. Readers get a representative Guest collection, warm and sentimental, from a poet whose verses hung in kitchens across the country.
2902-studies-and-essays-concerning-lette:
John Galsworthy collected his essays on writing in Studies and Essays Concerning Letters, opening with a warning from Anatole France that excess is always an evil. The contents include A Novelist's Allegory, Some Platitudes Concerning Drama, Meditation on Finality, and Wanted: Schooling. The allegory begins on a late autumn evening, with a prince riding through dusk streets on an amber-colored steed.

Galsworthy compares dramas to trees, springing from seedlings, shaping themselves by hidden laws, and growing until warped by the forces around them. The essays argue for restraint, form, and patience in fiction and theatre. They still appeal to readers interested in how a working novelist thought about his craft.
2903-studies-and-essays-the-inn-of-tranq:
John Galsworthy's Inn of Tranquillity and Other essays collect travel sketches and meditations on country life. The title piece finds a pink house on an Odyssean coast, bearing the sign Osteria di Tranquillita, among pines, junipers, cypresses, and olives above the waves. The travelers stop partly for the name and partly from surprise at finding any house in those goat-haunted groves.

Other essays follow sheep-shearing, riding in mist, and a magpie over the hill, with scenes where mist thickens to rain-dust and trees seem to lose one another. Black pigs scuttle past a farmhouse and vanish into white air. The book shows Galsworthy's quieter voice, attentive to light, weather, and the small peace of a remote place.
2904-studies-and-essays-quality-and-othe:
John Galsworthy gathered life essays in Studies and Essays: Quality and Others, again under Anatole France's warning that excess is always an evil. The title essay recalls a bootmaker known since the author's youth, who worked with his elder brother in two little shops let into one in a fashionable by-street. Quality, for Galsworthy, lives in work done slowly and well.

Other essays take up the grand jury, threshing, an old-time place, romance, memories, and felicity. One passage protests a woman dying at thirty of a creeping malady she might have checked, had she not spent herself on children and husband. The book rewards readers who enjoy Galsworthy the essayist, humane, observant, and quietly angry at waste.
29054-orthodoxy-its-truths-and-errors:
James Freeman Clarke wrote Orthodoxy: Its Truths and Errors, in a fourteenth edition published in Boston in 1880 by the American Unitarian Association.
