Clarke opens with Latin mottoes from Seneca and Thomas Burnet, and a preface that frames his aim: to find substantial truth and formal error in every great doctrinal system. The contents run through eleven chapters and many sections.

Early chapters define orthodoxy as right belief, as the doctrine of the majority, and as the oldest doctrine, raising objections to each. Later chapters treat natural and revealed religion, and the orthodox and liberal parties in New England. Readers get a liberal theologian's fair-minded survey, written to seek truth rather than to win a party fight.
29162-the-traitors:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published this novel in 1902, first issued in book form in New York in 1903 by Dodd, Mead and Company. Oppenheim, author of A Millionaire of Yesterday and The World's Great Snare, was already a popular writer of intrigue. The frontispiece shows a dramatic moment: Marie shoots a man through the heart.

The Traitors belongs to Oppenheim's world of secret dealings, betrayal, and high-stakes plotting, where loyalty is tested and a single shot can settle an account. The novel's chapters carry the reader through its web of conspiracy. Readers get an early Edwardian thriller, brisk and melodramatic, from a writer who made the intrigue novel his own.
29195-it-s-all-yours:
Sam Merwin Jr. wrote this science fiction story about a dying Earth ruled by a Chancellor named Bliss. Human life, the story says, is failing: where it spawns, it spawns monsters. Bliss, suspecting he may be a humanistic old fool, still clings to his duty in a world grown sick and strange.

The tale opens in luxury, in a washroom of black porcelain and gold, with mermaid faucets and a shower-steam room of every beneficial ray. That comfort only sharpens the ruin outside it. Merwin asks what rule means when there is almost nothing left to rule. Readers get a bitter, vivid portrait of a last ruler on a deformed world.
29252-war-taxation-some-comments-and-let:
Otto H. Kahn published this pamphlet on war taxation in 1917, gathering his comments with letters from readers. Kahn's original comments warned that if Canada kept low or no income taxes while America set oppressively high rates, capital would flow north and enterprising men would follow it. Readers wrote in, and Kahn answered their points.

Contents divide into comments, then letters on the income tax and on returns from taxable and tax-exempt securities. Kahn, a leading banker, argues as a financier worried about war finance driving wealth away. Readers get a contemporary debate on paying for war, in the voice of a man who believed high taxes could cost America more than they raised.
29291-the-pirate-and-the-three-cutters:
Captain Frederick Marryat wrote these two sea tales, published by Macmillan in 1897 with illustrations by Edmund J. Sullivan and an introduction by David Hannay. The Pirate opens in the Bay of Biscay and follows the Bachelor through a gale, a leak, and Sleeper's Bay to attack, capture, a sand-bank, escape, and a trial at the Caicos.

The Three Cutters follows three cutters in turn, from Portland Bill through chases and encounters at sea. Marryat, himself a naval officer, writes with a sailor's knowledge of ships and crews. Readers get two brisk nautical stories from a master of the sea tale, full of weather, seamanship, and the rough justice of the age of sail.
29405-the-gods-of-mars:
Edgar Rice Burroughs, author of Tarzan of the Apes and A Princess of Mars, sent John Carter back to Barsoom in this 1918 sequel, published by Grosset and Dunlap. Carter returns to a Mars of plant men, forest battles, chambers of mystery, black pirates, and the depths of Omean. At its heart stands Issus, Goddess of Life Eternal, whose cult hides a grim secret beneath its promise of paradise.

Chapters race through prison isles, doomed flights, death sentences, and breaks for liberty, with Thuvia and a fair goddess among Carter's allies. Burroughs writes at full pulp speed, with swordplay and wonder on every page. Fans of planetary romance will find one of the Barsoom tales at its most colorful and breathless.
29446-beside-still-waters:
Robert Sheckley's gentle tale follows Mark Rogers, a prospector who sought the solitude of deep space and found it on a half-mile-thick slab of rock. Rogers had hunted radioactives and rare metals across the asteroid belt for years, finding little, hopping from fragment to fragment. At last he settled where the air pump labored to turn rock oxygen into breathable air, and the air seeped in slowly.

His company on that lonely rock is Charles the Robot, and Sheckley plays their quiet life for warmth and wry humor. Getting away from it all, the tale suggests, means more than distance: it means choosing what, and whom, to keep. Fans of Sheckley will enjoy a soft, funny story about solitude, friendship, and a man born old.
29502-little-masterpieces-of-science-exp:
George Iles edited this 1902 volume of Little Masterpieces of Science for Doubleday, Page, gathering first-hand tales of exploration. Columbus, Lewis and Clarke, Zebulon M. Pike, Charles Wilkes, Clarence King, and John Wesley Powell stand among the explorers whose words fill the book. Justin Winsor's account of Columbus opens the set, from Palos on August 3, 1492, through a mishap to the Pinta, the Peak of Teneriffe in eruption, and the Canaries.

Each piece is chosen for vivid, plain narration: deep snow, hard journeys, friendly Indians and whites, and provisions at exorbitant prices. The aim is science made readable, through the voices of those who saw it. Readers of exploration history will find a compact, well-chosen anthology of discovery in the explorers' own words.
29720-hall-of-mirrors:
Fredric Brown builds this short tale on a single dread choice, stated in its epigraph. It asks whether a man would give up his life so he could live it over again. The tale opens in bright sun, in a patio at Beverly Hills, where a man sits in a canvas chair talking to Barbara, his fiancee, in a swim suit. Then sudden dark falls in the middle of the afternoon.

He finds himself standing, naked, in a closet about four feet square. A door leads to a lighted room he has never seen, with furniture of a strange style. Brown tells it all in the second person, so the reader feels each groping step. The tale is short, tense, and strange, and it ends on the choice its first lines pose.
29726-the-strollers:
Frederic S. Isham published this novel in Indianapolis in 1902, with pictures by Harrison Fisher. A prologue, The Marquis' Honeymoon, opens a tale in three books. Book one, On the Circuit in the Wilderness, follows travellers, a chariot, a manor attack, and a council at the town pump. Book two, Destiny and the Marionettes, moves to the races, Lear and Juliet, and a debut in the Crescent City.

Book three, The Final Cue, brings the threads home through garret and garden, a lawyer's tidings, and a meeting on the mount. The strollers of the title are travelling players, and the marquis threads their world. Isham writes with color and high spirits. The book is a full romance of the road, the stage, and old Southern life.
29749-the-flying-cuspidors:
V. R. Francis wrote this comic science fiction tale for Fantastic Universe, where the author had sold work at twenty-one. Its hero is Hotlips Grogan, a trumpet player in the fiscal year of 2056. The narrator, Eddie, plays piano for the band and calls Grogan the gonest trumpet-tooter this side of Alpha Centauri. On a clear day Grogan plays notes no one can hear without special gear.

One night Grogan plays strictly in three or four wrong keys, and Eddie knows love is the cause. A trumpet-tooter in love, the headnote says, is a wonderful sight, and worse when extraterrestrials get mixed in. Francis keeps the slang fast and the joke broad. The tale is a light, musical farce set among future bands and alien listeners.
29812-the-little-nightcap-letters:
Aunt Fanny, whose real name was Fanny Barrow, printed The Little Nightcap Letters in New York in 1869. The book was entered for copyright in 1860, and it is lovingly dedicated to her daughter, Little Alice. A front picture shows children coaxing Mr. Appleton to tell where Aunt Fanny lived. The letters that follow are written for children at bedtime.

Nightcap Letter Number 2 from Aunt Fanny opens the book, with a lady visitor and a dear little girl named Kitty, blue-eyed and brown-curled. An introduction to Bella's letters, an account of how the nightcap letters came to be written, and letters from Charleston follow. The Return closes the set. The book is a gentle, epistolary volume for young readers.
29915-about-sugar-buying-for-jobbers:
B. W. Dyer wrote this booklet for jobbers who sell sugar, printed by Lamborn and Company of New York in 1921. Its subtitle promises a plain account of how a jobber can lessen business risks by trading in refined sugar futures. The booklet is short, simplified, and non-technical, meant for men who know exchange work in general but not this new market.

Trading in refined sugar futures had just begun on the New York Coffee and Sugar Exchange. Dyer argues that men who once dealt in raw sugar as a guard for refined needs should now trade refined sugar direct. His opening image is Time, the croupier of business, dealing floods, wars, drought, great crops, and fair weather alike. The booklet is a clear, period guide to hedging a grocer's risk.
29958-the-law-breakers:
Ridgwell Cullum published The Law-Breakers in New York in 1914, with a frontispiece in color. Cullum was known for The Story of the Foss River Ranch and The Way of the Strong. The tale opens watching the line at White Point, with a hold-up and a scene at the foot of an aged pine. Bound for the southern trail, the man-hunters and Charlie Bryant enter a hard country of pursuit.

The soul-savers, a stray-hunter, and the brothers follow, with the discomfiture of Helen and the house of Dirty O'Brien. Adventures in the night, Bill peeping under the surface, and Bill's three discoveries lead to the far reaches. Word from headquarters, storm clouds, and the broken chain shape the close, with a hidden corral and a wager. Cullum writes a brisk western of law, love, and the men who break both.
30075-our-next-door-neighbors:
Belle K. Maniates writes a light domestic comedy about a narrator, Silvia, and the neighbors next door, with pictures by Tony Sarg. Polydores pester the household, boarders move in, a vacation is taken, and a flirt meets a woman-hater in turn. Ptolemy disappears, the narrator visits a haunted house, ghosts are seen, discoveries are made, and Uncle Issachar arrives to stir the pot further.

Little, Brown published the Boston volume in February 1917, and its twenty chapters move by small, funny crises rather than one grand plot. Letters, a midnight excursion, a reporter's friend, and money earned for the household all feed the fun. Readers who like period humor about houses, kin, and nosy neighbors will find the book easy, warm, and full of cheerful incident.
30138-the-seiners:
James B. Connolly follows a Gloucester seining fleet through a season of mackerel fishing, from the launch of a new vessel to the race home with a full catch. Minnie Arkell, Little Johnnie Duncan, Maurice Blake, and Clancy work the docks and the decks. The fleet puts out to sea, loses a seine, runs to harbor in a breeze, and tries night seining. A brush with the yachting fleet and trouble with Dominion cutters test the crews.

Copyright in 1904 by Charles Scribner's Sons, the novel draws its force from work detail. It shows how a school of fish is found, circled, and brought aboard, and how gossip on shore shapes life at sea. Connolly, author of earlier Gloucester tales, writes the fishermen in their own plain speech. The book stands as both an adventure story and a record of a vanished trade.
30143-out-on-the-pampas-or-the-young-set:
G. A. Henty sends the Hardy family out to settle on the South American pampas, where a new home must be built, cattle must be found, and neighbors must be won over. Chapters follow the start, the first farm work, visits and advice, lost cattle, and quiet times, while Seth tells a tale of the Mexican war to fill long evenings. A fight with a puma, shown in the front pictures, gives the young settlers their sharpest test.

Zwecker drew the illustrations for the London volume, and Henty writes for young readers who like plain adventure mixed with useful fact. Grassland, horses, and farm craft fill the pages, but courage and steady work matter most, as the family learns to live far from town. The book stands as a classic boys' tale of emigration, hardship, and a home made by hand.
30173-saint-ursula-i-the-story-of-st-urs:
John Ruskin retells the legend of St. Ursula in two short pieces, rescued from his letters in Fors Clavigera for a small Devin-Adair booklet in 1912. The story opens with Maurus, a just Christian king of Britain, and his wife Daria, whose daughter is born wrapped in a hairy mantle and famed as the fairest creature on earth. Ursula and her legions face death for a noble cause, and the tale honors holy living and unselfish dedication.

A second piece, the Dream of St. Ursula, takes its image from a painting by Carpaccio, shown as the frontispiece. The preface, signed by an Ursuline of New Orleans, presents the booklet to clients of the Celestial Lily, as Mother Church names the martyr. Short, devout, and lyrical, the pair suits readers who like medieval legend told in Ruskin's rich, earnest voice.
3020-table-talk-essays-on-men-and-manner:
William Hazlitt collected Table-Talk: Essays on Men and Manners as familiar essays on painting, genius, common sense, and human nature. Volume one includes On the Pleasure of Painting, On Genius and Common Sense, Character of Cobbett, On People with One Idea, On the Ignorance of the Learned, and The Indian Jugglers. Volume two adds a Poussin landscape, Milton's sonnets, going a journey, and coffee-house talk.

Hazlitt's prose turns on worldlings who cannot bear to fritter wealth away in charity, since it would no longer peer in monumental pomp over other men's heads. Even on the point of death, they call such giving madness, waste, and impiety. The essays remain a model of the familiar style, argumentative, personal, and quotable on nearly every page.
30238-the-claims-of-labour-an-essay-on-t:
An 1845 essay on the duties of employers to the employed argues that duty to the public outweighs mere self-preservation, in a second edition from William Pickering in London. Its epigraph, drawn from Bacon, sets out a double nature of good. Good in a thing itself counts less than good as part of a greater body, since the latter guards a more general form. Iron turning from loadstone to earth, the passage says, mirrors a patriot turning to his country.

A second essay added to the volume treats practical means of improving the health and increasing the comfort of the labouring classes. Together, the two pieces blend moral argument with reform proposals, aimed at employers who held power over workers' lives. Readers of Victorian social thought will find here an early, earnest case for employer duty as public duty.
30263-a-captain-in-the-ranks-a-romance-o:
George Cary Eggleston tells a romance of affairs in A Captain in the Ranks, published by A. L. Burt in New York in 1904, under a copyright by A. S. Barnes and Company. A final fight opens, with a hero alone in a high mountain and a new birth of manhood. He becomes a private in the army of work and then a captain in that same army. The sizing up of Guilford Duncan, duty, one night's work, and an alliance offensive and defensive follow.

Barbara Verne enters with a battle and an acquaintance, a social advance, and her coming out, while a new enemy, an old friend, and Dick Temple's plans and story widen the plot. An illustration promises the climax in plain words: you have saved the railroad. Eggleston, author of Dorothy South and Running the River, writes business and love with brisk, popular energy.
3028-the-peterkin-papers:
Lucretia Hale wrote The Peterkin Papers as family comedies about the literal-minded Peterkins, first told to the daughter of the lady from Philadelphia. The first story was accepted for Young Folks, the tales continued in St. Nicholas, and a second edition added The Peterkins at the Farm. Mrs. Peterkin puts salt in her coffee in the opening tale, and the family solves each small crisis with elaborate logic.

A Fourth of July passage has the family driven from sleep by crowing cocks, braying donkeys, horns, cheers, torpedoes, and Chinese crackers from the Antiques and Horribles. In despair of sleep they come down to breakfast. The papers remain a beloved American children's classic, gentle in humor and exact in its portrait of a family that reasons itself into trouble.
30325-the-elements-of-drawing-in-three-l:
John Ruskin teaches drawing in three letters to beginners, in a Library Edition volume of his complete works from the National Library Association. Letter 1 covers first practice, letter 2 sketching from nature, and letter 3 color and composition, with appendices on illustrative notes and things to be studied. Ruskin wrote the work in the winter of 1856, and a first edition followed in 1857, with a second the same year carrying additions and slight alterations.

A third edition ran through its sixth thousand in 1859, seventh in 1860, and eighth in 1861, and part of the work later appeared in Our Sketching Club by St. John Tyrwhitt in 1874. Ruskin writes as a teacher who believes close looking comes before fine finish, and his letters move from simple exercises to nature and color in clear, firm steps. Beginners still find the book direct, demanding, and practical.
30453-the-boy-scout-fire-fighters:
Irving Crump follows Quarry Troop Number One in a 1917 Boy Scout adventure built around fire work, rescue, and friendly contests. Jiminy Gordon opens the book breathless from running up Otter Creek Hill after a hay barn fire. He joins Bruce Clifford, leader of the Owl Patrol, at headquarters.

Sixteen chapters move from a motorcycle fire brigade and a firemen's tournament to a circus visit and movie making. Later scenes add a prize contest, a beach patrol, a big race, a narrow escape, and a Christmas close. Crump stresses resourcefulness, courage, and teamwork, with scouts learning to act fast, help neighbors, and earn trust. The tone stays brisk and wholesome throughout.
30606-the-landleaguers:
Anthony Trollope's The Landleaguers opens with his biography. At nineteen in 1834 he joined the British postal service as a junior clerk, struggled with superiors, and in 1841 took an Irish inspector post for ten years.

In Ireland his civil service career flourished and he began writing novels, several early ones set there, including The Macdermots of Ballycloran and Castle Richmond. Readers see his affection for the Irish people, especially the poor. By 1882 Ireland faced boycotts and near breakdown of law and order, and in May Lord Frederick Cavendish, new chief secretary, entered that crisis. Trollope's novel draws on that turmoil.
30682-buxton-and-its-medicinal-waters:
Robert Ottiwell Gifford-Bennet, senior acting physician to the Devonshire Hospital and Buxton Bath Charity, writes Buxton and Its Medicinal Waters, transcribed from the 1892 John Heywood edition. Gifford-Bennet knows from long experience the powerful action of Buxton medicinal thermal water on the human system.

He also knows the poor results from indiscriminate and incautious use, whether in baths or taken internally. In brief, practical pages, he offers suggestions for professional brethren who have had no chance to know the Buxton Spa firsthand. Written from Tankerville House, Buxton, in May 1892, the book guides doctors on safe, useful use of the waters.
30745-calamities-and-quarrels-of-authors:
Isaac Disraeli wrote this book on the hard lot of writers, held here in a new edition edited by his son, the Earl of Beaconsfield, and published by Frederick Warne in London. Its first part, Calamities of Authors, opens with authors by profession, including Guthrie, Amhurst, Drake, and Smollett, and a stated case for literary property. Later pieces cover the sufferings of authors, a mendicant author, and Cowley's melancholy.

Other chapters weigh bad temper in criticism, fastidious egotism, disappointed genius, the maladies of authors, and the despair of young poets. Disraeli writes with wit and sympathy, drawing on lives from earlier English letters. The book remains a lively, if old-fashioned, guide to why writing, for all its glamour, has so often meant poverty, quarrels, and wounded pride.
30749-ringan-gilhaize-or-the-covenanters:
John Galt wrote this Scottish novel about the Covenanters, with an introduction by Sir George Douglas in the 1899 edition held here. Its hero, Ringan Gilhaize, lives through a time when Scots who held to their own form of worship faced harsh rule and harsh punishment. The opening lines praise those who stayed firm in torture and in death, and the editor calls the book a work long passed over.

The tale follows Ringan through faith, conflict, and loss in seventeenth-century Scotland, where church and crown pull in hard opposite ways. Galt writes in Scots voice and dialect at times, and the story leans on old tales of steadfast men and women. For readers today it offers both a plain adventure and a window on why the Covenanters still hold a strong place in Scottish memory.
30778-rhymes-and-meters-a-practical-manu:
Horatio Winslow wrote this practical manual for verse writers, with a 1906 copyright and a 1909 printing by the Editor Publishing Company of Deposit, New York. Winslow says verse making needs no defense, since well known English writers have practiced it, and since it sharpens prose and opens the greatest literature. Courses in poetics at large universities, he notes, show how strong the interest had grown in America.

Twelve chapters move from verse making in general through meter, rhyme, stanza forms, and subtleties of versification, then to the quatrain, sonnet, ballade, song, and modern verse types. A closing part covers verse translation, reading aloud, hints for beginners, the verse market, and books to read. It is a plain, useful guide for anyone who wants to try writing poems well.
30797-the-thirst-quenchers:
This September 1963 Analog story by Rick Raphael turns on fresh water running short in a world full of salt water. Earth has more water surface than land, the story notes, yet America already presses the limits of its fresh supply. Two men of the Division of Agriculture, Troy Braden and Alec Patterson, ski through heavy snow in the Sawtooth Mountain range.

Above the timberline the full storm will hit them, and their talk turns to work that has stayed dependable while the world left the steel age behind for nuclear power. Raphael uses a cold, practical job in the mountains to frame a larger question: how a thirsty society finds, keeps, and shares clean water. It is a grounded tale of engineers, weather, and a resource we too often take for granted.
30804-applied-design-for-printers:
Harry Lawrence Gage wrote this 1920 handbook for printers, number forty-three in the Typographic Technical Series for Apprentices, published by the Committee on Education of the United Typothetae of America. Its full title promises the principles of arrangement, with brief comment on the periods of design that most strongly influenced printing. Gage writes for apprentices who must make printed work both useful and pleasing.

Contents move from an introduction and the surface through materials and qualities of design to proportion, balance, symmetry, variety, motion, and ornament. A later section treats the periods of design that most affected printing, with supplementary reading, review questions, and a glossary at the end. It is a clear, practical guide to layout, still useful for students of typography and book design.
3092-the-conquest-of-new-france-a-chroni:
George M. Wrong recounts how France lost North America to Britain. This 1918 volume belongs to the Chronicles of America series from Yale University Press. It covers the long colonial wars of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Quebec, Boston, Acadia, and Louisbourg are its main prizes.

Wrong moves chapter by chapter through Frontenac and Phips, the Ohio Valley fight, and the expulsion from Acadia. He writes a compact narrative history, not a source collection. General readers get the whole contest in one clear sweep, from coastal raids to a continent changing hands.
30988-the-junkmakers:
Albert Teichner wrote this science fiction story, printed in If: Worlds of Science Fiction in July 1961. Its tagline introduces Eric, the best robot they ever had, perfectly trained, ever thoughtful, and a joy to own, whom naturally they had to destroy. The story's hero is Wendell Hart, who drifted slowly rather than plunged into the underground movement called the Savers' Conspiracy.

Hart's awakening came a few short weeks before the Great Ritual Sacrifice, held only once a decade, on the great High Holy Day. For days before it, joyous throngs assemble old worn vehicles, machine tools, and computers in public squares, crowning proudly each pile with used, disconnected robots. In the evening, families proudly make private heaps on their lawns, traditionally of household utensils, heaters, air conditioners, and the family servant. It is a dark satire on a society that destroys its machines.
31045-frondes-agrestes-readings-in-moder:
Held here is Frondes Agrestes, readings in Modern Painters, chosen at her pleasure by the author's friend, the younger lady of the Thwaite, Coniston. It was published in London by George Allen in 1902, in its thirty-eighth thousand. The preface explains why the readings exist at all.

The author says he has often been asked to republish the first book the public noticed, which remains their favourite, in a more attainable form. He is resolved never to republish it as a whole, since some parts are rendered unnecessary by the established fame of Turner. Others praise excellence the public will never give the labour to discern. His friend, in advanced age retaining the cheerfulness of bright youth, had copied out many passages. He asked her to add to her own chosen passages, for readers who would enjoy his early writings. It is a selection from a work on art.
31048-a-battery-at-close-quarters:
Henry M. Neil, captain of the Twenty-second Ohio Battery, wrote this paper on a battery at close quarters. It was read before the Ohio Commandery of the Loyal Legion on October 6, 1909, and published by the Champlin Press in Columbus, Ohio, in 1909. Its subtitle gives its subject: the story of the Eleventh Ohio Battery at Iuka and Corinth.

Neil opens with Civil War artillery projectiles, divided by structure into solid, hollow, and case shot. Solid shot battered down walls or heavy obstructions, while hollow shell and shrapnel struck animate objects, set fire to buildings, and destroyed lighter obstructions. Case shot meant grape and canister, though grape is no longer used, having been superseded by the machine gun. Canister, a sheet iron case filled with bullets, works only at very short ranges. It is a vivid artillery memoir.
311-bunner-sisters:
Two sisters keep a tiny shop near Stuyvesant Square in old New York. Edith Wharton's Bunner Sisters, serialized in Scribner's in late 1916, follows Ann Eliza and Evelina through a shabby basement store. Their sign reads simply Bunner Sisters in blotchy gold.

Customers know the shop's local fame, though strangers cannot guess its trade. A clock, a lover, and a slow decline test the sisters' bond. Wharton writes poverty and devotion without sentimentality. The novella ranks among her most quietly moving works. Wharton wrote the sisters' tragedy from her own New York memories.
31123-the-observers:
G. L. Vandenburg's short science fiction tale of security and suspicion is set at Fort Dickson, home of the Army Weapons Development Center. George Fisher, a shy, diligent, trustworthy laboratory technician with no ambition beyond assisting the brains, turns up dead, and the coroner calls it suicide, to his superiors' quick relief.

Harry Payne, the civilian personnel director, must now find a replacement, starting with Fisher's file and his muddled secretary, Miss Conway. Behind the guarded fences, a new bomb may be taking shape, but Payne cares only about people. The story turns on who can be trusted when everyone after a key job seems to be hiding something.
31130-boys-book-of-frontier-fighters:
Edwin L. Sabin's 1919 book for boys retells frontier fights from 1676 into the 1860s in short, stirring chapters. Captain Church captures old chief Annawan, Major McColloch makes his great leap at Wheeling, and Betty Zane runs the powder exploit at Bryant's Station. John Colter races the Blackfeet, Hugh Glass meets the grizzly bear, and Kit Carson's couriers slip through enemy lines.

Each chapter centers on one deed of nerve or endurance, told in plain, fast-moving prose for young readers. The volume, with Custer's Last Stand as its frontispiece, belongs to an era of heroic frontier storytelling. It still reads as a lively introduction to the men and women of the American borderlands.
31133-home-life-of-great-authors:
Hattie Tyng Griswold's Home Life of Great Authors, in a seventh edition from A. C. McClurg of Chicago in 1902, sketches the private lives of famous writers for busy readers. Her preface states the aim plainly: not criticism or complete biography, but the home life commonly neglected in popular biographies, rewritten for people with little time to read.

Sketches run from Goethe, Burns, Madame de Staël, Wordsworth, and De Quincey through Scott, Lamb, Byron, Shelley, and Irving. They go on to Emerson, Hugo, George Sand, Macaulay, Tennyson, Hawthorne, Longfellow, the Brontës, Poe, Thackeray, Dickens, George Eliot, and Ruskin. Warm and anecdotal, the book lets readers meet great authors at home.
31229-pot-boilers:
Clive Bell's Pot-Boilers, published by Chatto and Windus in London in 1918, collects essays and reviews written to keep the pot boiling. Its contents run from Montaigne in facsimile, Ibsen, Miss Coleridge, Peacock, Boswell's letters, and Carlyle's loves and love-letters. They go on through the Lysistrata, Trelawny's letters, Sophocles in London, William Morris, and Persian miniatures.

Picture shows follow, on the London Salon, English post-impressionists, an expensive masterpiece, Marchand, and the Mansard Gallery, closing with contemporary art in England, art and war, and before the war. Bell's opening essay treats a facsimile Montaigne as a bibliophilic rather than literary event, setting the collection's witty, connoisseur tone.
31238-noah-webster-american-men-of-lette:
Horace E. Scudder's life of Noah Webster, in the American Men of Letters series edited by Charles Dudley Warner, was published by Houghton, Mifflin in 1890 with copyright dated 1881. It follows the lexicographer in eight chapters. It opens in West Hartford, a village of crossroads and slow change, much as it stood in 1758 when Webster was born.

Later chapters take up the Grammatical Institute, Webster as author and publisher, his political writings, excursions, preparations for the dictionary, and An American Dictionary of the English Language itself. Drawing on Gordon L. Ford's collection of Webster material, Scudder gives a compact, readable life of the man who defined American English.
31259-the-boy-with-the-u-s-life-savers:
Francis Rolt-Wheeler's 1915 boys' book, published by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard in Boston as part of the U. S. Service Series, tells the work of the Life-Savers in twelve chapters with forty-eight illustrations, nearly all from photographs lent by government bureaus. Its frontispiece shows a Coast Guard patrol burning the Coston light to signal a wrecked vessel that help is at hand.

Chapters follow a rescue by moonlight, lights that never sleep, heroes of the underground, snatching from frozen death, rescue by breeches-buoy, and a blazon of flame at sea. They go on to reindeer to the rescue, a volcano's death, defying the tempest, adrift on a derelict, wreckers of the Spanish Main, and the graveyard of the deep. Stirring and factual, the book honors the surfmen who risked all for strangers.
31313-the-forerunners:
Romain Rolland's Forerunners, translated by Eden and Cedar Paul and published by Harcourt, Brace and Howe in New York in 1920, gathers writings for an international. Dedicated to the martyrs of the new faith: Jean Jaurès, Karl Liebknecht, Rosa Luxemburg, Kurt Eisner, and Gustav Landauer. Victims of bloodthirsty stupidity and murderous falsehood, they liberated the men who killed them.

Twenty-six pieces follow, from Ara Pacis, an upward winding road, addresses to murdered peoples, the undying Antigone, freedom, and free Russia the liberator. Tolstoy the free spirit, letters to and from Maxim Gorki, and free voices from America follow. Next come young Switzerland, under fire, two Ave Caesar pieces, men in battle, a great European in G. F. Nicolai, an international of the mind, a call to Europeans, an open letter to President Wilson, and a declaration of the independence of the mind. The book is Rolland's conscience in full.
31343-the-invaders:
Murray Leinster's science-fiction novel The Invaders opens at Ardea, a village north of Salonika in rugged northern Greece, where Coburn is making a survey and struggling to start his car. A villager's shrill, panicked yell breaks the morning quiet, and from there the story races through revolution and an invasion from outer space, as the book's own headnote promises. Coburn is buried, in its phrase, to his ears in assorted adventures.

Leinster, praised in that headnote as a master storyteller, keeps the action swashbuckling and fast, with vivid characters and a weird mystery at the center. The novel mixes a Greek setting with alien invasion, a combination that gives the familiar invasion plot a fresh stage. It is pulp adventure at full speed, written to entertain rather than to pause for science.
31356-the-man-who-staked-the-stars:
Charles Dye's science-fiction story The Man Who Staked the Stars was printed in Planet Stories in July 1952. It centers on Bryce Carter, a man risen from Thieves Row to director of the famed U.T. Earth, Moon, and the Belt await his command for a grand coup. His cousin from Montehedo, presented in the story's headnote as star-sent help, arrives at a moment of high ambition. The tale opens aboard an Earth-Moon liner, where a young man tells Donahue he is a witch doctor.

That young man, registered as a psychotherapist, explains that witch doctoring ran in his family, through his grandfather and his father's father, and that he learned a special teaching. Dye mixes space opera with questions of belief, inheritance, and power, as Carter's scheme meets a stranger whose craft is older than rockets.
31422-the-kempton-wace-letters:
Jack London and Anna Strunsky wrote The Kempton-Wace Letters as an exchange of letters between two correspondents debating love, marriage, and the relations of men and women. The title page names both authors, and the book belongs to London's early-twentieth-century output, listed among his works in this edition. Its form is the debate itself: one letter answers another, and positions sharpen as the correspondence grows.

Readers get two minds arguing in earnest, not a narrator settling the question. The letters move from personal feeling to general principle, asking what love should be and what marriage should require. As a document of its period, the book shows how progressive writers of the time argued about sex, freedom, and commitment in public, through fiction shaped as argument.
31534-fifty-two-sunday-dinners:
Mrs. Elizabeth O. Hiller's Fifty-Two Sunday Dinners is a book of recipes arranged on a unique plan. It combines helpful suggestions for appetizing, well-balanced menus with the newest ideas and latest discoveries in tasty, wholesome cookery. Hiller, founder and principal of the Chicago Domestic Science School and a noted writer, planned the book well. A housekeeper could find in it a complete Sunday dinner for every week of the year. Each menu pairs dishes that belong together, with recipes to match.

The book belongs to the domestic-science movement, which brought laboratory order to the kitchen. Its menus reflect the tastes and budgets of middle-class America in its day, with Sunday dinner as the week's set piece. Readers who cook from old books will find a practical, charming guide, and a record of what American families ate on Sundays a century ago.
31591-language-of-flowers:
Kate Greenaway's illustrated Language of Flowers pairs flowers with the meanings and messages they were understood to carry. Each flower in the book stands for a sentiment, and the illustrations let a reader match bloom to meaning at a glance. The book belongs to the Victorian fashion of speaking through flowers, where a bouquet could say what words held back.

Its plates show the flowers in Greenaway's graceful style, and the text sets out what each stands for. As a reference for the language of flowers, it serves both the curious reader and anyone choosing a bouquet meant to carry a message of its own.
31619-the-planet-savers:
Marion Zimmer Bradley's short novel The Planet Savers, produced from Amazing Stories of November 1958, is introduced as a triumphant return. Its author had been away from the magazine's pages too long. The headnote calls Bradley one of the finest science-fiction writers in print, and says this story could well be her best to date. The novel opens with a narrator waking on a leather couch in a bare room with huge windows, alone, or so he thinks, and slowly coming to himself.

From that white room, the story moves to a planet in peril and the effort to save it, in Bradley's early manner. Readers of her Darkover work will recognize the blend of science fiction and romance, with a heroine's courage at the center. The Planet Savers stands as an early, compact example of Bradley's fiction, before her novels grew long and famous.
3163-birds-and-bees-sharp-eyes-and-other:
John Burroughs gathers his nature essays here, with an introduction by Mary E Burt and a biographical sketch. Birds, bird enemies, and the tragedies of the nests lead the contents. Bees follow, in an idyl of the honey-bee and a study of pastoral bees. Sharp eyes, named in the title, names the gift the whole book celebrates.

Burroughs was born, the sketch notes, just before the wake-robin shows itself in spring. That timing fits a writer who spent a life watching. The essays teach attention: a nest watched daily, a bee followed home, a song traced to its singer. They remain a fine entry to American nature writing, clear, patient, and full of outdoor fact.
31644-helpfully-yours:
Evelyn E. Smith's Helpfully Yours, illustrated by EMSH, appeared in Galaxy Science Fiction for February 1955. Its sidenote calls it a humiliating order for somebody with wings to be told to come down to Earth and stay there. Tarb Morfatch has read all the information on terrestrial customs in the Times morgue before leaving Fizbus, and she has eagerly studied her handbook of terrestrial manners.

Tarb knows the natives are non-alate, so she must not take wing on Earth, but she forgets to match that knowledge to her own vertical habits. Stepping from the tender that ferried her down from the Moon, she looks up instead of right and narrowly escapes a raging groundcar. Smith's comedy follows a winged visitor learning Earth the hard way.
31685-nuts-and-nutcrackers:
This illustrated collection of comic sketches appeared in its second edition from London and Dublin, dated 1845 in Roman numerals. It takes its title from John Bunyan's image of hard texts as nuts whose shells keep their kernels from eaters. Its pieces satirize courts, lawyers, priests, and statesmen, imagining, for example, judges settling cases by tossing a coin.

The humor is that of the 1840s press: sharp, topical, and fond of turning a public institution upside down to show its folly. Readers get a lively volume of Victorian satire, illustrated by Phiz, that cracks open the pretensions of law, church, and politics.
31699-bring-me-his-ears:
Clarence E. Mulford's western novel, published in October 1922, opens in the St. Louis of the early 1840s, outside a ramshackle saloon on Locust Street. A tall, lanky Missourian and a Mexican trader argue over a lost man, Tomaz Boyd, who knows too much and has insulted the governor.

The trader carries a message that gives the book its title: bring Boyd to the governor, or bring his ears. Readers get a frontier adventure from the author of the Bar 20 books, following a manhunt across the border country where a single insult can set a whole chase in motion.
31709-our-southern-highlanders:
Horace Kephart's book on the southern highlanders, first printed in November 1913 and issued here in the 1916 printing, studies the mountain people of the southern Appalachians. Kephart opens by recalling Poe's 1845 allusion to wild mountains in western Virginia tenanted by fierce and uncouth races of men, the first literary reference to these mountaineers.

He then tests the popular caricature, a tall, slouching figure in homespun with a rifle on his shoulder, against what he saw living among them. Readers get an early twentieth-century portrait of mountain life, sympathetic but unsentimental, illustrated with photographs including the bear hunter Big Tom Wilson.
31716-jimsy-and-the-monsters:
Walt Sheldon's short science-fiction story is set in a Hollywood studio that can handle just about anything, until a machine brings in two real aliens. Studio chief Mr. Maximilian Untz regards the monsters with a critical eye that script girls, cameramen, and even stars quail under, but the monsters do not.

The first has a round, globe-like head and several spidery legs, the second is willowy and long-clawed, and a third is covered with hair. When Untz calls for Jimsy LaRoche, the studio's child performer, the meeting of movie-making and real aliens drives the comedy. Readers get a light satire of Hollywood confronted by the genuine article.
31867-history-of-the-sixteenth-connectic:
B. F. Blakeslee's History of the Sixteenth Connecticut Volunteers was written by a late second lieutenant of Company G. It is an outline history compiled mostly from diaries Blakeslee wrote at a young age, when he did not grasp their future use. He regrets that no complete history of the regiment has been written, and says this volume is but a mere outline.

Its first chapter follows the regiment in 1862 from Camp Williams to Antietam. Its aim is a permanent record of marches, battles, and experiences for surviving members, and a sad memorial to friends of those lost in battle or prison. Readers get a veteran's modest, firsthand regimental history of the Civil War.
31878-the-tempers:
William Carlos Williams's 1913 poetry book The Tempers, published in London by Elkin Mathews and dedicated to Carlos Hoheb, gathers early lyrics and translations. Its contents include Peace on Earth, Postlude, Homage, The Fool's Song, Immortal, Mezzo Forte, Crude Lament, and The Death of Franco of Cologne, with translations from the Spanish Romancero.

The opening poem watches an archer wake, a swan flying, gold against blue, and hunting in heaven, bidding the reader sleep safe till tomorrow. Readers get the young Williams before his famous American idiom, writing musical, image-driven verse with a European ear.
32005-border-raids-and-reivers:
Robert Borland's Border Raids and Reivers, published at Dalbeattie in 1898, tells the story of the Anglo-Scottish border country. Borland, minister of Yarrow, opens with the auld enemy: widespread border reiving, plunder and reprisal, every class implicated, and a double dose of original sin.

Chapters follow Percy's pennon and the battle of Otterburn, where Earl Douglas was slain and Hotspur taken prisoner. They also follow the poor and lawless condition of Scotland, where barons were supreme and every man's hand was against his neighbor. Readers get a scholarly local history of raids, feuds, and border lawlessness, from Edward's sacking of Berwick onward.
32135-maids-wives-and-bachelors:
Amelia E. Barr's collection of essays, published by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1898, takes up courtship, marriage, and domestic life from a woman's side. Barr, author of Jan Vedder's Wife and A Bow of Orange Ribbon, arranges her pieces in order. They run from maids and bachelors through falling in love, engagement, and the ring on the finger, to wives, mothers, and children. The book speaks to readers weighing decisions that shape a household.

Its contents show the range. They cover the American girl, dangerous letter-writing, flirts and flirtation, dowries for daughters, flirting wives, and mothers-in-law. Good and bad mothers, unequal marriages, and discontented women follow, with women on horseback, domestic and professional work for women, and the servant-girl's point of view. Later essays cover naming children, the children's table, extravagance, mourning, and portraits. Readers get advice and observation, plain and firm in judgement.
32150-prison-of-a-billion-years:
C. H. Thames's short story, printed in Imagination in April 1956, follows a condemned man with nothing to lose. Adam Slade is making a break for it, though no one has ever escaped from the prison. The story wastes no time: Slade kills a guard with a length of iron pipe, though no one ever knew where he got it. The guard is dead, and Slade is on the loose.

Slade escapes with a hostage, Marcia Lawrence, twenty-two years old, pretty, and terrified. Before becoming a hostage, she was a reporter for Interplanetary Video, granted the final pre-execution interview with Slade. She had looked forward to it for a long time, but it did not work out as planned. Readers get a tense prison-break tale, where an interview becomes a kidnapping.
32173-under-boy-scout-colors:
Joseph B. Ames's Under Boy Scout Colors, published in New York by the Century Company in September 1917, was approved by the Boy Scouts of America. Ames, author of Pete, Cow-Puncher and The Treasure of the Canyon, supplied drawings by Walt Louderback. He dedicated the book to Troop Five, from their grateful scoutmaster. Its contents promise both sport and scouting adventure.

Chapters run from The Live Wire and The New Tenderfoot, through The Silver Lining and On the Gridiron, to Trouble Ahead, The Quarrel, and In the Last Quarter. A good turn, an odd Thanksgiving, and a surprise follow, before Elkhorn Cabin, a cry in the night, and what the boys found there. Readers get a period boys' story where football, troop loyalty, and a cabin mystery share the term.
32181-do-unto-others:
Mark Clifton's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in June 1958, takes the Golden Rule to another planet. Its tagline states the rule: do unto others as you would have them do unto you. It adds that Capella IV folk, deep thinkers by bent, would hardly brush it aside. The narrator is Hapland Graves. Christened after Earth President Hapland, a cousin by marriage, he was called Happy Graves at school.

His Aunt Mattie, Matthewa H. Tombs, president of the Daughters of Terra, calls him Haphazard Graves instead. She reminds him of how he lives his life and does things, or does not do them. She shudders at anything disorderly, which includes her nephew, and holds it her beholden duty to right anything that appears wrong. Readers get a science-fiction moral tale, where a ne'er-do-well nephew, an aunt, and a philosophical planet meet.
32197-poitiers:
Hilaire Belloc's Poitiers was published in London by Hugh Rees in 1913. It is a map-driven history, with a coloured battle plan as frontispiece and four more plans. Its parts run from Introduction and The Campaign through The Preliminaries of the Action and The Terrain. They continue to The Action, The Aspect of These Battles, and The Results of the Battle. Belloc treats Poitiers as the second great raid, ten years after Crecy.

Just as Crecy eased strain on Edward III's southern force in France and drew French troops north, Poitiers eased strain in the north and drew them south. It called pressure off English troops in the north and brought French levies southward. Edward's Normandy march had been a daring ride for plunder, Belloc notes. The Poitiers campaign follows the same raiding logic. Readers get a Hundred Years' War study of campaign design, terrain, and action.
32278-seven-graded-sunday-schools-a-seri:
Seven Graded Sunday Schools, a series of practical papers edited by Jesse Lyman Hurlbut, was published in New York and Cincinnati in 1893, with copyright by Hunt and Eaton. Hurlbut, secretary of the Sunday School Union of the Methodist Episcopal Church, opens with The Essentials of a Graded Sunday School, then presents seven working plans from seven towns. A Model Sunday School Room closes the book.

The seven plans are the Akron plan by Lewis Miller, the Wilkesbarre plan by George S. Bennett, the Detroit plan by Horace Hitchcock, the Erie plan by H. A. Strong, the Chicopee plan by L. E. Hitchcock, the Lynchburg plan by Irvine Garland Penn, and the Plainfield plan by Hurlbut himself. Readers get a practical handbook for grading a Sunday school by age and progress, with real schools as models rather than theory alone.
32284-the-hitch-hikers:
Vernon L. McCain's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in November 1954, is set on a drying Mars. The cover line says the Rell, an old and mighty Mars people, neared doom once their world lost all its water. Then a single stranger touched down on Mars one day: an odd biped made largely of water.

The planet's drying had taken centuries in all, the story explains, and the Rell were still a great race when drying began. Readers get a science-fiction fable of thirst and survival, where an ancient Martian people meet a creature made of the very thing they have lost. The title's hitch-hikers ride on the visitor's arrival, and on water itself.
32291-paul-bunyan-and-his-loggers:
Otis T. Howd and Cloice R. Howd present Paul Bunyan as the folk hero of the North Woods lumberjack, not as a figure from company reports. Their account roots the tales in the Lake States pine country, where logging grew fast after the Civil War and swept across Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota. By 1900, they note, little of the great pine forest remained except fragments and miles of stumps.

The book explains how camp life, hard work, and tall talk shaped stories about Bunyan and his crews. It treats the hero as a way for loggers to speak about scale, danger, and pride in their trade. Readers interested in American folklore, labour history, or the timber industry will find the lumber camp world described from the inside.
32322-the-boy-with-the-u-s-miners:
Francis Rolt-Wheeler's boys' book, copyrighted in 1922, follows a young hero into the world of the United States miners, with thirty-six illustrations. Early chapters face underground terrors, a boy entombed alive, the dangers of rescue, and eight days of dark. Later chapters turn to the lure of gold, nuggets, the forty-niners, and the great bonanza, before moving north and on to a Siberian adventure.

Mine rescue crews with oxygen-breathing apparatus feature in the frontispiece, exploring a mine after a disaster with help from the United States Bureau of Mines. The book blends adventure with plain facts about shafts, timber, gas, and rescue gear. It offers young readers danger and discovery while teaching how miners worked and how rescue teams saved lives.
32328-methods-of-authors:
William H. Hills's book, copyrighted in 1894, asks a simple question readers often ask after a fine novel or treatise: how was it written? Hills presents the volume as a novelty, noting that books about authors were common, while none, as far as he knew, described their methods of work. He gathered material with help from the Reverend Francis Jacox, an anonymous article in All the Year Round, and R. E. Francillon's essay on the physiology of authorship.

Jules Claretie of Paris and the late Dr. Meissner, among others, assured Hills that authors themselves wanted such a book. The result surveys habits, routines, and working tricks across many writers, showing how books were planned, drafted, and revised. It remains a useful early source for anyone curious about the daily craft behind finished prose.
32360-the-holes-around-mars:
Jerome Bixby's short tale follows the first crew to land on Mars, led by Hugh Allenby, a commander fond of puns. Soon after stepping from the ship, Allenby finds a neat, round hole running straight through a granite rock. The crew, including a pilot, a photographer, a botanist, a biologist, and a mineralogist, gathers to study it.

Measurement shows the hole is about four and three-eighths inches across and some sixteen inches long, with a clean, perfect circle at each end. No ordinary cause fits the mark, and the crew must weigh what kind of maker could have left it there. The story turns on that puzzle, and on how a small, odd find can unsettle a whole landing party.
3237-the-garotters:
William D Howells writes this farce under the title The Garotters, in an author's edition printed at Edinburgh in 1897 by David Douglas. A note reserves acting rights to the publisher. The first part opens at the window of a woman's apartment in a hotel, with Mrs Roberts, then Mr Roberts, taking the stage in turn. The scene is set for a comedy of manners.

Garotting, the crime of throttling from behind, gives the play its sensational hook, but Howells treats it as farce material. Respectable people, hotel rooms, and sudden alarms drive the fun. The piece shows Howells the dramatist at play, turning a newspaper horror into drawing-room laughter, with dialogue as the chief weapon throughout.
32464-a-supplication-for-the-beggars:
Simon Fish's Supplication for the Beggars, dated spring 1529 and reprinted in Edward Arber's English Scholar's Library in 1878, is a famous Tudor tract on beggars, monks, and the commonwealth. Fish, of Gray's Inn, addresses the king on behalf of beggars, arguing that idle religious houses drain alms that should support the truly poor. Arber's edition, number four in his old series, presents the tract for students of English literature.

The supplication became a landmark in Reformation debate, linking charity, work, and church wealth in plain, forceful prose. Readers meet a sixteenth-century voice calling for reform of begging, hospitals, and monastic riches, with arguments that later reformers echoed. The short tract remains essential reading for Tudor history, English prose, and the origins of poor relief.
32580-the-golgotha-dancers:
Manly Wade Wellman's tale, printed in Weird Tales in October 1937, follows a museum visitor who came to see Goya prints and instead finds a painting he has never seen. The Goya gallery is too crowded to enter, so he wanders past oils, Greek and Roman sculpture, medieval armour, Oriental porcelain, and Egyptian gods. By chance he reaches a rear stairway where Arnold Böcklin's Isle of the Dead usually hangs, with high brown rocks, black poplars, midnight sky, and a single white figure in a skiff.

In its place, arresting even in bad light from the stairs, hangs a gilt-framed painting new to him. Wellman's framing note calls the story a curious, terrifying tale of an artist who sold his soul to paint a living picture. From a museum stairway, the story moves toward that picture, its dancers, and the bargain behind its life.
32620-the-three-mulla-mulgars:
Walter de la Mare tells of three monkey brothers, Thumb, Thimble, and Nod, who live with their mother Mutt-matutta on the borders of the Forest of Munza-mulgar. The youngest, Nod, is restless and brave, and the brothers soon leave their tumble-down hut for a wider world.

Their journey takes them past fierce birds, mountain men, and the silver-haired guards of enchanted orchards, toward a Wonderstone and a Queen of the Mountains. De la Mare mixes adventure, fear, and wonder in a fairy tale about growing up and finding one's own path.
32649-the-middle-years:
Henry James recalls his middle years in this memoir, published by Scribner's in November 1917. It follows two earlier volumes of memory, and it opens by qualifying an old claim: an event early in 1870 had marked the end of his youth. James then rethinks what youth means, as a march with stragglers behind and skirmishers ahead.

From March 1869, when he neared twenty-six, James savors London life: hansom cabs on Piccadilly, Robertson's comedies, and Henry Irving's Shakespeare at the Lyceum. He also meets Tennyson and Renan, and finds the real men differ from his dreams. The book is a slow, rich record of growth.
32664-black-amazon-of-mars:
Leigh Brackett tells of Eric John Stark, an Earthman on Mars, who carries a dying Martian named Camar through the cold Norland night. Camar, born in the Thieves' Quarter, stole the talisman of Ban Cruach, a holy thing he was never meant to touch. He dies before he can reach Kushat, his home city.

Stark takes up his friend's burden, though hordes of Lord Ciaran hunger for the jewel in his belt. Ahead lie the dread Ice Creatures and a tower crowned with dark force, where small seven-fingered hands seize him in the cold. The novel mixes sword, sorcery, and a doomed quest for return.
32770-the-intriguers:
William Le Queux opens this novel on a snowy January night in 1888. The scene is Dean Street, Soho. There the young Italian musicians Nello Corsini and his sister Anita play for pennies in the street. A passing carriage holds Prince Zouroff, the Russian ambassador, and his young sister Princess Nada.

Nada pities the pair, but her brother roughly forbids her help. Nello's path soon crosses the singer La Belle Quero, a popular idol of the musical world. Love for the princess, revenge against her brother, and secret plotting carry the story on. Through drawing rooms and embassies, Nello schemes to win Nada and escape Zouroff's vengeance.
32795-three-thousand-dollars:
Anna Katharine Green tells a mystery of a safe, a scheme, and three thousand dollars, published by the Gorham Press in Boston in 1910. Twenty chapters carry titles drawn from the dialogue itself, from 'Do you know what would happen to him' to 'A jewel of far greater value.'

The tale opens in a forsaken old church near Avenue A, where two men on a long bench discuss a problem in near darkness. Fellows, a cracksman who calls himself Beau Johnson, and a fearless young woman named Miss Lee all circle the prize. The plot turns on what lies in the safe, and on who will take the blame.
32801-the-plotters:
Alexander Blade tells of Marko, a visitor from a far planet, in this story from Amazing Stories of December 1948. Marko wakes running through a storm, his nose bleeding, his mind gray and empty. He does not know where he is, who he is, or why he runs.

Pain breaks through the grayness when a tree limb pins him down, and with pain comes knowledge. Names return: Ristal, Kresh, Copperd, and Beth, the golden girl. Marko came to Earth to learn its secrets, but love for Beth upsets his mission. A kiss on a porch sweeps his purpose from his mind.
32904-the-huddlers:
William Campbell Gault reports from Venus on the strangest colony of bipeds imaginable, in a story from If Worlds of Science Fiction of May 1953. The narrator, a Venusian reporter named Fred, calls Earth people huddlers for the way they crowd together. One coastal crust holds eight million of them in a place called New York, living one above another in apartments.

Back at the Department, Jars and Deering divide over the cause: fear, says Jars, and love, says Deering. Earth has achieved nuclear fission, and a last war seems to be shaping up. Against orders, Fred falls in love with Jean, a woman who grew up in an old glass-walled house. Jars pleads for him before the assembly, while Fred admits he does not know where his wife is, or whether she will come.
32932-seven-frozen-sailors:
George Manville Fenn sends a secret Arctic voyage out under a sealing pretext, in a tale of seven frozen sailors. Captain Cookson accepts command from a hugely fat, hugely active backer who keeps his real object under seal. The crew is told seal, and a bit of sealing will be done on the voyage, but the true purpose waits.

Abram Bostock, tall and thin, brings in old bos'en Abinadab Scudds, who starts at the sight of the stranger. Below decks hides Miles O'Rourke, a man with two hundred pounds reward on his head, who has starved from fourteen stone to ten. Cookson once mistook him for a ghost and hugged him hard enough to break a strong man's ribs. The voyage north, its frozen sailors, and the secret its backer guards drive the story toward the Arctic circle.
32934-the-young-colonists-a-story-of-the:
G. A. Henty sends two Derbyshire farm boys to the wars of South Africa, in a volume from Blackie and Son of London. The Humphreys farm stands near Castleton, with a hundred acres of bottom land and five times as much upland grazing. Richard, about fourteen, and his brother John, three years younger, attend school at Castleton.

Henty's preface owns the pain of describing two campaigns of defeat. Isandula fell in the Zulu War, where a divided army lost touch with its detached force. Laing's Neck and Majuba Hill fell in the Boer War. Relief for the besieged came by swift ship, with the Shah turning back at Saint Helena and the Boadicea landing every man she could spare. England sent the 57th and 91st Regiments, with a hundred and sixty men from Mauritius. English pluck and daring, Henty promises, carry his hero through both disasters.
32944-ruba-iya-t-of-doc-sifers:
James Whitcomb Riley's Rubáiyát of Doc Sifers, published by the Century Company in 1897 and illustrated by C. M. Relyea, is a book of verses in the manner of Omar Khayyám, turned toward an Indiana country doctor. Riley dedicates it to Dr. Franklin W. Hays, the loyal chum of his latest youth, and the poems remember a figure found in a far-away that still seems near, a vagrant's friend from an earlier life.

The rubáiyát form, short quatrains on life, time, and fellowship, suits Riley's plain, musical voice, and Doc Sifers becomes a lens for memory, humor, and quiet philosophy. The book belongs to Riley's popular middle period, when his Hoosier poems reached a national audience. Readers who like verse that is easy to hear and hard to forget will find it here, warm rather than grand.
32979-interpreters:
Carl Van Vechten's Interpreters, in a revised edition of 1920 with sixteen illustrations and an epilogue, profiles the great singing actors of his day. Chapters take up Olive Fremstad, Geraldine Farrar, Mary Garden, Feodor Chaliapine, Mariette Mazarin, Yvette Guilbert. Waslav Nijinsky, each essay weighing voice, stage presence, and the art of turning a role into a living figure. Photographs of the performers in costume run through the book.

Van Vechten writes as a critic who loved the theater and knew its stars at close range. He dedicated the book to his wife Fania Marinoff, herself an interpreter of many roles. The essays are personal rather than scholarly, full of sharp judgments and affection. For readers interested in opera, dance, and the stage before recorded sound took over, they preserve performers who can now only be imagined.
33095-the-spanish-pioneers:
Charles F. Lummis's Spanish Pioneers, in a sixth edition from Chicago in 1914, retells the story of Spain's explorers and founders in the Americas for popular readers. A frontispiece shows Francisco Pizarro, and the book opens with a guide to pronouncing Spanish names. It gives a the sound of ah, e of ay, i of ee, and j of h, so readers can say the heroes' names aright. Lummis dedicates the work to Elizabeth Bacon Custer, as one of such women as make heroes and keep chivalry alive.

Lummis writes with enthusiasm for Spanish courage, endurance, and faith. His pioneers include conquerors, missionaries, and settlers whose roads, towns, and missions shaped the Southwest. Modern readers will weigh his admiration against later history, but the book remains a vivid, influential telling of a story long told from the other side.
3319-letters-to-dead-authors:
Andrew Lang writes letters to authors who cannot answer in this charming volume. Thackeray and Dickens lead the contents, with Pierre de Ronsard, Herodotus, and an epistle to Alexander Pope. Lucian of Samosata, Maitre Francois Rabelais, and Jane Austen follow, with Master Isaak Walton, M Chapelain, and Sir John Mandeville. Alexandre Dumas, Theocritus, and Edgar Allan Poe join them.

Sir Walter Scott and Eusebius of Caesarea round out a correspondence across two thousand years. Lang writes as a fan, a critic, and a friend, praising, teasing, and arguing with the dead. Lang's letters read one at a time, witty enough to reread, and learned enough to trust.
33321-two-plays-for-dancers:
W. B. Yeats's Two Plays for Dancers, printed by the Cuala Press in 1919, gathers plays shaped by the noble plays of Japan. The volume holds The Dreaming of the Bones, for which Yeats sought historical notes on Dervorgilla, and a second dance play in the same spare style. Yeats sets the action on an empty patch of floor near a wall, and the action moves through speech, dance, and music rather than scenery.

Yeats's plays are short, ritual, and haunting, aimed at readers and players who love poetry in motion. Their power lies in image and rhythm, not plot alone. For students of modern drama, the volume is a key example of Yeats's late style, where Irish myth and Japanese form meet in a new kind of theatre.
33471-stories-and-ballads-of-the-far-pas:
N. Kershaw's Stories and Ballads of the Far Past, translated from the Norse, Icelandic, and Faroese, with introductions and notes, was published at Cambridge in 1921. Its first part offers sagas, from the tales of Nornagest and Sörli to Hromund Greipsson and Hervör and Heithrek, with an appendix on the combat at Samsö. Kershaw's notes guide readers through a distant, heroic world.

The volume suits readers of Norse literature, offering translations that are both scholarly and readable. Its tone is learned yet lively, with introductions that set each saga in its place. For students of the sagas, it is a valuable, well-edited collection, bringing far-past heroes to modern English readers.
33667-two-prisoners:
Thomas Nelson Page writes a children's story of two prisoners in this 1903 volume, illustrated in color by Virginia Keep and first condensed in Harper's Young People under Alfred B. Starey. The story opens in a dingy house squeezed between older houses down a dirty, narrow, cobble-stoned street. Only the poorest and most unfortunate would remain in such a hovel.

Mrs. O'Meath rules the house, a short, red-faced woman who says she was once a wash lady. Within it, two young prisoners, a little girl and her world, find imagination and friendship against squalor. Illustrations show a bird flying straight away, a girl walking with her nurse, and a whispered word to a mother. Page writes tenderly about childhood resilience in hard places.
33846-the-tent-dwellers:
Albert Bigelow Paine, author of The Van Dwellers, writes a camping narrative in this 1908 Outing volume, illustrated by Hy. Watson. During holiday week, Eddie proposes a matter close to his heart. Tents, vari-colored flies, and the prospect of campfire smell make his straight, silvered hair bristle. They put a new glare into his wide, round spectacles, until he seems even more anarchist-like than in his old Heidelberg days, though he is truly a gentle soul.

The narrator, writing letters at his club, agrees to the plan, and the book follows their tent-dwelling expedition through woods and waters, with mishaps, fishing, and campfire talk. Paine writes with humor and affection for outdoor life. Readers who enjoy classic American camping literature will find a warm, leisurely account of friends, flies, and fires under northern stars.
33850-the-slizzers:
Jerome Bixby wrote this short science tale, first printed in Science Fiction Stories in 1953. Its narrator warns that slizzers live all around us, looking human and living beside us, while feeding on people in a way he likens to a need for maple trees. Because people act in so many odd ways, a small slip in disguise passes unnoticed.

The tale asks whether a friend, a spouse, or a neighbor next door might be one of them. Bixby keeps the danger low-key: slizzers are not killers or rampaging monsters. The story's chill comes from its calm claim that we would enjoy their company and never suspect a thing.
33892-regina-or-the-sins-of-the-fathers:
Hermann Sudermann wrote this novel, translated by Beatrice Marshall and published in London in 1907. It opens just after peace is signed and Europe, long the plaything of the great Corsican, comes to itself again, bruised and bleeding from a thousand wounds. Bells ring and prayers rise, while mourners hide their heads.

Regina's story grows from that aftermath, as the sins of fathers press on children who did not commit them. Sudermann writes of a continent remaking itself after war. The novel remains a powerful study of guilt passed down through a family and an age.
33907-one-act-plays-by-modern-authors:
Helen Louise Cohen edited this 1921 school anthology of one-act plays, with a long introduction on playmaking and the theatres of the day. She covers the commercial stage, the repertory idea, the little theatre, and the Irish National Theatre before turning to the craft of the short play itself.

The plays include work by Booth Tarkington, A. A. Milne, Lady Gregory, and others, each with a short introduction by Cohen. Teachers and student actors gain both scripts to stage and a guide to how a one-act play is built. The book still works as a compact survey of the short play at its early peak.
33944-how-to-observe-morals-and-manners:
Harriet Martineau published this guide in London in 1838, as the second work in a series on how to observe. The first, on geology, had appeared in 1835, and Martineau's volume extends the plan to social life: how a traveler should watch morals and manners abroad. She sets out what to ask, what to note, and how to judge fairly.

Martineau warns readers against hasty views and urges close, patient study of homes, laws, work, and faith. The book shaped travel writing and early social study alike. It still reads as a thoughtful manual for anyone who wants to see another society clearly.
33959-the-reclaimers:
Margaret Hill McCarter wrote this novel, published in New York and London in 1918 by Harper and Brothers. Its center is Eden, the country estate of Jerusha Darby, a wealthy Philadelphian, and her husband Cornelius, whose work is to guard her wealth. Parts follow Jerry, then Jerry and Joe, then Jerry, Eugene, and Joe, toward a postlude in Eden.

McCarter, author of Vanguards of the Plains, writes of faith, family, and the pull of the flesh-pots of the Winnwoc. A storm, a snare, and a crossing of the Rubicon mark the way. The novel ends, as its title promises, with reclaiming.
33997-the-jonathan-papers:
Elisabeth Woodbridge wrote this set of country papers, published in Boston and New York in 1912 by Houghton Mifflin. Woodbridge dedicates the book to Jonathan and to all perfect comradeship wherever its joyous spirit is found. The papers first appeared in the Outlook, the Atlantic, and Scribner's.

Contents run from a placid runaway and an unprogressive farm through a desultory pilgrimage and the yellow valley. Later papers treat larkspurs and hollyhocks, a farm Sunday, the country road, the lure of the berry, and comfortable books in the firelight. Woodbridge writes with gentle humor. The book offers a charming record of farm and friendship.
34200-story-lessons-on-character-buildin:
Loïs Bates's 1900 book gives teachers and parents short tales for teaching morals and manners to children. Each tale is short enough to tell aloud or read in class, and each ends with a clear point a child can grasp.

Stories are grouped by virtue: obedience, loyalty, truth, honesty, kindness, thoughtfulness, helpfulness, and courage, with homely scenes of homes, schools, and play. Bates wrote for the daily round of school and home, where the right tale at the right hour beats a scolding. Bates, author of a kindergarten guide, wrote these tales for telling as much as for reading.
3421-bramble-bees-and-others:
Jean Henri Fabre collects his essays on wild bees in this volume, drawn from his long Souvenirs entomologiques and translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. The book opens with bramble stems, which peasants cut while trimming hedges and which bees then use as nesting places. Later essays treat the Halicti and other solitary bees, leaving the mason bees to a separate volume.

Fabre watches how each kind of bee digs, builds, stores food, and guards its young. He explains the insects in plain terms, with the patience of a man who spent years in his own field. The volume suits nature lovers who want careful observation rather than theory, and it shows why Fabre earned his name as the poet of insects.
3469-the-hand-of-ethelberta-a-comedy-in-:
Thomas Hardy calls this novel a comedy in chapters, written as a light interlude between his more sober stories. Ethelberta is a young woman of humble birth who has married into a higher station. She must manage suitors, family, and reputation across scenes set in Sandbourne town, its moor and pier, and London drawing rooms. Hardy warns that strict probability was not his aim.

The fun lies in Ethelberta's poise and in the social climbing around her. She keeps her wits while men compete for her hand and her past threatens to catch up with her. Readers who know Hardy only from his tragedies will find a brighter, teasing side here, with the same sharp eye for class and village life.
3690-floor-games-a-companion-volume-to-l:
Herbert George Wells writes a companion to his Little Wars, this time about games played on the floor with simple toys. The jolliest indoor games, Wells says, demand a floor covered with linoleum or cork carpet, where toy soldiers stand up and cities can rise. His list of toys runs to soldiers and civilians, bricks, boards and planks, clockwork railway stock and rails, tin ships, and Easter eggs.

Games include the Wonderful Islands, the building of cities, funiculars, marble towers, castles, and war games, though Wells allows very little of war itself. The book suits parents, teachers, and children who want inventive play from plain materials, and readers who enjoy Wells as a father writing about his sons' games.
373-lay-morals-and-other-papers:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers essays and papers in this posthumous volume, with a preface by his wife. The pieces range from youth, marriage, and books to travel and moral choice. Many were written in his roaming years, and the preface recalls island days when leprosy touched every port they knew.

Stevenson argues in a warm, personal voice, mixing jest with stern sense. He praises courage, plain speech, and the habit of facing life as it is. Readers who know his tales will find the same mind here, turned to thought rather than plot, and just as keen on style and truth.
3761-this-country-of-ours:
Henrietta Elizabeth Marshall tells the story of America as a chain of tales for young readers. The book moves from early settlements through the colonial years, with governors, founders, and ordinary folk taking turns at the center. One vivid scene shows Boston gone mad with joy as two ships bring orders to proclaim William and Mary, with bells, bonfires, and a great procession to the town hall.

Marshall writes in a plain storyteller's voice, favoring deeds and scenes over dates and debates. Sir Edmund Andros sent home a prisoner marks one turning point among many. The book suits families and young students who want a first narrative of the United States, told as history that reads like a storybook.
386-virginibus-puerisque-and-other-paper:
Robert Louis Stevenson reflects on youth, love, and marriage in the title essay of this set, then turns to books, travel, and talk. He opens with Shakespeare's marrying men and asks why modern lovers fear vows that older folk took lightly. Later essays weigh idleness, talk, and the art of living well.

Stevenson writes with wit and a light, probing touch, never preaching at length. His sentences sparkle, yet his points bite: youth wastes time, love tests pride, and books shape conduct. The volume shows the essayist at his most personal, thinking aloud for readers who like a sharp mind at play.
3953-cinq-mars:
This edition collects all of Alfred de Vigny's Cinq Mars, with prefaces by Charles de Mazade and Gaston Boissier. The life of Vigny traces a reputation of extraordinary ups and downs. First lauded as precursor of French romantic poetry, then sunk in semi oblivion, he was recovered in the last years as a main illuminating force of the nineteenth century. He stands, the preface says, between Musset and Chenier, lyric and philosophic at once.

A tense passage shows the plot's heart, as the Cardinal's guards question Cinq Mars and allow him to advance only with De Thou. The Cardinal Duke says sharply that he has come too late to speak with the king. Then Louis the Thirteenth himself speaks, torn between irritation at his minister and knowledge that he owes him the day's success. Readers who want Cinq Mars whole will find conspiracy, friendship, and a king's divided mind.
399-cast-upon-the-breakers:
Horatio Alger Jr. tells of Rodney Ropes, a schoolboy left to a faithless guardian, in this rags-to-respect tale. Rodney learns his guardian has drained his funds, and he must leave school to earn his keep. Work, friendship, and pluck carry him through hard towns and harder masters.

Alger follows the familiar moral arc: honest toil beats sly schemes, and a true friend proves worth more than cash. David, a poor day scholar, opens the book as Rodney's first ally. The novel charms as a plain, hopeful tale for young readers, where grit and good conduct win out.
404-industrial-biography-iron-workers-an:
Samuel Smiles continues his Lives of the Engineers with this 1863 study of iron workers and tool makers. He traces iron from early smelters and smiths to the furnace masters who built modern British industry. Chapters follow the Forest of Dean, Sussex cannon works, and the shift from wood charcoal to pit coal.

Smiles profiles inventors and mechanics whose toil, thrift, and skill shaped trade and war. Dud Dudley, early coal smelters, and later engineers each get a clear, fact-filled life. The book praises useful work without show, and it still reads as a solid record of how iron made an age.
4218-sisters:
Ada Cambridge's novel Sisters follows a man who dreads a letter from his baby's caretaker, a lady of whom he stands in undignified dread. Mentioning the matter next day, he finds after breakfast a letter forwarded from Five Creeks, her handwriting paling his brown face.

His stout heart flutters at the sight, and he keeps the letter unopened for some time, afraid to know what he already guesses it contains. Cambridge writes Australian domestic life with warmth and humor. Readers who enjoy family novels of the colonies will find a charming, human story.
4274-wives-and-daughters:
