He writes the North as a moral climate. Cold, distance, and hunger strip men to what they are. Pierre, who has seen everything twice, narrates without surprise.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-2-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 2, by Gilbert Parker, gives Pretty Pierre five more northern tales. Parker opens with Malachi, in a room of gossips calmly predicting that a man will swing tomorrow. The door opens, the condemned man's friend Pierre steps to the fire, stretches his hands to the heat, and repeats the sentence himself in a soft ironical voice: Exit Malachi. The wind, Pierre says, does not tell where it has been.

The Lake of the Great Slave and The Red Patrol take the tales onto the water and the mounted police trails of the far North. The Going of the White Swan and At Bamber's Boom close the volume among river drivers and their booms of trapped logs. Parker's North West gives a hanging, a drowning, and a log jam the same weight of fate. Pierre's shrug there is a philosophy earned at forty below.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-3-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 3, by Gilbert Parker, places Pretty Pierre among the river drivers of the Madawaska. Parker opens The Bridge House with a building set on a wall between two small bridges, above channels that divide at its foundations. Spring floods batter the wall with logs, and a man can step from the back door into the river itself. The house was once a tavern, and the drivers who loved it were its true parish.

The Epaulettes, The House with the Broken Shutter, and The Finding of Fingall follow, with Three Commandments in the Vulgar Tongue to close. Soldiers, deserters, and river men pass through Parker's Ottawa valley, where French and English Canada meet on the drives. The Bridge House itself, rock like among the currents, stands for the book's method: fix one spot where wild lives converge, and let the river bring the stories past.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-4-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 4, by Gilbert Parker, opens with a Christmas tale told to power. In Little Babiche, Pretty Pierre faces the governor of the great Company, the Hudson's Bay chief, whose grey head and seamed face carry long solitary years in the northern fastnesses. Pierre corrects the record about a man he has known fifteen years, and promises the strange truth of a thing that happened at Noel, the day of the Great Birth.

At Point o' Bugles, The Spoil of the Puma, The Trail of the Sun Dogs, and The Pilot of Belle Amour complete the volume. Parker's tales keep returning to witnesses: men who were present, who knew, and who set a governor or a reader straight years later. The North of these stories is governed from fur trade posts and remembered in firelight, and its justice arrives, when it arrives, as testimony.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-5-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 5, by Gilbert Parker, closes the Pretty Pierre records with the longest tale in the set. The Cruise of the Ninety-Nine follows a big gulf yawl, handy enough for a man and a boy, with high old fashioned bulwarks and a tolerable record for speed. Her captain was Tarboe the smuggler. He named her after a parable. The parish priest came seeking the one lost sheep. Tarboe replied that he was the ninety nine, needing no repentance. He offered the cure his excellent smuggled brandy.

A Romany of the Snows and The Plunderer fill out the volume. Parker ends his northern cycle on salt water. Customs officers wink there, and priests drink with their parishioners.
a-woman-s-love-letters: Sophia Margaretta Hensley writes a woman's love letters in verse in this volume of the Fleur de Lis Poets, published at New York in 1895. The contents run from A Dream and Dream-Song through Doubt, Anticipation, Misunderstanding, Shadow-Song, and Revulsion to a Song of Dawn, Weariness, a Song of Rest, Death, and Battle-Song. Content, Sea-Song, Gratitude, Prayer, Loneliness, and To-morrow close a sequence of feeling in short lyrics.
aboriginal-american-authors: Daniel Garrison Brinton surveys native American authors and their works, with special attention to writing in the native languages, as a chapter in the history of literature. A new introduction notes that the work, published in 1883, suits a time when the native movement stresses an Indian telling of history. Interest in native literature, it argues, reinforces identity among American Indians today, and Brinton's survey remains a foundation for that reading.
across-the-years:
Eleanor H. Porter gathers eighteen stories reprinted from magazines such as the Ladies' Home Journal, Harper's Bazaar, and the Century, as her contents page records. The titles sketch her world. They include When Father and Mother Rebelled, Jupiter Ann, and The Price of a Pair of Shoes. The Bridge Across the Years, A Belated Honeymoon, and When Aunt Abby Waked Up follow.

The first story opens a month before Christmas with old Samuel Bertram sighing to his wife Lyddy Ann. Porter's people are elderly couples, country girls, and tired workers, and her plots turn small sacrifices into glad outcomes. The author of Pollyanna writes here for adults, with the same faith that gladness is a duty and a medicine.
addams-twenty-years:
Jane Addams published Twenty Years at Hull-House in 1910, looking back on the settlement house she co-founded in Chicago in 1889. Hull-House stood in a poor immigrant ward on Halsted Street. Addams lived there among her neighbors for decades.

She describes the neighbors who came: Italians, Greeks, Jews, Bohemians, each with old-country ways and new-world troubles. Hull-House offered classes, a nursery, art, and help with jobs and law. Addams also traces her own growth toward labor reform and peace work. The book helped invent American social work and remains its founding memoir.
american-merchant-ships-and-sailors: Willis John Abbot traces American merchant ships and sailors, opening with the shallop and moving through the age of sail. The book follows vessels, crews, and the commerce they carried, with stories of voyages and hardships at sea. Abbot gives a lively history of the merchant marine that built American trade.
americans-and-others: Agnes Repplier gathers essays in Americans and Others, with pieces on counter-currents, a happy half-century, convent days, compromises, and books and men. The essays mix wit, learning, and a conservative's scepticism toward fashion, praising good sense and good talk. Repplier's voice, urbane and sharp, made her one of America's best-loved essayists.
among-the-mushrooms-a-guide-for-beginner: Ellen Markoe Dallas and Caroline A. Burgin guide beginners among the mushrooms, with a preface and contents suited to first study in the field. The book teaches readers to know common kinds, their marks, and where they grow. Written for amateurs in Philadelphia's Drexel Biddle edition, it opens a hobby that joins walking with close looking.
an-englishwoman-s-love-letters: Laurence Housman presents an Englishwoman's love-letters, published in New York by the Mershon Company. The letters trace a love affair in the writer's own voice, from hope and delight to doubt and parting. The epistolary form gives the romance an intimate, confessional force. The voice stays frank, even where hope fades.
arkansas-governors-and-united-states-sen: John L. Ferguson compiles brief lives of Arkansas territorial and state governors and United States senators, leaving out brief acting holders. Each entry gives birth, schooling, work, marriage, and term dates, starting with James Miller in 1819. The result is a handy desk reference for students of state politics, not a set of full biographies. Its value lies in dates and facts kept in one plain sequence.
bandelier-delight-makers:
Adolph Bandelier founded much of Southwestern archaeology in the United States. His novel The Delight Makers first appeared in 1890, here in a 1918 edition. He set the tale among the Pueblo peoples in the age before Spain came.

Bandelier builds daily life from the ruins and records he knew best. Corn fields, clan rites, hunts, and feuds fill the prehistoric village. A young hero moves through custom, duty, and secret plots. Few novels of the ancient Southwest rest on such deep field knowledge. Science wears the dress of story here, with rare skill and care throughout.
barchester-towers:
Anthony Trollope returned to Barchester in Barchester Towers, and the cathedral town is asking who will be the new bishop. The answer is Dr. Proudie, whose wife rules the palace and whose chaplain, Mr. Slope, schemes to rule the diocese. Against them stand Mr. Harding, the gentle ex-warden of Hiram's Hospital, the old dean and chapter, and the whole habit of Barchester life.

Chapters promise war, receptions, and Slope versus Harding, while the Stanhope family, including the fascinating Signora Neroni, stirs the drawing rooms. Trollope treats church politics as high comedy with real stakes: livings, sermons, and souls. This second Barsetshire novel made the series famous, and Mrs. Proudie remains one of fiction's great commanding wives.
barford-abbey-a-novel-in-a-series-of-let:
Susannah Gunning published this novel in letters at London in 1768, printed for T. Cadell in two volumes. Lady Mary Sutton opens the correspondence from the German Spa, writing to Miss Warley — her dear Fanny — in England. A death has just thinned their circle, and Lady Mary weeps over Fanny's mournful detail while praising the departed saint's god-like virtues.

Suitors write in the confessional mode of the period. One tells Molesworth that absence and time cannot deaden the exalted image: it neither sickens nor dies, but blooms to immortality, and parting from mere beauty is not his wound. Gunning, a prolific novelist of sensibility, builds the plot from such letters alone — visits, rumours, and hearts laid open page by page in the manner Richardson made fashionable.
barks-and-purrs:
Colette, signing herself Colette Willy, wrote these animal dialogues, translated here by Maire Kelly. Her bulldog Toby and her cat Kiki-the-Demure hold long conversations about their mistress, her callers, her country house, and the small politics of the hearth. A prefatory sketch teases the author as a countrywoman whose orchard, stable, and beehive hold no mysteries for her.

Toby-Dog sniffs back tears while Kiki consoles him with the cool philosophy of cats: pleasures and friends will return, and the farmer's dog crunching bones outside proves the world goes on. Colette gives each beast a voice true to its species — the dog all heart, the cat all reserve — and turns pet-keeping into a two-handed comedy of manners, love, and jealousy.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-08-great:
John Lord's eighth Beacon Lights volume treats great rulers, and Alfred the Great opens it with the Saxons in England. Contents follow the conversion of the Saxons, Caedmon and Bede, Alfred's succession in Wessex, Danish invasions, his humiliation and defeat, then conquest, forts, a reorganised army and navy, laws, shires, and parishes. Alfred stands as Lord's model of the Christian king.

Later rulers carry the story toward modern Europe, where Lord's real subject is the power of ideas. Thinkers set nations in motion as Rousseau would later do; the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries belonged to divines, he argues. Luther's private judgment, Calvin's majesty of God, Latimer's personal responsibility, and Gustavus Adolphus fighting for religious liberty show rulers and reformers sharing one stage in Lord's providential history.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-10-europ:
John Lord's tenth Beacon Lights volume treats the leaders of Europe in the nineteenth century. It opens with William IV and reform in England. The contents run through the whole reform age: Lord Grey at the head of the government, Lord John Russell, and the Reform Bill's final passage. Brougham, Melbourne, and Peel all take their turns in office. Irish troubles under O'Connell, the end of slavery in the West Indies, town government reform, trade unions, and penny postage fill out the list.

A later talk weighs Napoleon III with grudging care. The usurper fed French pride with dreams of martial glory, his uncle's old trick. Yet he gave much to the middle and lower classes, spurred trade, and graced Paris with grand new works. Most Frenchmen, Lord admits, found the reign kind and lucky. Reform at home and empire abroad balance the scales of the volume.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-11-ameri:
John Lord's eleventh Beacon Lights volume gathers his lectures on the American founders. A publishers' preface explains the regrouping: the old Warriors and Statesmen lectures were redistributed for the new edition. Hamilton and Webster, once placed elsewhere, are brought into closer relation with the founding generation here. Lord rewrote and extended the lectures for the purpose.

The founding itself is told as deliberation. Delegates differed in temper, the preface of one lecture concedes, but all stood united on independence and distrust of monarchies. Debates turned first on the powers of the executive, judicial, and legislative branches. Their work was consummated, Lord writes, in the glorious Constitution, our marvel and our pride. Washington, Franklin, and their peers appear as character studies in his familiar lecture manner.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-12-ameri:
John Lord's twelfth Beacon Lights volume treats American leaders of the middle republic. The publishers moved the Daniel Webster lecture here from Warriors and Statesmen, judging Clay and Calhoun its natural neighbourhood. A preface hopes that, the Civil War era having passed, Northerners and Southerners can now take dispassionate views and find honourable reasons on both sides.

One eulogy shows Lord's measure of greatness. At a leader's grave even enemies felt that a great man in Israel had fallen. His defects were towering: intellectual pride like Chatham, austerity like Gladstone, indifference to money obligations like Pitt, Fox, and Sheridan. Warmth of affection for faithful friends and simplicity of manners outweighed them all. Orators and sectional champions fill a volume built on balanced, post-war judgment.
bears-i-have-met-and-others:
Allen Kelly published this book of bear-hunting stories at Philadelphia in 1903, with illustrations by Ernest Thompson Seton and others. Kelly, a California newspaperman, writes of the grizzly when it still ruled western mountains. Contents promise the California grizzly, the story of Monarch — the great bear captured for a San Francisco menagerie — chronicles of Clubfoot, and the adventures of Pike.

Kelly is honest about the odds. In one season north of Yosemite he cut the trails of thirteen bears in two days and followed several. He hustled two out of a walk into a lope, yet never saw hair through his rifle sight. Without dogs, still-hunting a grizzly is mostly walking. The distinction between bear-hunting and bear-killing, he says, he and the Captain learned keenly that year.
bengal-dacoits-and-tigers:
Sunity Devee, Maharani of Cooch Behar, collected these true tales of Bengal in two parts: dacoit stories and tiger stories. Dacoits — armed robber gangs — fill the first: the Jhee's discovery, Raghu Dacoit, a girl as Kali-Ma, a deputy magistrate, two Chinese dacoits, and an unfaithful servant. The opening sets a young Bengali lady travelling in the scorching month of Jaishta, while the earth prays for the barsat rains.

One tale traps Ethel in a bedroom as a robbery begins. She hides her evening dress under the bedclothes and a pillow over her head, feigning sleep, until two Chinamen slip noiselessly through the door and advance. Tiger tales follow: through the roof, the palki and the tiger, a Cachar tiger, and a maharajah's adventures. The Maharani writes as an insider of princely India, retailing the perils her world still remembered.
billy-baxter-s-letters:
William J. Kountz Jr. of Pittsburgh wrote himself into these comic letters as Billy Baxter, a young blade writing home to his friend Jim. Billy reports a Minnesota hunting trip where he cannot open his borrowed gun, then moves through society calls, courtship, and a jaunt to New York. The letters first appeared as advertising booklets for a Pittsburgh distributing company and sold by the thousand.

Kountz died in August 1899, not yet thirty-two, and his brother gathered the letters as a tribute. Billy's slang, boasting, and sudden collapses of dignity drive the jokes. Read as a period piece, the book catches American young-man humor just before the twentieth century, pleased with itself and quick with a wisecrack.
birds-and-bees-sharp-eyes-and-other-pape:
John Burroughs's nature papers are collected in this volume, which opens with a biographical sketch of the author and an introduction by Mary E. Burt. The sketch fixes his beginnings: born at Roxbury in the Catskills on April 3, 1837, and raised on his father's farm. He was schooled in district schools, and drawn from the first to the essay form. The contents then divide into birds, bees, and other papers.

Bird Enemies and The Tragedies of the Nests give the bird section its edge; nesting is a dangerous business. An Idyl of the Honey-Bee and The Pastoral Bees turn to the hive and the bee-keepers. Sharp Eyes, the title piece of the remaining papers, trains the reader's own observation. Burroughs writes as a walker and watcher, and the book is meant to send its readers outdoors with better eyes.
birds-and-poets-with-other-papers:
John Burroughs's Birds and Poets, volume three of his collected writings, opens with a preface dated at Esopus-on-Hudson in March 1877. Burroughs explains that he has coupled outdoor nature sketches with chapters of a literary kind. Audubon, he argues, had the eye and heart of a poet though not the tongue. The title essay follows.

Touches of Nature and A Bird Medley carry the field observation, with April and Spring Poems for the turn of seasons. An essay on Emerson honours his master, and The Flight of the Eagle closes on Walt Whitman. Burroughs had championed Whitman when America mostly scorned him. His method is the naturalist's eye turned on books: close, patient, and affectionate. The volume helped found the American nature essay as literature, neither science nor sermon but a walk with a companionable mind.
bits-about-home-matters:
Helen Hunt Jackson published these essays on home matters in 1873, signing herself H. H. beside her Verses and Bits of Travel. Contents read like a conscience for parents: the inhumanities of parents in corporal punishment, needless denials, and rudeness; breaking the will; the awkward age; and the republic of the family. A day with a courteous mother stands as the pattern household.

Prisons test her metaphor in one essay, Friends of the Prisoners. A story of double walls of iron grating, with a cruel, empty space between crowded with words and looks, haunted her for days. Then she turned it: who of us is not in prison, living behind bars of custom and fear? Jackson's domestic essays mix nursery government with sudden depths, the same moral pressure she later turned on the nation's treatment of its Indians.
books-fatal-to-their-authors:
P H Ditchfield wrote Books Fatal to Their Authors, a study of writers ruined by their own pages. Ditchfield opens with a preface to the book lover on Fortune's cruelty to scribes. Critics are the least of it, he warns: some authors lost liberty or life for a book.

Case after case follows, from early printers to the age of Henry the Eighth. The Pole family shows how a cardinal's defiance could cost his kin their heads. Ditchfield sorts the fallen by their fates, with scaffold, prison, and exile all in the list. Anecdote carries the argument more than theory does. Book men of his day got a warning and a feast of stories at once. The moral is plain: print has always been a risky trade.
bramble-bees-and-others:
Jean-Henri Fabre wrote the essays in Bramble-Bees and Others from his patient studies of wild bees in southern France, translated here by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. Fabre collected the pieces from his Souvenirs entomologiques, leaving the mason-bees to a separate volume. His subjects live in bramble stems, reeds, and old walls. Careful watching, not laboratory theory, drives every chapter.

Opening essays follow bramble-dwellers and the Osmiae, a family of solitary bees. Fabre then asks how a mother bee controls the sex of her eggs. Leaf-cutters, cotton-bees, and resin-bees each get a chapter. Two closing groups study the Halicti, small bees with parasites and portresses. Readers get exact natural history written like storytelling, where an insect's nest becomes a small household with work, danger, and design.
brentano-aus-der-chronika-eines-fahrende:
A wandering scholar's chronicle gives Brentano his frame in Aus der Chronika eines fahrenden Schuelers, presented in German. The traveling student moves through a Germany of inns, roads, and chance meetings. Youth and freedom breathe through the fragmentary tale, part picaresque and part meditation.

Episodes gather like entries in a travel diary, warm with the poet's verbal music. The open road itself becomes the hero's teacher, as in so many Romantic daydreams. Melancholy underlies the charm; wandering also means never quite arriving. Brentano left the work in a loose, songlike form that suits its subject. Readers who love the Taugenichts spirit will feel at home here.
britannica-1911-abbreviators:
Abbreviators receives an office entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The abbreviators were writers in the papal chancery who sketched bulls, briefs, and decrees in draft. Scriptores then wrote the acts out in full. John the Twenty-second's Extravagantes first name the body.

Sixtus the Fourth fixed their count at seventy-two, split between a greater and a lesser park, named for the grated space where they sat. The greater park's men ranked as prelates and led the chancery once protonotaries left drafting to them. Martin the Fifth made their signature key to an act's validity. Privileges grew with the years. Pius the Tenth suppressed the body in 1908, passing its work to participating protonotaries.
britannica-1911-abhorrers:
Abhorrers receives a party entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The name fell in 1679 on those who declared abhorrence of the Petitioners, men signing calls for Charles the Second to summon Parliament. Anti-Catholic feeling and the Exclusion Bill against James of York drove the crisis.

Charles dissolved one Parliament and prorogued the next unmet. Petitions flooded in for a sitting. Sir George Jeffreys and Francis Wythens raised counter-addresses of abhorrence, and the frolic, in Roger North's phrase, went all over England. King and court gained a loyal chorus against the petition trade. Whig and Tory, the entry closes, were first pinned on English parties in this very quarrel.
britannica-1911-algae-colouring-matters:
Colour decides how deep an alga can live, and Colouring Matters, a part of the Algae article, tells why. All algae hold chlorophyll, the green stuff that lets a plant feed on carbonic acid gas in sunlight. Added tints change the game. Phycocyanin, phycophaein, and phycoerythrin each bend the plant's absorption spectrum, the band of light hues it soaks up.

Engelmann found a neat way to test it: watch where oxygen pours out most freely, for that marks where carbon is taken in fastest. The peak sat in the band of hues each tint drinks in. Light fades by hue as it sinks in the sea: red gives out for growth at thirty-four metres down, yellow at 177 metres, green at 322 metres. So a tint fits its plant to the depth where its own light still lives.
britannica-1911-algiers:
Algiers, the capital and largest city of Algeria, is described at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its Arabic name Jezair means the Islands. The city stands on the west side of a Mediterranean bay that bears its name, built on the slopes of the Sahel hills. It is the seat of the governor-general, a court of appeal, and an archbishop.

Seen from the sea, Algiers looks like dazzling white terraces rising from the water, which earned the Arab comparison of a diamond set in an emerald frame. Two cities compose it: the modern French town on level shore ground, and the ancient city of the deys climbing the steep hill behind. The kasbah, or citadel, crowns the climb at four hundred feet above the sea. The article also notes the city's college, with its schools of law, medicine, science, and letters.
britannica-1911-all-fours:
Four points make a hand at All Fours, the card game Americans also call Seven Up, Old Sledge, or High-Low-Jack. High goes for the highest trump out, low for the lowest trump dealt, Jack for the knave of trumps, and game for the most pips won in tricks. Two players usually sit down, though four may play, with a full pack and seven counters apiece.

Each player gets six cards, and the thirteenth turns up to fix trumps. Holding a poor hand, the non-dealer may beg for a fresh deal; the dealer can refuse, at the cost of a point, or deal extra cards instead. Tricks then decide the rest, under rules for following suit and trumping, with a fresh deal allowed after a dealing error.
britannica-1911-angers:
St Maurice's cathedral leads the old buildings of Angers, a city of western France and capital of Maine-et-Loire. Raised mainly in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, it holds fine stained glass and prized tapestry hangings. The abbey-church of St Serge and the church of La Trinité stand nearby, and the prefecture fills the old abbey of St Aubin.

Angers spreads over rising ground along the Maine's two banks, joined by three bridges, and counted 73,585 people in 1906. Wide straight streets and tree-lined boulevards ring it, placing it among France's most pleasant towns, while the country round it is famed for nurseries and market gardens. Its past includes English rule in the twelfth and fifteenth centuries, a Huguenot seizure in 1585, and a noted university that lasted until the Revolution.
britannica-1911-avars:
Avars, also called Avari, are an East Caucasian people of central Daghestan, described as the most renowned of the Lesghian tribes. The entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica stresses that they differ from the Avars whose Danube empire Charlemagne broke.

One mark sets them apart among Lesghian tribes: they alone had a written language, using Arabic characters for it. The writer Komarov is cited for holding that the tribe is of more recent origin than its famous namesakes. Their name, he held, is Lowland Turki for vagrant or refugee. Readers are pointed to the Lesghians article for the wider group.
britannica-1911-avengers: Avengers, or Vendicatori, were a secret society formed in Sicily about 1186 to avenge wrongs done to common people. Vendicatori is Italian for avengers, and the group took justice into its own hands outside the courts. King William II, the Norman ruler, finally suppressed the society. He hanged its grand master and branded the members with hot irons, a punishment meant to mark them for life and end their work of private revenge.
britannica-1911-bashkirs:
Bashkirs are a people of Russia living in the governments of Ufa, Orenburg, Perm, and Samara. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places them on the Ural slopes and the plains beside them. They speak a Tatar language, though some authorities held them to be a Finnish people reshaped by Tatar influence. Their name appears first in the tenth century in Ibn-Foslan, who met them among the Volga Bulgarians and called them warlike idol-worshippers.

Submission and revolt mark their history with Russia. Strong and independent before the Mongol arrival, the Bashkirs accepted Russian supremacy in 1556. They paid a fur tax, while Ufa was founded for their defence. They rose in rebellion in 1676, again in 1707 over ill-treatment by officials, and once more from 1735 in a rising that lasted six years. They are last divided into settled farming, cattle-rearing, and bee-keeping communities and nomadic groups.
britannica-1911-bass-brewers:
Bass is the name of a family of English brewers of Burton-on-Trent, traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The founder, William Bass, born in 1720, began as a carrier whose clients included a Burton brewer. By 1777 he had saved enough to brew for himself, selling Burton beer to St Petersburg through Hull. When Russia shut Burton ales out with a heavy duty in 1822, the firm turned to the home market and to London.

India pale ale made the firm's fortune. Asked to supply a beer that would survive the Indian climate, William Bass produced the lighter pale ale that became popular across India. A shipwreck whose salvaged Bass beer reached Liverpool opened trade in the north-west by accident. Draught Bass at the 1851 Exhibition spread its London fame. The business became a limited company in 1880. William's grandson Michael Thomas Bass added philanthropy in Burton and Derby to brewing.
britannica-1911-bazigars:
Bazigars are a nomad folk of India, found across the whole peninsula. They are also called Panchpiri, Nats, Bediyas and other names in different parts of the country. They live apart from the Hindu people around them and keep a clear sense of their own identity.

Their living comes from juggling, dancing, basket-weaving and fortune-telling, trades long linked with wandering peoples. Each clan has its own king, much as among the gipsies of Europe. The entry is brief, giving their range, their other names, their trades and their clan order in a few lines.
britannica-1911-berbers:
Berbers is the name covering the many branches of the native “Libyan” people of North Africa. Since the dawn of history they have held the land between the Mediterranean and the Sahara, from Egypt to the Atlantic. The name’s source is doubtful: some trace it to the Greek and Roman word for barbarians, others to the Arab conquerors.

Egyptian records name kindred tribes as early as 1700 and 1300 B.C., and the Berbers may be close kin to the old Egyptians. Conquest after conquest, Phoenician, Greek, Roman, Vandal, Arab and French, failed to change their physical type or temper. The long article treats their villages, ruled by an assembly of grown men, their dress, crafts, women’s standing and a language still spoken by millions.
britannica-1911-blachford-frederic-roger:
Frederic Rogers Blachford (1811–1889) was a British civil servant who spent most of his career in the Colonial Office. Born in London, he studied at Eton and Oriel College, Oxford, won high honours in classics and maths, and became a fellow of Oriel. He was called to the bar in 1837 but never practised law.

The entry follows his move into public work, first as registrar of joint-stock companies in 1844 and then as commissioner of lands and emigration. From 1860 he served as permanent under-secretary for the colonies under six secretaries of state. On retiring in 1871 he was raised to the peerage as Baron Blachford. A volume of his letters, edited in 1896, is noted at the close.
britannica-1911-brierly-sir-oswald-walte:
Sir Oswald Walters Brierly (1817–1894) was an English marine painter born at Chester into an old Cheshire family. He studied at Sass's art school in London and learned naval architecture at Plymouth, showing ship drawings at the Royal Academy in 1839. A love of the sea shaped everything that followed.

In 1841 he sailed round the world with Benjamin Boyd in the Wanderer, settled for ten years at Auckland, and gave his name to Brierly Point. Voyages in HMS Rattlesnake in 1848 and with Sir Henry Keppel in the Meander in 1850 fed his art, and he pictured Keppel's cruise in an 1853 book. Crimean War service with Keppel led to 1855 lithographs of the English and French fleets in the Baltic. Royal favour followed: he joined sea tours of the duke of Edinburgh and the prince of Wales and became marine painter to the queen in 1874.
britannica-1911-broadstairs:
Broadstairs is a watering-place in Kent, England, 3 miles south-east of Margate on the South-Eastern and Chatham railway, in the Isle of Thanet division. Its urban district, Broadstairs and St Peter's, held 6466 people in 1901. Charles Dickens made it his favourite summer resort from 1837 to 1851 and sketched it as Our English Watering-Place.

Dickens called it a place left high and dry by the tide of years. Summer visitors grew the seaside village, with its half-circle sweep of houses, into a real town of hotels, boarding houses, libraries, a bathing house and a fine promenade. His home there, Fort House, became known as Bleak House by link to his novel, though the book was written after his last visit. A small fishing pier first built under Henry VIII, an archway of 1540 by George Culmer.
britannica-1911-carabiniers:
Carabiniers were mounted troops armed with the carbine. They began in the French army. This 1911 Britannica article traces the name in three armies. In 1690 each French cavalry regiment kept one company of them. Their duties matched those of infantry grenadiers. They scouted, did detached work, and fought in sieges. They fought mounted and on foot alike.

At Neerwinden in 1693 the companies were joined in one body. Louis XIV then made them a permanent regiment. It took the name Royal Carabiniers after that action. The regiment survived the French Revolution under a new title. Its heir in the modern French army is the 11th Cuirassiers. The British carabiniers date from 1685, the entry notes. They took the title in 1692, from their carbines. For years they were called the 3rd Irish Horse. Since 1788 they have been the 6th Dragoon Guards, the Carabiniers.
britannica-1911-celsius-anders:
Anders Celsius (1701–1744) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Swedish astronomer born at Upsala. He held the chair of astronomy at the university of his native town from 1730 to 1744. During 1732 and the years after, he travelled in Germany, Italy, and France. At Nuremberg in 1733 he published a collection of 316 observations of the aurora borealis. They covered the years 1716 to 1732 and drew on his own work and that of others.

In Paris Celsius urged the measurement of an arc of the meridian in Lapland. In 1736 he joined the expedition the French Academy organised for that purpose. Six years later he described the centigrade thermometer in a paper read before the Swedish Academy of Sciences. He wrote on the distance of the sun and on the figure of the earth. He died at Upsala on 25 April 1744. The entry closes with references to his memoir on the thermometer scale.
britannica-1911-centaurs:
Centaurs is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a race of beings in Greek mythology, part horse and part man. They dwelt in the mountains of Thessaly and Arcadia. Myth made them the offspring of Ixion and Nephele, the rain cloud. They are best known for their fight with the Lapithae. At the wedding of Peirithous they tried to carry off the bride, Deidameia. Theseus helped to drive them off.

The entry gives their general character as wild and lawless. They were slaves to their animal passions. Pholus and Chiron stand as exceptions. Later art shows them drawing the car of Dionysus, or bound and ridden by Eros. Scholars explained them in many ways: as cloud shapes, as spirits of torrents, or as sun rays. One suggestion is that early Greeks, new to riding, took northern horsemen for single creatures. Their defeat figured the struggle of civilisation against barbarism.
britannica-1911-checkers: Checkers is a very short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, a single sentence long. It records the name by which the game of draughts is known in America. The entry adds one point of origin: the name checkers shares its origin with the name of chess. For the game itself, its board, and its rules, the entry sends the reader to the article on Draughts, and for the name's root it points to the article on Chess.
britannica-1911-contributors:
Contributors is the roll of the men and women who wrote for the encyclopaedia itself. Names run in letter order from A onward, each with initials in brackets. After each name stands the work that person supplied. Matthew Arnold, for one, gave the piece on Sainte-Beuve. Graziadio Ascoli gave part of the piece on the Italian language.

Thomas Ashby gave the geography and statistics of Italy, plus pieces on Italian sites and old remains. Charles Francis Atkinson gave a long list on war. The American Civil War, arms and armour, artillery and infantry all bear his mark. The roll runs to some 37,000 bytes in the hosted text. It forms a map of who wrote what across the whole work. A reader can trace a signed piece back to its author's name and field.
britannica-1911-covenanters:
The Covenanters were a party that grew out of the Reformation movement in Scotland. They played a great part in Scottish history in the 1600s, and a lesser part in England's. Their name came from the bands or covenants they signed. In those bands they bound themselves to keep Presbyterian doctrine and church order. That faith was to stand as the sole religion of their country.

Far more weight sits on the covenant of 1581. John Craig drew that text up as Roman Catholics strove to win Scotland back. Men call it the King's Confession or the National Covenant. It rests on the Confession of Faith of 1560 and damns the pope in strong terms. The General Assembly took it up, and King James VI signed it with his household. In 1637 Scotland stood in turmoil once more. Charles I and Archbishop Laud had just met a sharp reverse.
britannica-1911-cowley-fathers:
The Cowley Fathers are the members of the Society of Mission Priests of Saint John the Evangelist. The society is an Anglican religious community with its headquarters at Cowley Saint John, close to Oxford in England. The Reverend R. M. Benson founded it in 1865. Its set aim was a life given to God by the rules of poverty, chastity and obedience.

School work and mission work fill the society's days in equal shares. It keeps a house in London for its home work. Branch houses stand far past the seas as well. Bombay and Poona in India hold two of them. Cape Town and Saint Cuthbert's in Kaffraria hold two more in South Africa. Boston in the United States holds a fifth. The dress of the Fathers is plain and set. A black frock or cassock, bound by a black cord, is worn with a long black cloak over it.
britannica-1911-cuirassiers:
Cuirassiers are a kind of heavy cavalry grown out of the men-at-arms of feudal armies. Their mark was full armour, kept long after other troops had dropped it. That armour gave them their name. The first Austrian corps was formed in 1484 by the emperor Maximilian, at a strength of 100 men. By 1705 Austria held twenty regiments of them. After the war of 1866 those regiments were turned into dragoons.

Russia likewise cut its cuirassiers to a few guard regiments in modern times. Prussian cuirassiers bore a great part in Frederick the Great's wars, then left the cuirass off on service until after 1814. Captured French cuirasses then re-equipped them, and the plate survives for ceremonial parades. In France the arm dates from 1666 and grew to fourteen regiments by 1812. The French alone in Europe, the entry notes, wear the cuirass at all parades and manoeuvres.
britannica-1911-elster-rivers:
Elster is the name of two rivers of Germany, and the entry treats both in turn. The Schwarze, or Black, Elster rises in the Lausitz range on the southern border of Saxony. It flows north and north-west and, after a course of 112 miles, enters the Elbe a little above Wittenberg.

The Weisse, or White, Elster rises in the north-western corner of Bohemia, a little north of Eger. It cuts through the Vogtland in a deep, pretty valley, passing Plauen, Greiz, Gera, and Zeitz on its way north to Leipzig. Below Leipzig it receives its chief tributary, the Pleisse, then divides. The main stream turns north-west and enters the Saale above Halle. The other arm, the Luppe, enters the Saale below Merseburg. The White Elster's total length is 121 miles, with a total descent of 1286 feet.
britannica-1911-ethers:
Ethers, in organic chemistry, are compounds of the general formula R·O·R′, where R and R′ are alkyl or aryl groups. They count as anhydrides of the alcohols, formed by dropping one water molecule from two alcohol molecules. Matching radicals give simple ethers, and differing ones give mixed ethers. Concentrated sulphuric acid on an alcohol yields them, and the process can run continuously. Williamson prepared ether from sodium ethylate and ethyl iodide in 1851 and fixed the structural formula.

The ethers are neutral, volatile liquids, though methyl ether is a gas at ordinary temperatures. Phosphorus pentachloride turns them into alkyl chlorides, and nitric and chromic acids oxidize them. Methyl ether, first made by Dumas and Péligot in 1835, boils as a liquid at 23.6 degrees. Methyl ethyl ether boils at 10.8 degrees. Heating alkyl halides with silver oxide is another route to the class.
britannica-1911-executors-and-administra:
Executors and administrators, in English law, are the persons to whom a dead person's property passes. An executor is appointed by the testator's will, expressly or by implication. His estate vests from the moment of the testator's death. An administrator is appointed by the probate division of the High Court. His title vests only at that appointment, held meanwhile by the probate judge. Apart from these two points, their rights and duties match.

Before the Land Transfer Act 1897, real estate bypassed the representative and vested in the devisee or heir. That act made the personal representative the real representative too. Joint tenancy land and copyholds remain exceptions. The representative stands in the dead man's shoes and may sue on his contracts and debts. First among duties comes burial suited to the estate left. Funeral costs rank ahead of every duty and debt, though extravagant spending falls on the representative personally.
britannica-1911-flanders:
Flanders, in Flemish Vlaanderen, is a territorial name for part of the Netherlands in Europe. It first meant only Bruges and its near neighbourhood. In the eighth and ninth centuries it spread over the whole coast region from Calais to the Scheldt. In the middle ages the land split in two, one part looking to Bruges and the other to Ghent. The name survives in the Belgian provinces of West and East Flanders.

West Flanders, capital Bruges, holds Ostend, Courtrai, Ypres and Roulers along a coast of a little over 40 miles. Its 1,263 square miles held 845,732 people in 1904, farmed with famous care on sandy dune soil, with fishing on the coast. East Flanders, richer still, reaches toward Antwerp. The long entry then turns to the counts of Flanders, from Baldwin onward, and the medieval history of the county, its towns, weavers and wars.
britannica-1911-fochabers:
Fochabers is a burgh of barony and village of Elginshire, Scotland, with 981 people in 1901. It sits pleasantly on the Spey, about nine miles east by south of Elgin. A branch of the Highland railway ends there, joining the main line at Orbliston Junction. The town was rebuilt on its present site at the end of the eighteenth century. Its earlier site was wanted for changes in the grounds of Gordon Castle, where the old town cross still stands.

The rebuilt town's streets all run at right angles to a central square where fairs and markets are held. Its public buildings include a library and reading-room, the court-house and the Milne school. That school is named for Alexander Milne, who endowed it with a legacy of 20,000 pounds. Gordon Castle adjoins the town in a park of fine old trees.
britannica-1911-francs-archers:
Francs-archers were parish bowmen raised in France under an ordinance issued at Montils-les-Tours on 28 August 1448. Each parish had to pick its most apt man, free him from the taille tax and some other duties, and keep him practising with the bow on Sundays and feast days. He had to march, fully equipped, at the first signal.

The entry calls the corps the first attempt at regular infantry in France. Under Charles VII the francs-archers fought in many battles against the English and helped drive them from the country. In later reigns the force faded, and by the middle of the 16th century it had vanished. The men were also known as francs-taupins.
britannica-1911-francs-tireurs:
Francs-tireurs, meaning free-shooters, were irregular French infantry who fought in the war of 1870-1871. They began as rifle clubs and volunteer societies formed in eastern France during the Luxemburg crisis of 1867. Members wore no uniform, carried the best rifles they could get, and chose their own officers, which made the government keen to bring them under army control.

In July 1870 the societies passed to the war minister, and that November they came under the generals in the field. Working mostly in small bands, they blew up culverts, cut off patrols, and surprised small posts. Deeds singled out include the blowing of the Moselle railway bridge at Fontenoy in January 1871 and the defence of Châteaudun. Captured men faced death at German hands, yet their work tied down large enemy detachments.
britannica-1911-gaveston-piers:
Piers Gaveston (died 1312), earl of Cornwall, was the favourite of England's Edward II. The 1911 Britannica entry makes him a Gascon knight's son, raised at Edward I's court beside the future king. Banished early in 1307, he returned on Edward I's death and at once became chief adviser.

Made earl of Cornwall, married to the king's niece, and regent during the king's absence in France in 1308, Gaveston roused the barons' anger. They forced his exile to Ireland, then perpetual banishment under the Ordinances of 1311. He slipped back to England, was restored, and surrendered at Scarborough in May 1312. The earl of Warwick seized him, and he was beheaded on Blacklow Hill on 19 June 1312. His body was buried at King's Langley in 1315.
britannica-1911-gisors:
Gisors is a town of France in the department of Eure, in the pleasant valley of the Epte, 44 miles north-west of Paris on the Dieppe railway. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 4,345 people in 1906. A feudal stronghold, built chiefly by the kings of England in the 11th and 12th centuries, dominates the town.

The outer walls cover over seven acres, with a round donjon added by Philip Augustus, and an older octagonal keep on a mound at the centre. The ramparts now serve as promenades. The church of St Gervais, founded by Blanche of Castile in the mid-13th century, mixes Gothic and Renaissance work and is rich in sculpture. The entry also notes the town's felt-making, bleaching, dyeing and leather-dressing, and its old place as capital of the Vexin.
britannica-1911-givors:
Givors is a manufacturing town of south-eastern France, in the department of Rhone, 14 miles south of Lyons on the Lyons to St Etienne railway. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 11,444 people in 1906. It stands on the right bank of the Rhone, here crossed by a suspension bridge, where the Gier and the Givors canal join the river.

Its chief industries are metal-working, engineering construction and glass-working, and coal mines lie nearby. On the hill above the town stand the ruins of the chateau of St Gerald and the convent of St Ferreol. These are remains of the old town, destroyed in 1594. The notice is a short industrial gazetteer entry, giving position, works and the one historical note of the ruined hill.
britannica-1911-glanders:
Glanders, or Farcy, in the 1911 Britannica medical entry, is a specific infective disease caused by the parasite Bacillus mallei. It chiefly attacks the horse, ass and mule, and it can pass from them to man. The entry deals with the human disease, leaving the animal side to veterinary science.

Human cases are rare, and they fall on those who work with horses: grooms, coachmen, cavalry soldiers and veterinary surgeons. The bacillus enters through a wound or scratch, or through the lining of the nose or mouth, and symptoms follow in three to five days. They begin with general illness and pains in the limbs and joints like acute rheumatism. An ulcer forms where the poison entered, with swelling along the lymph vessels. The entry then follows the disease's course and its grave outlook.
britannica-1911-hawkers-and-pedlars:
Hawkers and pedlars are itinerant dealers. They carry goods from place to place for sale. Hawker entered English from German or Dutch in the early 1500s. An act of 1533 already complains of haukers in brass and pewter. Huckster is the older word, found by 1200. Both may come from a root meaning to squat or crouch. Pedlar derives from pedder, a carrier with a ped, or basket.

French colporteur names the book-hawker specifically. Religious bodies adopted it for Bible sellers. British law long regulated both trades carefully. The Pedlars Act 1871 defines a pedlar in technical terms. Hawkers need certificates; pedlars need licences under the acts. Exemptions cover fair sellers and the makers of goods. Penalties punish infringements of the rules. In the United States state and federal licences are required.
britannica-1911-higham-ferrers:
Higham Ferrers is a market town and municipal borough in Northamptonshire, England, 63 m. N.N.W. from London. Its population was 2,540 in 1901. It stands on high ground above the south bank of the river Nene. St Mary's church ranks among the finest in the county, with an Early English chancel and a wide Decorated north aisle like a second nave.

Near the church stand the school-house and Bede House founded by Archbishop Chichele in 1422, and remains of his college survive. Shoemaking is the local trade. The place was a large village before the Domesday Survey and passed in 1199 to William Ferrers, earl of Derby. A Ferrers charter of 1250 freed ninety-two persons and made it a free borough. Its castle, noted in 1322, was destroyed by 1540. A mayor, 4 aldermen and 12 councillors govern the town.
brook-farm-historic-and-personal-memoirs:
John Thomas Codman wrote a first-hand history of Brook Farm, the famed shared-life farm of the 1840s. Five long chapters frame the tale, each with full sub-heads. Growth of the movement holds the first place. George Ripley, the Transcendental Club, and the farm's first folk fill it, with Hawthorne among the names.

Re-shaping under Fourier's social code holds the second place. Codman's own road to the farm and life on the place fill the third. Work years and their folk fill the fourth: Margaret Fuller, Emerson, and Theodore Parker walk its pages. Rush and hum of work fill the fifth. Groups and series, the workshop, dances, and a death and funeral on the farm all show there. Names came from the author's own years on the ground, which gives the book its weight as a source.
bruges-and-west-flanders:
G. W. T. Omond wrote the text for a picture tour of Bruges and its shire, with plates by Amédée Forestier. Eleven chapters frame the trip. Market place, belfry, and the town's early tale hold the first place. Baldwin Bras-de-Fer and the murder of Charles the Good hold the second.

Béguinage, churches, and the relic of the Holy Blood come next. Bruges Matins and the Battle of the Golden Spurs fill the fourth. Damme, the sea fight at Sluis, and the town's fall from trade fill the fifth. A still, dead Bruges gets a chapter of its own. Ypres and the plain, Furnes and its penitents' march, and Nieuport and the Battle of the Dunes spread the net wide. Coast and dune lands close the tour. Index and plate list end the book.
bunner-sisters:
Edith Wharton wrote Bunner Sisters in 1892, though it waited until 1916 for book publication. Ann Eliza and Evelina Bunner keep a tiny shop in a poor New York street, selling notions and mending, and live together in the room behind it. A clock bought for Ann Eliza's birthday brings Mr. Ramy, the clockmaker, into their lives, and both sisters quietly hope for the marriage that would change everything.

He marries the younger, Evelina, and the tale that follows is one of slow ruin: a drug habit, poverty, a lost child, and a return too late. Wharton tells it with pity and a steady eye. The tale is an early proof of the power she later brought to The House of Mirth.
cabbages-and-cauliflowers:
James J. H. Gregory wrote a hands-on guide to growing cabbages and cauliflowers, lodged at Washington in 1889. Gregory bills himself as first bringer of six named cabbages: Marblehead, Deep Head, Warren, All Seasons, Hard Heading, and Reynolds. Full points on each step form the vow of the title page.

Soil choice and soil prep open the frame. Manure — what kind and how to lay it — takes two parts. Hill making and seed work come next in the list in view. Crop care, keeping, and sale to market fill the rest of the plan. Seed trade craft from a man who sold the seed forms the base. Plain steps, timed to the season, are the book's whole method. Backyard patch and market field both sit in its aim.
calamities-and-quarrels-of-authors:
Isaac Disraeli wrote a set of tales of authors' woes and fights, in a new edition set right by his son, the earl of Beaconsfield. Frederick Warne of London put out this copy. Warburton and his rows hold a long place, with a sketch of his bent as a man of letters.

Pope fills much of the frame: rows at large, the Curll case of his letters' print, Cibber, and Addison. Bolingbroke and Mallet fight Pope from past the grave. Lintot's account book shows the trade side in cold sums. Pope's first satire and the Royal Society get their own takes. Sir John Hill's wars with the Society, Fielding, and Smart fill a late slot. Boyle and Bentley close the list in view. Print shop spite and pen pride form the stock.
captain-macklin-his-memoirs:
Captain Macklin: His Memoirs, by Richard Harding Davis, pretends to be the life story of a young American soldier of fortune. Davis gives his narrator a West Point opening and a frank excuse for writing young: soldiering is hazardous, and tomorrow might not come, so the record must be made now. Walter Appleton Clark illustrated the volume, and the frontispiece shows a cavalry farewell, a captain crying God bless you to his horse.

Macklin's road runs from the Military Academy through revolutions and filibustering expeditions in Central America, the world Davis reported as a correspondent. Camp moons, barrack yards, and cabin fights fill the illustration list. The memoir form lets Davis string his war reporting into one swaggering career. It is half confession and half recruiting poster. The narrator calls soldiering the noblest profession a man can follow. Then he sets out to prove the price of believing it.
captains-all-and-others:
W. W. Jacobs wrote a set of sea-side tales, dated 1911, with Captains All at its head. Nine tales line the contents page. The Boatswain's Mate comes next. The Nest Egg and The Constable's Move fill the first run.

Bob's Redemption and Over the Side mark the heart. The Four Pigeons and Samuel Burge's hard choice come next. Mr. Lister's mad turn and The White Cat close the list. Plate lines give the tone in the men's own speech. One shows two quid paid ere a man steps in doors. One shows old Sam home like a dream walker. His bag of oranges was one he did not want. Night watch talk, inn talk, and boat talk form the stock. Small ports and small wages hold big jests in Jacobs's hands.
captivating-mary-carstairs:
Henry Sydnor Harrison called his first long story a story rather than a novel. A signed note dated 1914 tells how it was planned in 1900 and rewritten many times. It was first published under a pen name in February 1911. The action centres on the town of Hunston, where two young men arrive bent on a scheme the early chapter titles call a crime.

Politics and local quarrels fill the opening chapters before Mary Carstairs herself is introduced in the fifth. From there the plot mixes small-town manoeuvring, romance, and the fallout of the scheme the pair brought with them. Harrison's own account of the book's long road to print frames a lively, talk-driven tale of ambition and attraction.
cast-upon-the-breakers:
Horatio Alger Jr opens Cast Upon the Breakers with schoolboy Rodney Ruland, a star boarder whose rich guardian pays all his bills. Rodney soon learns the money is gone, spent by that faithless guardian, and he must leave school and earn his living. The first chapter sends his friend David off to learn the carpenter's trade instead.

Rodney heads west, guards a casket of his dead mother's jewels on a train, loses it to thieves, and works his way up through honesty and luck. Alger's formula is complete here: a boy cast on the world, tempted, tested, and rewarded. Young readers of the 1890s made such tales bestsellers, and this one shows why.
catherine-memoirs:
Catherine the Great wrote her memoirs in French over many years, and they surfaced long after her death in 1796. The German princess had come to Russia as a bride and seized the throne from her husband in 1762. Her own account stops before that coup.

She describes the court of the Empress Elizabeth, her loveless marriage to Peter, and her reading of the French thinkers. Intrigue, loneliness, and ambition shape her rise, told in a cool, observant voice. The memoirs break off in 1759, before the seizure of power. Even so, they remain the key source for her early life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbreviators:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on abbreviators describes those who shorten a long work into an abstract, tightening its words and sentences. Abbreviation took two forms: a single letter for a single word, and a mark standing for a word or phrase, both common among the Romans.

Emperor Justinian forbade abbreviations in the Digest and later in all writings, but the ban was not universally obeyed, and abbreviators kept the practice for convenience and interest, especially at Rome. Early Christians used abbreviated writing as an easy, safe way to communicate and guard secrets from enemies. In time the Apostolic Chancery adopted it as curial style, further dropping diphthongs and punctuation marks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acts-of-the-m:
Acts of the Martyrs, strictly speaking, are the official records of early Christian martyrs' trials, made by court notaries. In a wider sense the title covers all narratives of a martyr's trial and death. The entry classifies them with care. Official reports of interrogatories survive in few numbers, like the Acta Proconsulis for Cyprian, and reach us only in editions shaped to edify the faithful. The Passio Cypriani and Acta of the Scillitan martyrs typify this class.

Non-official records by eyewitnesses or contemporaries form a second class. It includes the Martyrium of Polycarp, with its pious fancy, and the Acta of Perpetua and Felicitas, most famous of all, holding autograph notes of Perpetua and Saturus. The letter of the churches of Vienne and Lyons on their martyrs belongs here too. Later classes, legends and romances, demand sharper criticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-algiers:
Algiers, ancient Icosium, is an archdiocese covering Algeria province in French Africa, with Oran and Constantine as suffragans. Missions rose in 1632, and an apostolic vicar soon followed. Late in the seventeenth century he oversaw Tunis's pro-vicar and Tripoli's prefect. The second-century Icosium see died under the Arabic conquest and revived in 1838 as Aix's suffragan. Dupuch was its first bishop until 1845, Pavy served from 1846 to 1866, and Lavigerie became its first archbishop in 1867.

The church honours Mercedarian confessors, including thirteenth-century Peter Armengaud at Algiers, and venerates Raymond Lully, dead at Bougie in 1325, and Geronimo, buried alive at Algiers in 1569. At the end of 1905 the diocese counted 230,843 European-born inhabitants besides the army, 8 first-class and 101 second-class parishes, 25 vicariates, and 24 auxiliary priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angers:
Angers, anciently Andegavum, is a diocese covering Maine-et-Loire in France. It was a suffragan see of Tours under the old regime and the Concordat. The first known bishop is Defensor, who in 372 opposed Saint Martin's nomination at the Tours election. The legend of an earlier bishop Auxilius belongs to the Saint Firmin cycle, against Angevin tradition before the thirteenth century.

Early names include Saint Maurilius, hermit of Chalonnes, who stood against idolatry and died in 427, and Thalassius, bishop in 453, who left a brief compendium of canon law. Modern bishops include Cardinal de la Balue, caged by Louis XI from 1469 to 1480, the Jansenist Henri Arnauld, Freppel, and Mathieu, later cardinal and academician. The twelfth-century cathedral of Saint Maurice, without side aisles, shows Angevin architecture. Medieval Angers held six great monasteries, including Saint Aubin and Saint Serge. In 1905 the diocese counted 514,658 inhabitants and 543 parishes and vicariates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anglican-orde:
This article treats the validity of orders conferred in the Church of England. In Catholic belief, Holy Order is one of the seven sacraments, giving the priesthood's powers to consecrate the Blessed Sacrament and administer Confirmation, Penance, and Extreme Unction. Holy Order has three degrees, bishops, priests, and deacons, with bishops holding the priesthood in full, able to exercise and transmit it. Only a bishop ministers Holy Order, and validity requires his valid consecration and a rite keeping all Christ's essentials.

From the start, Catholic writers attacked the Edwardine Ordinal for an insufficient rite. The article traces the debate through the Parker succession and Rome cases, where re-ordination was the practice. Leo XIII's Bull Apostolicae Curae pronounces Anglican ordinations absolutely null and void, on defect of form and defect of intention. The Bull caused excitement in England, and Anglicans showed no disposition to accept its arguments or decision.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-annals-of-the:
The Annals of the Four Masters are Ireland's most extensive ancient annals. They run, nominally at least, from A.M. 2242 to A.D. 1616. Entries, bare early, grow fuller as the Annals progress, and towards the end become almost like history. The principal compiler was Michael O'Clery of Donegal, a trained antiquary and poet who joined the Franciscans at Louvain. Father John Colgan sent him back to Ireland to collect saints' lives. Many lives he copied from Ireland's old vellum books are preserved.

The name comes from the four compilers, most learned masters in antiquarian lore. Written in archaic language, difficult even then except for the learned, the Annals give reigns, deaths, genealogies, and dates. They cover high-kings, provincial kings, chiefs, and family heads, men of science, historians, and poets. They record saints, abbots, bishops, and dignitaries, and the foundation and occasional overthrow of countless churches, castles, abbeys, and convents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-exa:
Apostolic examiners, named by the Apostolic See for work in Rome, were instituted by Pius V in 1570 to examine candidates for holy orders and confessors. Chosen by the pope, they swear before the cardinal vicar. Under a constitution of Alexander VII in 1662, examinations for orders take place in the vicariate before at least three examiners. Only after consulting the pope may the vicar dispense a candidate, except for tonsure, the first clerical rite, which one examiner may test privately.

All candidates, whether tied to Rome or not, must pass this examination. Anyone in Rome four months or more who plans to return must face examination in the vicariate before receiving orders elsewhere, on pain of suspension. Canons of St. Peter's are examined by their cardinal archpriest. The entry is a precise guide to how Rome guarded entry to the priesthood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-exp:
Apostolic expeditors are officials who handle the sending of bulls, briefs, and rescripts, papal documents, issuing from the Apostolic Chancery, Dataria, Sacred Penitentiaria, and the Secretariat of Briefs. In a narrow sense they are laymen approved by the Dataria, after examination, to act as agents for bishops and others before the Dataria or Chancery. They count as members of the Roman court. They are not solicitors, who merely prepare documents as assistants to procurators, and from procurators or agents in general.

An expeditor deals more with matters of favour, privileges, and dispensations than with cases in litigation, and the Dataria and Chancery do business only with authorized agents of this kind. Their office is to draw up and sign needed documents, receive the answer, and forward it, for a fixed fee per transaction. The entry opens a window on the paperwork engine behind papal government.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-let: Apostolic letters carry two meanings in this short entry. First, they are the letters of the apostles to Christian groups or to those in authority. They are the Pauline epistles, including the letter to the Hebrews, together with the seven general epistles of the other apostles. Second, they are documents issued by the pope or under his name, such as bulls and briefs, the formal and less formal papal letters that govern, teach, or grant favours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assessors:
Assessors, in church law, are learned persons whose task is to advise a judge with whom they sit in trying cases. They are called assessors since they sit beside the judge, from Latin assidere. They must examine documents, consult precedents, and explore laws for points bearing on the case at issue.

A judge overburdened with business or conscious of inexperience in law may voluntarily take assessors, or superior authority may assign them. Assessors should be beyond suspicion of partiality, with conceded learning, and if a judge's acts are appealed, they make unexceptionable witnesses. As advisers, not judges, they hold no jurisdiction and bear no public character, attending trials in a private capacity, though they may take part in examining witnesses and evidence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berengarius-o:
Berengarius of Tours, an eleventh-century teacher condemned for his views on the Eucharist, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Tours about 999, he died in 1088 after study at Chartres under Fulbert, whose anxiety over his pupil's bold opinions already showed. As head of the school of St. Martin at Tours, his fame drew students from far away.

His teaching held that the bread and wine of the altar are figures and memorials of Christ's body, not that body itself in the sense later defined. Lanfranc attacked him, councils at Rome and Vercelli condemned him in 1050, and repeated retractions followed. The entry traces a brilliant mind caught in the age's fiercest doctrinal fight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cahors:
Cahors covers the whole French department of Lot, once under Bourges, then from 1676 under Albi, and after the Revolution restored in 1822 to near its old bounds under Albi. Tradition sends Saint Martial to Cahors in the first century. The first bishop known to history is Saint Florentius, correspondent of Saint Paulinus of Nola at the end of the fourth century.

Its bishops include Saint Rusticus, murdered in office, his brother Saint Desiderius, steward of King Dagobert, and Guillaume de Cavaillon, who joined the Albigensian crusade. Cahors gave birth to Jacques d'Euse, who became Pope John XXII in 1316. The Venerable Alain de Solminihac, bishop from 1636 to 1659, ranks among the great reformers of the seventeenth-century French clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-hou:
A canonical hour is each fixed portion of the Divine Office the Church appoints to be said at set hours. The term came from Jewish custom into early Christian speech, and Acts shows prayer named by its hour. Once the observance turned from optional to obligatory for certain classes by church canons, each portion took the name canonical hour, and the whole day's prayers took the name canonical hours. The term spread even to the prayer book itself, the book of hours.

The Rule of Saint Benedict is among the oldest documents using the phrase, and it passed into common speech by the next century, as Saint Isidore of Seville shows. The Breviary article treats the Office's parts, their origin, and their history. The duty itself binds daily, at least in private, all clerics in holy orders, all beneficiaries, and religious bound by rule to choir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-orde:
The Catholic Orders of Foresters were three fraternal insurance societies built on the plan of the Foresters' courts. The first, the Massachusetts Catholic Order of Foresters, was organized on 30 July 1879 by members of Boston's St. Vincent de Paul Society. By January 1909 it counted 235 courts and 27,757 members, nearly ten thousand of them women, with $27,757,000 of insurance in force.

A second body, the Catholic Order of Foresters of Illinois, followed in Chicago in 1883, moving from a flat one-dollar death assessment to a graded system after an 1895 convention. It had paid over ten million dollars in death claims by 1908. A Women's Catholic Order of Foresters, founded in Chicago in 1892, counted 54,350 members with courts across many states.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-john-:
An encyclopedia life of Charles John Seghers, the Belgian-born bishop who became known as the Apostle of Alaska. Born at Ghent in 1839 and left an orphan while still young, he was raised by uncles, trained at Louvain, and ordained a priest in 1863. Within months he sailed for Vancouver Island, where he spent a decade working among settlers and native peoples before becoming bishop there.

Seghers twice crossed into Alaska, setting up missions along the Yukon and on the island's west coast, then served briefly as Archbishop of Oregon City. He gave up that higher post to return to Victoria and resume the Alaskan work, founding missions at Sitka and Juneau in 1885. On a fifth northern trip he was murdered by a travelling companion, and his remains were later moved to Victoria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-bro:
An entry on the Brothers of the Christian Schools, a society of male religious who take no holy orders. They devote themselves to the Christian education of youth, above all poor children and artisans' sons. Founded at Reims in 1680 by Saint John Baptist de La Salle, then canon of the city church, it runs any boys' school except one teaching Latin. Its chief work is free elementary schooling.

De La Salle was moved by the ignorance of the people in knowledge and religion. He built the institute almost without a set plan, first steadying a congregation for poor girls, then backing a layman's schools for poor boys. The entry warns against thinking the Church neglected popular schooling before him, citing councils from Vaison in 529 to Trent in 1547 that ordered free teaching of the poor. It then traces the brothers' spread, rule, and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercian-ab:
Villers, on the borders of Villers and Tilly in Brabant, was the first Cistercian monastery in that territory. In April 1146 twelve monks and five lay-brothers went from Clairvaux to Boverie, sent by Saint Bernard under Abbot Lawrence. After more than a year of discouragement they moved about three miles to a better site and raised a modest oratory and dwelling. Local nobles gradually came to their aid.

Abbot Charles, from 1197 to 1209, laid the foundations of the great church, finished only about 1300. By the mid-thirteenth century Villers stood at its height, with over a hundred monks and three hundred lay-brothers, and more than fifty of its members are honoured as saints or blessed. Later, sovereigns claimed the choice of abbots, unworthy prelates intruded, and political disorder once drove the whole community away for nearly twenty years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercian-si:
The first Cistercian house for women was founded at Tart in the Diocese of Langres in 1125. Its sisters came from the Benedictine monastery of Juilly, with the help of Saint Stephen Harding, Abbot of Citeaux. Tart founded Ferraque in 1140, Blandecques in 1153, and Montreuil-les-Dames in 1164. In Spain the first house was Tulebras in 1134, followed by Las Huelgas de Burgos, Alfonso the Eighth of Castile's 1187 foundation and the most celebrated of all.

Eighteen French abbesses held their first general chapter at Tart in 1190, but Trent's cloister decrees ended the chapters and visitations. Reforms followed: Jeanne de Courcelles restored Tart's discipline and moved it to Dijon in 1625, while Angelique Arnauld reformed Port-Royal, suppressed by royal order in 1710. After the Revolution, Dom Augustin de Lestrange rebuilt the sisterhood as Trappistines, who returned to France in 1816. By 1908 the Reformed nuns held twenty-one houses with about two thousand religious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-co-consecrato:
Co-consecrators assist the presiding bishop in consecrating a new bishop. Church rule strictly requires two assistants, three bishops in all. Missionary countries, where gathering so many proves impossible, may use two priests as assistants with Holy See leave. In the present Roman Pontifical the assistants help place the Gospels on the elect's shoulders, join in laying hands on his head, and say over him Accipe Spiritum Sanctum. The consecrator alone says the Eucharistic prayer, the essential form of the rite.

So it was in ancient Western rites, where the words are a late medieval addition. In earliest times as many bishops as possible gathered, with the comprovincials at least taking part under the metropolitan. Since that proved impracticable, Nicaea enacted choice by all his province's bishops. If necessity or journey length prevented it, at least three bishops could proceed with written permission of the absent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-covenanters:
This historical entry explains who the Covenanters were: the Scots who subscribed the National Covenant of 1638 and the Solemn League and Covenant of 1643. Though the covenants as national bonds ended with Cromwell's conquest, a remnant kept them alive after the Restoration.

At stake was a struggle for supremacy between king and Kirk over who should decide Scotland's religion. Charles I sought to impose bishops and a new liturgy, while Presbyterians held that the Kirk, not the crown, governed the Church. The entry traces that clash from the Reformation under Knox and Melville through persecution and resistance, drawing on standard histories of the Scottish Kirk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crutched-fria:
This entry describes the Crutched Friars, or Crossed Friars, a mendicant order that reached England in the thirteenth century from Italy. There they were called Fratres Cruciferi. They first appeared at a Rochester diocesan synod in 1244, bearing papal documents and asking leave to settle. Each friar carried a wooden staff topped by a cross and wore a red cloth cross on his habit.

Their rule was that of Saint Augustine, and their habit, first brown or black, was changed to blue by Pius II. They founded eight or nine English houses. The first stood at Colchester or Reigate in 1245, and London followed in 1249, lending their name to the district still called Crutched Friars near Tower Hill. Their claimed first-century founding by Saint Cletus is treated as uncertain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-teniers:
An art entry untangles two Flemish landscape painters both named David Teniers, father and son. The elder was born at Antwerp in 1582 and died there in 1649. He trained under his brother, entered Rubens's school for a time, and studied under Elsheimer at Rome. He returned in 1606 to paint landscapes, rural sports, and classical scenes.

The younger was born at Antwerp in 1610 and died at Brussels in 1694. He far eclipsed his father. Likely trained in his father's studio, he married Anne Brueghel in 1637, with Rubens at the wedding. After her death in 1656 he married Isabel, daughter of Brabant's council secretary. Rich from both marriages and picture sales, he bought a chateau and served as court painter. The Louvre alone holds nearly forty of his works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-definitors-in:
A canon law entry describes definitors in religious orders, generally the governing council of an order. Usage varies: with Dominicans, all sent to represent provinces in a general chapter are definitors, and Cluniacs had a similar rule, though Benedictines normally have none. Franciscans, Carmelites, and Augustinian Hermits elect definitors in general and provincial chapters to assist superiors in government.

In that case definitors act as a kind of executive committee for the chapter, subject to its legislation. Strictly so called, they hold a decisive vote in congregation equal to the superior's, unlike mere consultors such as the Jesuits have. No superior may act in weightier matters without their vote. A definitor votes only when present, must speak candidly in conscience even against the majority, yet must sign the minority report after the vote.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dimissorial-l:
Dimissorial letters, from the Latin for letters of dismissal, are papers a church superior gives his subjects for use outside his own bounds. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains their proper sense, letters by which a bishop or regular prelate lets his man be ordained by another bishop. The name is also stretched to cover testimonial and commendatory letters for traveling clergy.

Letters of excorporation, by which clerics pass from one diocese to another, belong to the same family. The entry sets out when such letters are required and when they are merely fitting. For readers of canon law, it offers a compact guide to the paper trail that lets priests cross diocesan lines in good order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diocesan-cons:
In American dioceses, a group of priests serves as the bishop's official advisers, under the name of diocesan consultors. Together they stand in for the cathedral chapter found elsewhere under church law. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces their start to the Second Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1866. The Third Plenary Council of 1884 made them a diocesan council and fixed their rights and duties.

They number six, or at least four, where possible, and hold office for three years with renewal allowed. The entry sets out how they are chosen and what matters call for their counsel. It gives American readers the rules of a body that stands close to the bishop in governing his diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominique-bou:
Dominique Bouhours was a French Jesuit author born at Paris on 15 May 1632. At sixteen he entered the Jesuits, then taught grammar and rhetoric in Paris, Tours, and Rouen. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes his works against the Jansenists, above all two letters to a lord of the court and to the gentlemen of Port-Royal. They won wide circulation and set him among the leading critics of the seventeenth century.

He also turned the New Testament into French, a version often reprinted. English readers know him best by his lives of Saint Ignatius from 1679 and Saint Francis Xavier from 1682, both translated at London. His Art of Criticism, on thinking well in works of wit, appeared in London in 1705. He died in 1702.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Ecclesiastical letters are publications of church authority, above all of popes and bishops, sent to the faithful in letter form.
