A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that synods also issue them, but popes led the way, using the primacy to lay down laws for the whole Church and for single persons. Such letters went out on the pope's own motion or on appeal from synods, bishops, or single Christians.

Apart from the epistles of Peter, the first example is the letter of Pope Clement the First to the Corinthians, written when grave dissension split that community. Few papal letters survive from the first three Christian centuries, and the entry traces the growth of the form. It cites Laurentius and Sagmuller on a genre that carried church government by post.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-familiars:
Familiars were lay people attached to a religious house as servants. They lived under the regular prelate and shared in the house privileges. These included absolution, Easter Communion, and the last sacraments in the house. The term covered household staff and servants, not friars or monks.

The Council of Trent set rules for ordaining such household members. A man needed three years' residence in the house and a benefice before ordination. The article explains how familiars differed from oblates and servants. It also notes their share in the community's spiritual goods and prayers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family-of-rue:
The Rueckers were celebrated organ and keyboard builders of Antwerp. Hans Rueckers, who died in 1640 or 1641, joined the Guild of St Luke. His spinets used two keyboards coupled together to sound an octave apart. His son Andreas, born in 1579, carried on the family workshop.

Andreas the Younger became a maker of world renown in his own turn. Rueckers instruments reached wealthy buyers across Europe, including England. Some were later broken up so that their painted lids could be sold. The article values their sweet tone, fine craft, and painted decoration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flanders:
Flanders is a low, flat land by the North Sea, once flooded at high water. Its poor soil was made fertile by careful farming; flax, hemp, linen, and dairy goods lead its trade. The county was founded in 864, when Baldwin Iron Arm received the land from Charles the Bald. Baldwin's successors ruled a county split between a French fief and an imperial fief.

Later counts added lands, granted privileges to communes, and joined the crusades. Baldwin IX became the first Latin Emperor of Constantinople and died fighting Bulgarians in 1205. Countess Jeanne ruled wisely through her husband's captivity after Bouvines in 1214. On Margaret's death in 1279, Hainault went to the Avesnes children and Flanders to the Dampierres.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-forty-martyrs:
The Forty Martyrs were soldiers put to death for their faith at Sebaste in Lesser Armenia during the persecution of Licinius after 316. The earliest account is a homily by St. Basil of Caesarea, preached on their feast only fifty or sixty years after the event. Forty soldiers who had openly confessed their Christian faith were condemned to stand naked on a frozen pond through a bitter night. Warm baths stood nearby to tempt anyone who gave in.

One man yielded, but a guard who saw a strange brightness over the sufferers declared himself a Christian and took his place, keeping the number at forty. At dawn their bodies were burned and the ashes thrown into a river, yet Christians gathered the remains, and relics spread widely. Churches rose in their honour, and their feast is kept on 9 March in both the Greek and Latin churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fossors:
Fossors, from the Latin for diggers, were the grave diggers of the Roman catacombs in the first three or four Christian centuries. Once the Church resolved to bury its dead in cemeteries reserved for Christians alone, it needed workers to cut the underground galleries. Those workers soon ranked among the lower clergy, a rise in standing that the entry contrasts with the low esteem of pagan burial workers, the vespillones.

By the fourth century their corporation could sell burial plots, and the work also covered tomb decoration, so some fossors were painters or sculptors as well. The entry cites named fossors at Cirta in 303, a fresco of the fossor Diogenes with pick, sack, and lamp, and a second-century painting in the catacomb of St. Callistus. Fossors also kept unauthorized people out of liturgical gatherings held in the cemeteries for martyrs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-four-crowned-:
The Four Crowned Martyrs, the Quatuor Coronati, are a group venerated at the catacomb of Sts. Peter and Marcellinus on the Via Labicana outside Rome, where pilgrims came to their grave. Their story is tangled. Five sculptors from the quarries of Pannonia, named Claudius, Nicostratus, Simpronianus, Castorius, and Simplicius, refused to carve a statue of Aesculapius for a pagan temple, though they had made other pagan images. They were drowned in leaden caskets in the River Save toward the end of 305.

Later a Roman legend told of four Christian soldiers martyred at Rome for the same refusal. Because their true names were unknown, Pope Melchiades ordered them honoured on 8 November under the sculptors' names. A basilica on the Caelian Hill, first mentioned in 595, still stands as their titular church, and about 850 Pope Leo IV moved relics there from the Via Labicana. Both groups are commemorated on 8 November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-foxe-s-book-o:
John Foxe, born at Boston in Lincolnshire in 1516 and educated at Oxford, wrote the vast Protestant martyrology known as Foxe's Book of Martyrs. An extreme reformer under Edward VI, he fled to Germany in Mary's reign, worked for the printer Oporinus at Basle. He published a large Latin folio in 1559 tracing persecution from Wyclif to Cranmer. Back in England he translated and enlarged it as Acts and Monuments, published in 1563.

The book grew through editions in 1570, 1576, and 1583, and five more within a century. By 1684 it reached three folio volumes, packed with documents, letters, and woodcuts of martyrs' sufferings. Convocation ordered copies kept in cathedrals in 1571, and it became beloved in Puritan and Low Church homes. Yet the entry judges Foxe untrustworthy with evidence, sometimes mutilating documents, and notes that Catholic critics attacked him in his own day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-karl-mo:
Franz Karl Movers, born at Koesfeld in Westphalia on 17 July 1806 and died at Breslau on 28 September 1856. He was a German exegete and scholar of Scripture and eastern languages. Schooled at Koesfeld and Munster, he studied philosophy, theology, and eastern languages at Munster Academy under Laurenz Reinke and was ordained at Paderborn in autumn 1829. He continued eastern studies briefly at Bonn, tutored for Baron von Geyr at Rath, became pastor at Berkum in 1833. He became professor of Old Testament exegesis at Breslau, extraordinary in 1839 and ordinary in 1842.

His studies include critical work on the biblical Chronicle in 1834, on the Greek and Hebrew recensions of Jeremiah's prophecies in 1837, on passages illustrating the Old Testament canon in 1842. His essays in theological journals included articles in the first Kirchenlexicon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fredegis-of-t:
Fredegis of Tours, an Anglo-Saxon monk of the ninth century, studied under Alcuin first at York and then at Charlemagne's court. Known in the palace school by the name Nathaniel, he followed his teacher to Tours and succeeded him as abbot there in 804, keeping his ties to the emperor. He died at Tours in 834 with a name for deep learning.

Besides poems, Fredegis wrote a short letter-treatise asking whether nothing and darkness are real things, a question raised by their use in the opening of Genesis. He answered yes, arguing from authority and from reason, though his view never won general assent. The entry values the piece for its early use of the logical method that later grew into scholastic debate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-free-thinkers:
Free-thinkers are people who take no religious teaching on authority and rest belief on reason alone. The Catholic Encyclopedia entry defines free-thought as an extreme form of private judgment, the idea that each mind must judge doctrine for itself. A free-thinker accepts only what he feels he can prove and gives assent to nothing else.

The name arose among the English Deists, and Collins gave the movement its label in a 1713 Discourse of Freethinking. But the entry finds the same spirit far earlier, in classical scoffers at old myths and in medieval schoolmen who reasoned revelation away. From the Deists onward, it says, free thought spread from learned studies into the wider public mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-g-henry-woute:
G. Henry Wouters, a Belgian historian born at Oostham in 1802, taught church history at Liège and Louvain for over forty years. He became professor of moral theology at Liège in 1829, then moved to the restored Louvain in 1834 as professor of church history, holding the chair until 1871. He drew on Baronius, Pagi, and Noël Alexandre.

His three-volume Compendium of Church History, issued in 1842 and 1843, won wide fame and became a classic handbook in many lands. A four-volume set of dissertations followed between 1868 and 1872, meant to treat disputed questions down to Trent, but it stopped at the fourteenth century. Wouters saw church history as a helper science to theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gemblours:
Gemblours, a suppressed Benedictine monastery nine miles from Namur in Belgium, was founded about 945 by Saint Guibert. Guibert, aided by Erluin, a canon turned monk, built it for Saint Peter and the martyr Exuperius on the river Orneau. Kin challenged the gift as fiscal land, but Otto I, pleased by their defense, confirmed the house by diploma in September 946.

Erluin, its first abbot, was beaten by reform-hating monks of Lobbes in 958 while trying to renew that house. Under Olbert, abbot from 1012, discipline returned, a new church rose in 1022, and a rich library grew. Thietmar's age saw the chronicler Sigebert, whose world chronicle from 381 to 1111 Anselm continued to 1136, with Gottschalk carrying on its abbots' history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-count-o:
French historian Henri, Count of Boulainvilliers, born in 1658, pioneered the history of France's institutions as a long plea for feudalism against monarchy. A soldier until his father's death in 1697 forced him into estate research, he argued, saturated with aristocratic conviction like Saint-Simon, that conquering Franks divided Gaul among themselves as free peers. The king was a mere magistrate to settle disputes.

Crusade mortgages let wealthy commoners buy fiefs and corrupt the nobility. Ignorant lords handed justice to clerks who became the robe nobility, and Capetian kings gathered fiefs, dazzled lords into courtiers, freed communes, and packed the States General with clergy and freed serfs. Written for his grandchildren and published after his death, his works found their school only in the last twenty-five years, in Fustel de Coulanges and his followers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herbert-golds:
Herbert Goldsmith Squiers, an army officer and diplomat born at Madoc in 1859, was educated at several academies and Fordham University. He became a second lieutenant in 1877 and served with the 7th Cavalry at Wounded Knee before resigning in 1891. In diplomacy he was second secretary at Berlin in 1894 and first secretary at Peking in 1898, where Archbishop Favier received him and his family into the Church.

During the siege of the legations in 1900 Squiers served as chief of staff under Sir Claude Macdonald, who with the Russian minister called his services invaluable amid exaggerated racial feeling. He was thanked by Britain and by President McKinley. As minister to Cuba from 1902 and to Panama from 1906, his tact and firmness helped settle questions of those early days. His health broken by eight years in the tropics, he died in London in 1911, leaving burses for Catholic students and a collection of Chinese porcelain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-orders:
Holy Orders is the sacrament by which grace and spiritual power for church offices are conferred. Order first means the right arrangement of things, giving each its proper place, as Augustine defines it. It then came to mean rank itself, applied to clergy and laity, and later restricted to the hierarchy and the ranks of the clergy. It also names the outward action, ordination, by which clergy rise to that rank.

Tertullian and early writers already used the word in this sense, often with a qualifying adjective. The entry traces how Christ founded the church as a supernatural society with ordered ministry, and how the sacrament's nature, matter, and effects were understood across the ages. Readers find the theology of ordination set out from its scriptural roots to its developed form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hospitallers:
Hospitallers were religious who served the sick and poor in the hospitals of the medieval West, the Maisons-Dieu or Hôtels-Dieu. Men and women lived under one roof, followed the Rule of St. Augustine, and vowed perpetual chastity and service to the sick. Paris's Hôtel-Dieu stood out above all houses.

There, in the early 1600s, Mère Geneviève Bouquet opened a novitiate and began the custom of taking a saint's name. The congregation survived the Revolution and the disorders of 1830. Military orders of the Crusades likewise cared for the sick, aided by women's communities under the same rules, such as the Hospital Sisters of St. Lazarus and the Hospitaller Sisters of St. John of Jerusalem, founded for pilgrims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-imposters:
This entry rounds up shady figures too slight for their own articles, yet too notorious or disruptive in Church life, through lies or base conduct, to skip outright. Christ warned in the Gospels that men would use pious show to hide wicked plans.

He told hearers to watch for false prophets in sheep's clothing who were inwardly ravening wolves. He also said false Christs and false prophets would arise, working signs and wonders to mislead even the elect if they could. Other New Testament writings strike the same note: false prophets abroad in the world, lying teachers yet to come among the people. The Didache and Justin Martyr, writing about A.D. 150, show these warnings coming true early.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-institutes-of:
Looking after the sick in their own homes is the chief aim of this society, second only to the personal holiness of its members, as its constitutions put it. Its nursing sisters care for sick people at home, rich and poor alike, nursing the poor for nothing while those who can pay do so. Sixteen houses stood in France; Ireland had four, England one, the United States two, and Belgium one.

Paris kept the motherhouse, where Archbishop de Quélen started the Bon Secours sisters in 1822. Pope Pius IX gave them formal approval in June 1875. The sisters dressed in a black habit, a white frilled cap, and a black veil. The Paris congregation, the first of France's nineteenth-century home-nursing congregations, is taken up here before the others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irish-confess:
Persecution in Ireland between about 1540 and 1713 fills this long martyrology, opening with Henry VIII's break with Rome. Local acts set up the king's church supremacy, abolished papal jurisdiction, and suppressed religious houses, with the act against the pope in force from 1 November 1537. Its penalties were terrible, the entry says, and the license of enforcers worse.

Within little more than a year the Bishop of Derry told Paul III a grim tale. The king's deputy and his men were burning houses and wrecking churches. They were robbing and killing unoffending people. They were murdering priests who prayed for the pope or kept his name in the Mass. Torture awaited preachers who would not deny papal authority. The entry then names confessors and martyrs across nearly two centuries of that pressure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-japanese-mart:
No people in church history offer annals as glorious, or a martyrology as lengthy, as Japan's people, this entry claims at its outset. In January 1552 St Francis Xavier noted the early converts' proselytizing spirit. He wrote that he saw them rejoicing in successes, showing ardent zeal to spread the faith and win pagans they met to baptism. He foresaw obstacles blocking faith's progress in certain provinces, above all the absolutism of daimyo lords, then very independent of the Mikado and in revolt against his supreme authority.

In Hirado province, where Xavier made a hundred converts, six years later 600 pagans were baptized in three days. Yet a Christian woman, the proto-martyr, was beheaded there for praying before a cross. In 1561 a daimyo forced Christians into new trials. The entry follows Japanese Christianity from Xavier's hopeful start through persecution toward the great martyrdoms of Nagasaki and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-pierre-m:
Jean-Pierre Minkelers, inventor of illuminating gas, was born at Maastricht in 1748 and died there in 1824. At sixteen he went to Louvain, studied theology and philosophy at Falcon College, and became professor of natural philosophy there in 1772.

When ballooning gripped scientists, the duke of Arenberg set a committee to find the best balloon gas, and Minkelers served on it. Heating oil sealed in a gun barrel in a forge, he drew off a remarkably light gas, best for balloons, and published his memoir in 1784. His pupil records that he also lit his workshop with it, an early hint of gas lighting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-judaizers:
The Judaizers were Jewish Christians in the early Church pressing Gentile converts to accept circumcision and the Mosaic Law. At first the apostles and their converts still kept Jewish customs and ate no unclean food. They worshiped in the Temple, looking from outside like one more Jewish sect.

When the Gospel reached Gentiles, the question turned sharp: must converts take the Law, or may Jews relax the barriers that kept them apart? Most Palestinian Jews favored imposing the Law, yet the entry argues that neither forcing circumcision nor treating Gentiles as second-class could serve a Church meant for all nations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kafirs:
Kafir was a name Arab traders of the East African coast gave to nearly all South Africa's natives. It means unbeliever; the peoples themselves do not use it, distinguishing their many tribes instead. The legal list runs from Zulu, Basuto, and Bechuana through Pondo, Fingo, Griqua, Damara, Koranna, Bushman, and Hottentot. Nearly all speak Bantu, whose Kafir group divides into Xosa, Zulu, Tabele, and Mfengu.

Jesuits and Dominicans evangelized these peoples' ancestors from the fifteenth to the eighteenth centuries, but converts relapsed when the missionaries were driven out. The Zulu chief Chaka's wars at the start of the nineteenth century are said to have killed over a million people. Wars with the British and Dutch followed until 1879. South of the Zambesi there were then some five million natives. A South African commission of 1903-1905 held that only Christian faith and morals could raise their standard of conduct.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lay-brothers:
Lay brothers were religious given wholly to manual labour and a monastery's secular business, distinct from choir monks devoted to the divine office and study. They appear under names like fratres conversi, laici barbati, and illiterati.

Their origin is disputed. Mabillon credits St. John Gualbert at Vallombrosa about 1038. Yet Fonte Avellana about 1000 already set religious servants apart for manual work. Camaldoli about 1012 certainly had brethren apart from choir monks. Early Benedictine monks, mostly not clerics, all laboured by hand. By the eleventh century study had grown, more monks held orders, and illiterate recruits crowded in. Hired servants needed ordering into the family. Cistercians, Carthusians, Grandmont, and most later orders all kept lay brothers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-co:
Liturgical colours are the hues the Church assigns to vestments and altar drapery, matched to the feast or season of the day. The entry takes up their number, the garments they touch, how binding they are, how old the usage is, and what each colour is meant to signal.

Since Pius V the Roman Rite has used five: white, red, green, violet, and black, with rose on two Sundays alone. White marks feasts of the Lord, of Mary, of angels, and of non-martyr saints. Red marks martyrs, apostles, and the Passion. Green fills ordinary time, violet marks Advent and Lent, and black marks mourning and funerals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-adolphe:
Louis Adolphe Thiers was a French statesman and historian, first president of the Third Republic, born at Marseilles in 1797 and dead at Paris in 1877. As editor of the Constitutionnel he rose in the liberal press, and his ten-volume History of the French Revolution made his literary name.

Le National, founded by Thiers, Mignet, and Carrel in 1829, helped topple the Bourbons in 1830, and Thiers served often as minister under Louis-Philippe. His twenty-volume history of the Consulate and Empire followed, and after 1848 he swung toward church interests, backing the Falloux school law and the Roman expedition. In 1871 he became chief of state and president.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mendicant-fri:
Mendicant friars belong to religious orders that, by vow of poverty, gave up ownership not only singly but also in common, unlike monks, living by their own work and the faithful's charity. Hence the name begging friars. Four great mendicant orders survive from the Middle Ages, recognized by the Second Council of Lyons in 1274. They are the Order of Preachers, the Friars Minor, the Carmelites, and the Hermits of St. Augustine.

Later congregations won the same privilege, and the Council of Trent granted all mendicant orders except the Friars Minor and Capuchins the freedom of corporate possession. The entry sketches first the mendicants' origin and character, then the opposition they met. Roots are plain. After the investiture struggle, ill will toward church property lingered. Arnold of Brescia preached that propertied monks and clerics could not be saved, and John Valdes founded the Poor Men of Lyons, with similar sects following.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-minor-orders:
Minor Orders, in Latin Ordines Minores, are the lower degrees of the hierarchy, as opposed to the major or sacred orders. At present the ranks of the clergy are entered by the tonsure, after which all the orders are received in succession without omission. As a general rule ecclesiastics no longer remain in the lower orders. Clergy in higher orders now perform those liturgical tasks, as with exorcism, or layfolk do, as with singing and altar service.

In earlier times, appointment to any task reserved to churchmen marked one's entry into the clergy. The article surveys the four minor orders, porter, lector, exorcist, and acolyte, with the subdiaconate once counted among them, tracing their origin, functions, and the ceremonies of conferral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-modeste-demer:
Modeste Demers, the Pacific Coast apostle of North America, was the first Catholic missionary to most Indian tribes across Oregon, Washington, and British Columbia. He was born at St. Nicholas, Quebec, on 11 October 1809 and died at Victoria, British Columbia, on 21 July 1871. His parents, Michel Demers and Rosalie Foucher, were upright French Canadian farmers.

Sensitive in conscience and deeply drawn to religion, the young Demers chose the priesthood, learning first on his own and then at Quebec's seminary. Bishop Signay ordained him on 7 February 1836, and he spent fourteen months in parish work. He then headed for the Pacific Northwest, where he worked among natives and settlers and in time became the first Bishop of Victoria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-music-of-vesp:
The Music of Vespers deals with the texts sung at evening prayer: antiphons, psalms and hymns that change with feast and season. They follow the Ordo wherever public recitation of the Canonical Hours is obligatory. The Second Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1868 ordered complete vespers on Sundays and feasts wherever possible after the Roman fashion, never replaced by other devotions.

To spread the practice, the council ordered Gregorian chant rudiments taught in parish schools so congregations could join ministers and choir in song. A rescript of 1882 banned the custom of singing only some verses of psalms, and the Third Plenary Council of 1884 commanded integral psalms wherever vespers are performed. The entry then surveys chant books, harmonisations and the practical problems of preparing changing antiphons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nevers:
Nevers is a diocese covering the Department of Nievre in France. Suppressed by the Concordat of 1801 and united to Autun, it was restored in 1823 as suffragan of Sens, taking parts of the former dioceses of Autun and Auxerre. Gallia Christiana names Saint Eladius, healed in Clovis's reign by Saint Severinus, as its first bishop.

Duchesne counts Tauricanus, present at Epaon in 517, as the first authentic bishop. Several later bishops are venerated as saints, including Arey, Agricola, and Jerome, who rebuilt the cathedral for martyrs Quiricus and Julitta. Notable bishops include the future cardinal Pierre Bertrandi, who defended church immunities against barons in 1329 to 1330. Charles de Bourbon, whom the Leaguers wished to make King of France as Charles X, also held the see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-taci:
A Franciscan scholar of Scripture from the Low Countries, Nicholas Tacitus Zegers worked at Louvain in the first half of the sixteenth century. Trained in Greek and Hebrew, he took over the chair of biblical explanation there in 1536 and gave it up in 1548 to write full time.

Zegers left many books, with notes on all the New Testament books and corrections to the New Testament text. He also made a kind of concordance and translations of devotional works from Flemish and French into Latin. He died at Louvain in 1559. His Greek and Hebrew learning set his criticism apart in an age when such judgment was rare.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-non-jurors:
The Non-Jurors were Anglican clergy and laity who in 1689 refused to swear allegiance to William and Mary. Their episcopal leaders, Sancroft of Canterbury with Turner, Lloyd, White, Thomas, Ken, Lake, and Cartwright, faced suspension by August and deprivation by the following February if they held out.

Most held out and lost their sees, joined by some four hundred clergy including Hickes, Collier, Kettlewell, and Nelson. Though five bishops had resisted James II, they would accept William only as regent, not as king, and their schism shaped Anglican life for decades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notre-dame-de:
Notre-Dame des Ardilliers, a shrine at Saumur in France, centers on a statue found by a spring in 1454. A monastery Charlemagne founded there fell to Normans, and its last monk kept only a statue of Our Lady in a cave by the spring, the image later recovered and honored.

Miracles at the spring, whose waters were held healing, led to a chapel dedicated in 1553, enlarged notably by Richelieu, and entrusted to Oratorians in 1614. Louis XIII, Anne of Austria, and Marie de' Medici numbered among its pilgrims, and Sulpician founders sought inspiration there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-prea:
The Order of Preachers, or Dominicans, joins friars, sisters, and lay penitents under Dominic's preaching mission, and this entry covers all three branches. Dominic's preaching in Languedoc against Albigensians led Innocent III's letters of 1205 to shape a new kind of apostolic preacher, patterned on the apostles.

Legislation for friars and sisters grew together, and the historical survey follows foundations, studies, missions, and the Inquisition's shadow. The entry details constitutions, government, habit, and the order's schools, saints, and missions across eight centuries. The order’s legislation grew closely with its history, a point the entry stresses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pamiers:
Pamiers is a French diocese covering the department of Ariege, suffragan of Toulouse. Joined to Toulouse by the Concordat of 1801, it rose again by the Concordat of 1817. The new diocese took effect only in September 1823. It united old Pamiers and Couserans with most of Mirepoix and Rieux and a deanery of Alet. A 1910 decree restored the titles of Couserans and Mirepoix.

Tradition names Saint Antoninus, born near Pamiers and martyred in his home country, as first apostle of the region. His abbey, founded about 960, passed to Girona in 1034 and to Cluny in 1060. Roger II of Foix built a castle on the site called Appamia, whence Pamiers. Boniface VIII raised the see by bull of 23 July 1295, named Bernard Saisset its bishop, and fixed bounds carved from Toulouse, despite the Toulouse bishop's opposition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parochial-reg:
Parochial registers are the five books a pastor must keep to know his flock: baptisms, confirmations, marriages, deaths, and a census of souls. Trent's command that a shepherd know his subjects, plus the historical weight and legal proof of public records, grounds the rule. Set forms govern entries, and every public paper must show place, date, and nature of the act, officiant, parties, witnesses, and official signature.

Church law adds parentage and parish for each person, the officiant's office, and full detail to remove doubt over validity or form. A baptism entry thus notes legitimacy, birth date, and names given, plus private, conditional, or supplied ceremonies where they apply. Foundlings' entries record where, when, and by whom they were found, with apparent age, and later pages cover corrections, secrecy, and custody of the books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrician-bro:
The Patrician Brothers, or Brothers of Saint Patrick, were founded by Daniel Delaney, Bishop of Kildare and Leighlin, at Tullow in County Carlow, on the Purification feast in 1808. Their aim was religious and literary schooling for youth and instruction of the faithful in Christian devotion. Catholic Ireland was just emerging from penal-law times, when procuring Catholic schooling for a child counted as treason.

Young and old alike thus lacked teaching, and Delaney chose seven Sunday-school catechists as the new order's nucleus. Under his own training and his successor Doyle's direction, the congregation took root as a diocesan body. Daughter houses spread through Ireland, and bishops invited the brothers to Australia and India, where several foundations rose. Later pages follow their schools, rules, and growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-melchers:
Paul Melchers was Cardinal Archbishop of Cologne, born at Muenster in Westphalia on 6 January 1813 and dead at Rome on 14 December 1895. He read law at Bonn from 1830 to 1833, practised briefly at Muenster, then studied theology at Munich under Klee, Goerres, Windischmann, and Doellinger. Ordained in 1841, he served at Haltern village, became seminary vice-rector in 1844, rector in 1851, cathedral canon in 1852, and vicar-general in 1854.

Pius IX made him Bishop of Osnabrueck in 1857 and Archbishop of Cologne in 1866. There he laboured zealously and launched the annual Fulda meetings of German bishops in 1867. Though he always taught papal infallibility, he judged its definition untimely, saying so with thirteen bishops in 1869. At Vatican I he voted against it on 13 July 1870, yet refused to join fifty-five others in a protest departure, and later submitted fully.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulist-fathe:
The Paulist Fathers are a community of priests for missions and apostolic works, above all winning converts to Catholic faith. Founded at Rome and New York in 1858 by Isaac Thomas Hecker, with Augustine Hewit, George Deshon, Francis Baker, and Clarence Walworth, they had all belonged to the Redemptorists. Suspected of disloyalty and accused of disobedience, they sought to explain themselves to their superior general, and Hecker, reaching Rome in 1857, was expelled from the Redemptorists three days later.

Appeal to the Holy See failed to win approval of the expulsion, and at their own request the priests were dispensed from vows and formed the new community. Propaganda letters warmly commended Hecker and his fellows to American bishops. Long before, Hecker felt distinct intimations that he was set apart to lead his country's conversion in some conspicuous way, and he told many, singly and together, of those supernatural visitations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-penitential-o:
Penitential orders were religious congregations bound to harsh works of penance, or to helping others atone for grave faults. This Catholic Encyclopedia survey names the great families first. They run from Capuchins and Carmelites to the Third Orders of Dominic and Francis and the Sisters of the Good Shepherd, each treated under its own heading. It then lingers on smaller and stranger communities that fit the same pattern.

Hermits of St. John the Baptist in Navarre lived eight to a hermitage in silence and mortification, wearing rough brown habits and heavy wooden crosses. A French reform of hermit life under Michel de Sabine admitted only men of proven character and delayed final vows until age forty-five. The survey closes with the Polish and Bohemian Order of Penance of the Holy Martyrs, whose origins writers disputed back to Pope Cletus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-donders:
Peter Donders was a Dutch missionary to lepers in Suriname, born at Tilburg in 1807. A childhood wish for the priesthood survived factory work and service in a college, where a benefactor's help finally let him study at Herlaar. Reading the Annals of the Propagation of the Faith fixed his call abroad. Accepted for Dutch Guiana in 1839 and ordained in 1840, he reached Paramaribo in 1842.

He baptised 1,200 plantation workers by 1850, caught the epidemic of 1851 himself, and recovered to work among the Saramaca Indians too. From 1855 he lived at Batavia, ministering nearly thirty-two years to 600 lepers, leaving them only to visit blacks and Indians. When Redemptorists took the colony in 1865 he joined them, learned music to cheer his charges, and laboured to the end in 1887.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-of-poit:
Peter of Poitiers was a French scholastic theologian, born near Poitiers about 1130. He studied at Paris, taught theology there for thirty-eight years, and succeeded Peter Comestor in the scholastic chair in 1169. His lectures shone so brightly that Walter of St. Victor, a fierce foe of scholasticism, mocked him with Abelard, Gilbert de la Porrée, and Peter Lombard as one of the Four Labyrinths of France.

In 1179 he published five books of sentences summing up his lectures. His teaching stayed orthodox, yet the entry finds more empty subtlety than scriptural theology in it, grist for critics who call scholasticism mere wordplay. As chancellor of Paris he cared for poor students, having lecture synopses engraved on classroom walls since books cost too much. He died at Paris in 1215, chancellor still, not bishop of Embrun.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poitiers:
Poitiers is a French diocese covering the departments of Vienne and Deux-Sèvres, suffragan to Bordeaux. The Concordat of 1802 joined to the ancient see part of the diocese of La Rochelle and Saintes. Its earliest episcopal catalogue, a twelfth-century tradition, lists twelve predecessors of Saint Hilary, though Duchesne doubts they were truly bishops of Poitiers.

Hilary, bishop from about 350, is the first with solid historical evidence. Among his successors were Fortunatus, Gilbert de la Porrée, and a long line of cardinals, from Arnauld d'Aux in 1312 to Pie, made cardinal in 1879. As early as 312 the bishop founded a school near his cathedral whose pupils included Hilary himself, Maximus of Trier, and the poet Ausonius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presentation-:
In the early nineteenth century, as the Penal Laws eased, the long ban on Catholic schooling of youth in Ireland lifted. Irish Catholics seized their new freedom, and several new religious congregations of men and women sprang up. Among them stood the Institute of Presentation Brothers, Edmund Ignatius Rice's 1802 foundation. The Brothers stayed a diocesan congregation approved by Rome until 1889, when their constitution changed to speed growth.

All houses then came under one superior general, and Leo XIII approved the new constitutions. Since then the order has spread fast. It holds several branches in each Irish province, and stands also in England and Canada. The Brothers run colleges, primary schools, industrial schools, and orphanages, and a new novitiate and training college rose at Mount St Joseph, Cork. The Commissioners of National Education fully approved the institute's training methods and recognized the training college.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-queen-s-daugh:
The Queen's Daughters form a religious and charitable society founded at Saint Louis, Missouri, on 5 December 1889, by Mary Hoxsey. This encyclopedia entry explains its purpose: to supplement the home visits to the poor made by members of the Conferences of Saint Vincent de Paul. The Very Reverend P. P. Brady approved and encouraged it in his parish. Papal sanction and blessing followed on 17 July 1894.

Since then the society has spread to many American parishes, with thirty-five associations joined to the Saint Louis centre. Its constitution sets government by a general council, made up of subordinate councils and associations. Five or more associations in a diocese may form a subordinate council with its own bylaws and officers. The Blessed Virgin stands as patroness. The motto runs Ad Majorem Dei Gloriam. One house in Providence keeps a day nursery and visits the sick poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regulars:
Regulars takes its name from the Latin regula, rule: observance of the Rule of Saint Benedict won monks the name at an early date. The Council of Verneuil in 755 uses it in its third canon. Its eleventh canon sets the ordo regularis against the ordo canonicus, the canons living under their bishop by canonical regulation. A rule for canons also grew up, drawing on the rule Saint Chrodegang, Bishop of Metz, framed from the sacred canons in 766.

When canons split into two classes in the eleventh century, those who added religious poverty to common life were called regulars, and those who gave up common life were called seculars. The entry adds two cautions. Novices count as regulars only in a wider sense, and writers disagree whether members of other orders merit the name before solemn profession, under Gregory the Thirteenth's constitution Ascendente.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scala-sancta-:
The Scala Sancta, or Holy Stairs, are twenty-eight white marble steps at Rome near the Lateran. Tradition calls them the staircase to Pilate's praetorium at Jerusalem, made holy by Christ's footsteps during his Passion. Their entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows the monument from Jerusalem to its present site.

Historians of the shrine say Helena, mother of Constantine, brought the stairs from Jerusalem to Rome about 326. In the Middle Ages they were known as Pilate's Stairs, leading to a Lateran corridor near St Sylvester's chapel, roofed over, with side stairs for ordinary use. When Sixtus V razed the old papal palace in 1589 and built anew, he moved the stairs before the Sancta Sanctorum, the Holy of Holies chapel of St Lawrence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seekers:
An obscure Puritan group that rose in England in the middle 1600s, the Seekers claimed to be hunting for the true Church, Scripture, ministry, and sacraments, which they held to be lost. This short Catholic Encyclopedia entry leans on the contemporary account of Richard Baxter. He reported their teaching that present Scripture was uncertain. He said they held that fresh miracles were needed for faith. He added that they counted existing ministry and worship as nothing.

Baxter also charged, in a claim the entry flags as absurd, that Catholics had hatched the group. Other writers linked the Seekers with the Vanists or read millenarian hopes into them. The entry concludes that the name likely marked a school of thought rather than a firmly organized body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seven-robbers: Seven robbers martyred on Corcyra, now Corfu, in the second century are commemorated in this brief entry. Their names were Saturninus, Insischolus, Faustianus, Januarius, Marsalius, Euphrasius, and Mammius. Saints Jason and Sosipater, preaching on the island, were thrown into a dungeon where the seven were held. They converted the robbers, who were then taken outside the city and martyred in cauldrons of seething oil and pitch. Greek menologies mark them on 27 or 29 April, while the Roman martyrology keeps 20 April.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sicilian-vesp:
The Sicilian Vespers is the traditional name for the rising that broke out at Palermo on Easter Tuesday, 31 March 1282, against the rule of Charles of Anjou. The name itself, and the legend of Easter bells calling rebels to arms, arose only in the fifteenth century, during the excitement over Charles VIII's passage in 1494. Charles, Count of Provence and brother of Saint Louis, had received the crown of the Two Sicilies from Urban IV after it was taken from the Hohenstaufens.

Having beaten Manfred and crushed the Ghibelline revolt of Conradin in 1268, with 130 barons condemned to death, Charles stood master of the Two Sicilies and aimed at dominion across the Mediterranean. He bought claims to Jerusalem, held Armenia's protection, drew tribute from Tunis, and planned a crusade against Constantinople. The Palermo rising wrecked those plans and opened a long, fruitless war against the House of Aragon, settled only by compromise in 1302.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-fr:
The Society of Friends, an Anglo-American religious sect first calling themselves Children of Truth and Children of Light, were nicknamed Quakers in scorn. Founder George Fox, a weaver's son born at Fenny Drayton, Leicestershire, in July 1624, was apprenticed to a shoemaker after rejecting a hireling ministry. In his nineteenth year a voice he believed from heaven told him to forsake all and be a stranger to all, and he wandered seeking light.

Fox taught reliance on the inward light over rites and sacraments. His followers refused tithes, oaths, and army service, drawing persecution. Under Charles II some 13,562 Quakers were imprisoned in England, 198 transported, and 338 died in prison or from assaults. William Penn shielded them and gave them refuge in Pennsylvania. After James II persecution eased, and later acts removed their legal disabilities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-ma:
The Society of Mary, or Marist Fathers, is a religious order of priests devoted to the Blessed Virgin. The idea arose in Lyons in 1816 among seminarians, but Jean-Claude-Marie Colin was the real founder. Bishop Devie of Belley authorized Colin and companions in 1823 to form a missionary band for rural districts. Gregory XVI approved the Priests of the Society of Mary definitively in 1836, and Colin became superior general that September.

Under four superiors general to 1910 the society worked in France, the British Isles, the United States, New Zealand, and Oceanica. French provinces counted 340 priests, 100 novices, and 34 lay brothers before the Association Act of 1901 dissolved communities and seized property. The society then counted six provinces, with American houses in eleven states and training houses at Washington.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-desiderius:
Desiderius of Cahors moved from the Merovingian court to a bishop's throne. This entry follows a career built on loyalty, learning, and steady administration. He was born to a noble Frankish family of Aquitaine. Schooled at the court of Chlotar II, he served as royal treasurer under Dagobert. He became bishop of Cahors after his brother Rusticus was murdered in 630. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 gives his death as 15 November 655.

Court life did not loosen his discipline. The piece stresses the monk-like seriousness he kept amid royal business. His mother's pious letters had shaped him. His brothers rose beside him: one to Cahors before him, one to high civic office. So the entry also sketches a family woven into Frankish power. It ends as a portrait of a bishop formed by the palace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gregory-of:
Gregory of Tours, bishop and historian, wrote the Franks' story while governing a city through civil war. Born in 538 or 539 at Arverni, modern Clermont-Ferrand, to a distinguished Gallo-Roman house, he was first called Georgius Florentius. He later took Gregory for his maternal great-grandfather, bishop of Langres. Losing his father young, he was raised by his uncle Gallus of Clermont, then by the priest Avitus. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Tours to 17 November 593 or 594.

An illness turned him toward church service. His History of the Franks preserves his age's voice. As bishop he faced kings who increased power by violence, until endless civil war made might seem right itself. During Sigebert and Chilperic's war he cried that the woes of his people hurt the Church more than Diocletian's persecution. The entry joins pastor and chronicler in one troubled reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hilary-of-:
Hilary of Poitiers, bishop and doctor, turned a noble pagan's learning into the West's great defence against Arianism. Born at Poitiers early in the fourth century, he came of a noble, very probably pagan family. He mastered profane learning, then studied Scripture. There he found the truth he ardently sought, renounced idolatry, and was baptized. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Poitiers to 1 November, or 13 January 368 by the Breviary.

About 350 his learning and zeal won him governance of Poitiers' faithful, a body existing since the third century. Hilary is the first of its bishops about whom true information survives, thanks to his part against heresy. Arianism had ravaged regions and threatened invasion, while papal power in practice could neither prevent nor stop internal discord. The entry follows a convert bishop into theological war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-martin-of-:
Born at Sabaria in Pannonia around 316, Martin of Tours first served as a Roman soldier before he became one of Gaul's most beloved bishops. At Amiens he famously shared his cloak with a shivering beggar, then sought baptism and freedom from the army. He joined St Hilary at Poitiers, lived as a hermit at Ligugé, and drew so many followers that a monastic community grew around him.

Dragged almost against his will to the see of Tours in 371 or 372, he kept his plain hermit habits while ruling the diocese, founding the monastery of Marmoutier across the Loire. He preached through central and western Gaul, pleaded at Trier for condemned men, and resisted handing the heretic Priscillian to secular courts. He died at Candes, most probably in 397.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-statute-of-pr:
The Statute of Provisors, the English act 25 Edward III, statute 4, of 1350 to 1351, curbed papal appointments to English benefices. It arose from the long and angry controversy, in Lingard's phrase, between English kings and Rome. The quarrel concerned filling church livings by papal provision, whereby the pope suspended a patron's right and nominated his own candidate, called a provisor.

Possession of English livings by Italians provoked at one thirteenth-century period acts of lawless violence. Gregory IX had pronounced against provisions infringing lay patrons' rights, and Innocent IV expressed general disapprobation in 1253. From the statute's recitals it appears that papal bestowal of English benefices and their revenues had grown intolerable. The entry sets a famous act within a century of crown and papacy contention.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stedingers:
The Stedingers, Frisian peasants along the shore of northern Germany, revolted against their lord, the archbishop of Bremen, and were crushed by crusade. Their name means those living along a shore. They refused tithes and forced labour as serfs, duties demanded with considerable severity, and Archbishop Gerhard II sent troops against them.

His troops lost in 1229. The Stedingers then wrecked churches and monasteries, and abused and slew priests. A Bremen synod on 17 March 1230 accused them of contempt for church authority and sacraments and of superstitious practices, and excommunicated them. Refusing submission, they faced a crusade preached by Gregory IX's bull of 9 October 1232, after Frederick II had banned them. An army advanced and subdued them in battle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-surnames-of-f:
Medieval custom gave celebrated doctors surnames that summed up their excellence, and this entry lists the principal examples with death dates. Theology supplies Angelicus for Thomas Aquinas, dead in 1274. It also gives Arca testamenti for Anthony of Padua, dead in 1231, Eximius for Suárez, dead in 1617, and Dulcifluus for Antonius Andreas, dead in 1320.

Law supplies its own roll. It includes Speculator for William Durandus, dead in 1296, Speculum Juris for Bartolus of Sassoferrato, dead in 1359, and Pater Juris for Innocent III, dead in 1216. Dozens more names fill both lists, from Acutissimus for Sixtus IV to Subtilis for two later writers, making the entry a handy key to medieval nicknames.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synodal-exami:
Synodal examiners are chosen in a diocesan synod, and this entry sets out Trent's rules for them. Trent requires at least six, while the Congregation of the Council fixed twenty as ample. Their chief task is running competitive examinations, called concursus, though they may be assigned other examinations as well. Candidates are proposed singly each year by the bishop or his vicar-general.

Each nominee needs the synod's approval by majority vote, secret or public as the bishop decides, and should hold at least a licentiate in theology or canon law. Once appointed, examiners serve until the next synod, swear to act without prejudice or favour, and must refuse presents on pain of simony. If their number falls below six within a year, the bishop with his chapter may fill it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-apostolic:
Christian writers of the first and second centuries who knew the Apostles, or were shaped directly by their teaching, are gathered under this name. Though some use the term only for actual disciples, it stretches in practice to cover nearly all surviving primitive Christian writing before the great apologies of the second century. These works form the bridge between the New Testament and later tradition.

Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Polycarp, the Didache, the Shepherd of Hermas, and the Epistle of Barnabas all appear, with accounts of each text, its date, and its witness. Jean-Baptiste Cotelier's 1672 edition gave the group its modern label. For students of early faith, the entry maps a small but vital body of writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-crosiers:
Canons Regular of the Holy Cross, called Crosiers, are the order traced here from a Liège canonry to wide lands. Théodore de Celles, after following Frederick Barbarossa on crusade, won a canonry at Saint Lambert's, Liège. On Holy Cross Exaltation, 14 September 1211, he and four fellow canons vowed before Liège's bishop, who gave them Saint Theobald's church at Claire-Lieu near Huy for their first house.

Innocent III approved the order by word in 1215, Honorius III in writing, confirmed by Innocent IV on 3 May 1248. France, Netherlands, Germany, and England soon held Crosier houses. Preaching to Albigenses with Dominic, martyrdom in Livonia under Prague's Bishop Albert in 1246, and service with Saint Louis on crusade mark their early zeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-military-:
Brotherhoods of knights, sacred and secular, crowd this survey, numbering near a hundred once sham and stillborn orders are struck out. War and religion, the twin trades of the Middle Ages, explain their appeal. Kings later turned the idea to their own ends, founding royal orders to reward loyal nobles until no country lacked its princely order.

Private adventurers joined the trade, decking dupes with sham insignia sold at a price. Marino Caraccioli, a Neapolitan noble, passed himself off as grand master of an order in 1624, a cautionary tale among many. Genuine orders, their rules, crusading service, and decline receive the main attention, mapping chivalry's sacred and courtly faces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-ten-thous:
Two groups of ten thousand martyrs, entered in the Roman Martyrology on different days, are sifted here. March 18 reads: at Nicomedia ten thousand holy martyrs put to the sword for confessing Christ. June 22 reads: on Mount Ararat ten thousand holy martyrs crucified. The first likely honours victims at Diocletian's persecution opening in 303, as Eusebius and Lactantius confirm.

Numbers need not exaggerate, the entry argues, given the scale of that persecution. June's entry rests on a legend translated from a lost Greek original by Anastasius Bibliothecarius, who died in 886, and dedicated to Peter, Bishop of Sabina. Emperors Adrian and Antoninus marching against Gadarenes opens a tale the entry treats as pious fiction, not history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-third-orders:
Third Orders are lay men and women joined to a religious order while still living ordinary lives outside a monastery or convent. They may wear the order's habit, share in its prayers and good works, and follow a rule fitted to life in the world. The Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces this pattern from early lay associates of monks through its full growth in the thirteenth century.

Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites, Servites and others each get their own section, with separate treatment of secular tertiaries and regular communities. Readers also find rules for members, lists of privileges, and reports on the orders in Canada, Britain, Ireland and the United States. It suits anyone tracing how laypeople took part in monastic life without leaving home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-three-chapter:
The Three Chapters were three sets of writings condemned in the sixth century. They were the person and works of Theodore of Mopsuestia, certain works of Theodoret of Cyrus, and the letter of Ibas to Maris. Emperor Justinian's edict of late 543 or early 544 anathematized them, hoping to win back the Monophysites, who charged the Church with Nestorianism. Those who refused the condemnation were said to defend the Chapters.

The quarrel runs in three stages. They stretch from the edict through Pope Vigilius's time at Constantinople and his ratification of the Second Council of Constantinople, to the healing of the Western schisms that followed. Greek bishops mostly yielded under pressure, while Latin bishops, including Dacius of Milan and Facundus of Hermiane, stood firm. Facundus's Defence of the Three Chapters remains the classic plea for their side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tours:
Tours is an archdiocese covering Indre-et-Loire in France, re-established by the Concordat of 1801 with Angers, Nantes, Le Mans, Rennes, Vannes, Saint-Brieuc and Quimper as suffragans. Rennes became a metropolitan see in 1859, taking the last three, while Laval, created in 1855, stayed subject to Tours. Its early history rests on Gregory of Tours's chapter on the bishops of Tours.

Gregory names Gatianus, one of seven apostles sent from Rome to Gaul in the mid-third century, as founder, though Duchesne doubts the date 250 and admits only a Constantinian founding. After Gatianus came Litorius, then the great Martin, bishop from 372 to 397, then Brice. The city later opened its gates to Clovis in 507, faced Saracens in 732 and Northmen from 853 to 903, and passed to English rule until 1214.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tunkers:
A Protestant sect named from the German tunken, to dip, also called Dunkards, Dunkers, Brethren and German Baptists. Besides Baptist teaching they hold distinctive practices: the candidate kneels in the water and is dipped forward three times, honouring the three Persons of the Trinity.

Communion follows the primitive pattern, held in the evening, preceded by the love-feast or agape and followed by the kiss of charity, with foot-washing on certain occasions. Founded by Alexander Mack at Schwarzenau in 1708 with seven companions, the body emigrated to America between 1719 and 1729 and organized its first church at Germantown in 1723.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
The University of Angers probably grew from the cathedral school of that city. Early in the eleventh century the school became famous under Marbodus, later Bishop of Rennes, and Ulger, later Bishop of Angers. Both men had studied under the famed canonist Fulbert de Chartres. In 1229 the school was enlarged by students, many of them Englishmen, who fled Paris to escape the direct control of the French king. Angers then became a centre for civil law.

It counted as a studium generale, though it was officially recognized as such only in 1337 by an episcopal ordinance. In 1364 King Charles V granted it a charter with the same privileges as the University of Orléans. Only in 1432 did it gain a faculty of theology, the entry notes, with medicine and arts following. The result is a compact history of a provincial university shaped by exile, law, and royal favour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-use-of-beads-:
Beads strung in set kinds, orders, and numbers help Catholics keep count in prayers that repeat their parts, a common expedient in forms of devotion. Made from plain wood or natural berries up to costly metals and precious stones, beads may be blessed with prayer and holy water, becoming sacramentals. In that character most religious orders, of men and women alike, prescribe them for personal use or as part of the religious habit.

Today beads appear mostly as the Dominican Rosary, or Marian Psalter, but Catholics also know Brigittine beads, Dolour beads, Immaculate Conception beads, and the Crown of Our Saviour. The entry traces the counting device from early knotted cords to the modern rosary, explaining each form's prayers and indulgences. It offers a practical guide to a humble tool of prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-mathew-fl:
Mathew Flathers, alias Major, was an English priest and martyr born probably about 1580 at Weston in Yorkshire, who died at York on 21 March 1607. Schooled at Douai and ordained at Arras on 25 March 1606, he was sent to the English mission three months later. Government agents, redoubling their hunt for priests after the Gunpowder Plot, discovered him almost at once.

Tried under the statute of 27 Elizabeth on the charge of receiving orders abroad, he was condemned to death. By an unusual act of clemency the sentence was commuted to lifelong banishment, but after a brief exile the undaunted priest returned to England to fulfil his mission. After ministering a short time to his oppressed fellow Catholics in Yorkshire, he was seized again, tried, and executed at York.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vespers:
Vespers is the evening office of the Church, treated here under six headings: its sixth-century form, its origin, its medieval variations, its latest changes, its symbolism and hymns, and its importance. In the sixth century, as described in St Benedict's Rule, the evening gathering comprised four psalms. A short reading, a response, a hymn, a versicle, the Gospel canticle Magnificat, litany, Lord's Prayer, prayer, and dismissal.

Pliny's early second-century letter already mentions Christian gatherings morning and evening, making Vespers, with Vigils, among the most ancient offices known. Later sections trace how Compline reshaped the old lucernarium, the lamp-lighting service, how psalm choices varied between the Benedictine arrangement and the Roman order's five psalms. How hymns entered the Roman evening office only in more recent times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vivarini-fami:
The Vivarini were a family of Venetian painters, and the entry's centre is Alvise Vivarini, born in 1446 or 1447 and dying in 1502. Son of Antonio and pupil of his uncle Bartolomeo, little is known of his youth. In 1488 he begged the Signoria to let him prove his skill beside the two Bellini in decorating the Grand Council's hall.

Granted, his pictures there have vanished, but in 1492 he received the honorary title Painter in the Great Council and five ducats a month. Long dismissed by critics as Bellini's pupil, foreman, or unimportant Murano imitator, Alvise was restored by Bernhard Berenson's work on Lotto to his rightful place. He stands as an eminent, original Venetian master of the fifteenth century, no follower of Bellini but great in his own right. He was master of Cima, Lotto, Mantegna, and Bonsignori, exercising a great and lasting influence on his successors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-viviers:
Viviers is a French diocese covering the Ardèche, suppressed by the Concordat of 1802 and joined to Mende. Then restored in 1822 from most of old Viviers plus parts of Valence, Vienne, Le Puy, and Uzès, as suffragan to Avignon. St Andéol, disciple of Polycarp, evangelized the Vivarais under Septimius Severus and was martyred in 208, his body buried by Blessed Tullie.

The Old Charter of 950, drawn up by Bishop Thomas, is the fullest document on Viviers' primitive Church, naming five bishops at Alba Augusta, Januarius, Septimus, Maspicianus, Melanius. Avolus, the last a victim of the barbarian Chrocus's invasion. After Alba's ravages, St Auxonius moved the see to Viviers about 430. Later canonized bishops include Lucian, Valerius, Venantius, present at councils in 517 and 535, Melanius II, Eucherius, Firminus, Aulus, Eumachius, and Longinus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-white-fathers:
The White Fathers, Missionaries of Our Lady of Africa of Algeria, known in French as Pères Blancs, were founded in 1868 by Algiers's first archbishop, later Cardinal Lavigerie. The famine of 1867 left many Arab orphans, and educating and instructing those children occasioned the society's founding. From the start Lavigerie aimed at converting the Arabs and black peoples of Central Africa.

Mission posts arose in Kabylia and the Sahara, and in 1876 and 1881 two caravans from southern Algeria and Ghadames, seeking Sudan missions, were massacred by their guides. Upper Congo, with French Sudan founded in 1894 and Sahara missions grouped in a prefecture. In 1880, at the Holy See's request, the White Fathers opened a Greek Melkite seminary at Jerusalem. Though bound by oath to labour for Africa's conversion, they are not strictly a religious order and may retain personal property.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilhelm-wilme:
Wilhelm Wilmers was a Westphalian Jesuit who taught philosophy and theology across Europe and wrote widely used religion textbooks. Born at Boke in 1817, he died at Roermond in 1899. He joined the Jesuits in 1834, was driven from Switzerland with his order in 1847, and took orders in France in 1848. Teaching posts followed at Issenheim, Louvain, Cologne, Bonn, Aachen, and Maria-Laach.

Wilmers served as a theologian at the Cologne provincial council in 1860 and at the Vatican Council in 1870. Later he taught at Poitiers, Saint Helier, and Jersey, then gave himself wholly to writing in England and Holland. His textbooks on religion, first issued in the 1850s and 1870s, ran through many editions and several languages. His last works, on revealed religion and the Church, appeared in 1897, with a third volume finished after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-abbot:
William, Abbot of Marmoutiers, was a Breton monk who fought his archbishop over the terms of his blessing. Born in Brittany, he died at Marmoutiers on 23 May 1124. He had served as Archdeacon of Nantes, gave up that rank to enter the Benedictine house at Marmoutiers, and was chosen abbot in 1105 after Hilgotus died. Archbishop Rudolph II of Tours, who had often trampled the abbey's rights, refused him blessing unless he swore loyalty and pressed his right hand into the archbishop's.

William would swear but not yield his hand, and Saint Ivo of Chartres backed him in letters to Pope Paschal II. William went to Rome and took his blessing from the pope himself. Through Ivo and other bishops, abbot and archbishop made peace around 1115. William sat at the Poitiers synod in 1106 and gained the Abbey of Cellen-Brie from the Bishop of Meaux in 1107.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-po:
William of Poitiers was a Norman historian and chaplain to William the Conqueror, whose life of the king survives in a single battered manuscript. Born of a noted family at Préaux about 1020, he studied at Poitiers and fought as a knight in several battles. Then he took orders and became the Conqueror's chaplain, resolving to write his history. Hugh of Lisieux made him archdeacon, serving under Hugh and Gilbert Maminot in a circle debating astronomy and mathematics.

William knew Greek and Latin letters and taught verse to young students, earning praise from Ordericus Vitalis. His Gesta Guilelmi, offered to King William between 1071 and 1077, survives only in a Cottonian manuscript, its opening to 1047 and its close from 1068 lost. Drawing on Dudon, lost annals, witnesses, and his own memory, he gives a careful if panegyrical contemporary source, prized for Harold's stay in Normandy and the Conquest itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-weath:
William Weathers was titular Bishop of Amycla and the long-serving president of Saint Edmund's College, Old Hall. Born on 12 November 1814 to Welsh Protestant parents, he died at Isleworth in 1895. His mother and children converted after his father's death. Schooled by Franciscans at Baddesley and at Old Hall, he stayed forty years there, holding every office. He was master before ordination in 1838, prefect of discipline, vice-president, prefect of studies, and president from 1851 to 1868.

Weathers's presidency reshaped college rules and welcomed lay convert Ward as theology lecturer from 1852 to 1858. When Manning tried to hand the seminary to the Oblates of Saint Charles in 1855, the chapter appealed to Rome and the Oblates withdrew in 1861. In 1869 Manning moved the divines to Hammersmith and made Weathers rector until Vaughan closed it in 1892. Weathers, a bishop from 1872, then served as chaplain to the Sisters of Nazareth at Isleworth and wrote on electricity and magnetism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-xaverian-brot:
Xaverian Brothers are an institute founded by Theodore James Ryken at Bruges in 1839 under episcopal approval. Ryken crossed to America in 1837 seeking views, winning letters from seven bishops. Back in Europe, Bishop Boussens sanctioned his plan if Ryken first spent a novitiate with the Redemptorists at Saint-Trond. After it, Ryken set up his congregation at Bruges, where trials nearly killed it: recruits failed to stay, and bread came only through effort.

By June 1840 the brotherhood counted three members, but a banker's gift in 1841 bought Het Walletje, their home. A giver's mission fund helped too, and Sallust's motto, concord makes small things grow, became theirs. A boys' sodality, a school, catechism at Notre-Dame, deaf-mute training, and Bruges schools in 1844 followed, with members sent to Saint-Trond. England called them to Bury in 1846 and Manchester, and America to Louisville in 1854 under Spalding, then Baltimore Saint Mary's and Saint Xavier's.
certain-personal-matters:
H. G. Wells gathered some forty short essays and sketches into a volume published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1901. The first piece remembers his Aunt Charlotte, who hated cheap veneer, plated goods, and the word trashy, and who corrected a child for calling a penny a copper. Cheapness, in things and in people, is Wells's opening theme.

Later pieces take up the choice of a wife, conversation, schooling, house-hunting, chess, and staying at the seaside. A few are tales rather than essays, among them Dunstone's Dear Lady. Others look far ahead, to the extinction of man and life seen through a microscope. Wells writes lightly on small subjects and lets the large ones arrive unannounced.
christ-in-flanders:
Honore de Balzac dedicated Christ in Flanders, translated by Ellen Marriage, to Marcelline Desbordes-Valmore, a daughter of Flanders of whom modern days may be proud. The tale opens at a dimly remote period in Brabant, when a ferry boat crossed between Cadzand island and the Flemish coast. Ostend then was an obscure haven of a few hundred hearths.

A storm rises, the rich passengers crowd the safe end, and a quiet stranger in poor clothes calms the waters after the pattern of the Gospel. Balzac divides the boat into two ends of society, terror and wailing among the worldly, peace near the stranger. This short legend belongs to his Philosophical Studies, where faith gets gentler treatment than usual.
cinq-mars:
Alfred de Vigny published Cinq-Mars in 1826 as a founding novel of romantic fiction. This English edition carries prefaces by Charles de Mazade and Gaston Boissier of the French Academy. Essays trace De Vigny's rise, neglect, and revival as a genius. The novel retells the fall of Louis XIII's favorite in 1642.

Henri de Cinq-Mars climbs from gentleman to king's favorite while Richelieu rules France behind the throne. Love for Marie de Gonzague feeds an ambition that favor cannot satisfy. Plotting with the king's brother and Spain, he signs a treasonable treaty against the cardinal. His friend De Thou, a counsellor, follows him from loyalty rather than belief. Arrest, trial at Lyon, and scaffold close the story for both men. De Vigny mixes invented scenes with documents and speeches, in Walter Scott's manner. Readers rank the book as a study of ambition, and this file holds it whole.
clairvoyance-and-occult-powers:
Clairvoyance and Occult Powers is a set of lessons issued in 1916 under the name Swami Panchadasi, author of The Human Aura and The Astral World. Its synopsis lists the course lesson by lesson. Lesson I treats the astral senses, and Lesson II sets telepathy against clairvoyance as two distinct powers.

The introduction explains the book's method by contrast. Students in India, the author says, accept a teacher's statements without demanding proof. Western students ask for evidence, so the lessons proceed in the opposite way, with cases and instances. One case tells of a willed visit to a house at Kew: the writer willed himself into a front bedroom at midnight, and was seen there.
concerning-animals-and-other-matters:
Concerning Animals and Other Matters, by Edward Hamilton Aitken, collects natural history essays first printed in the Strand Magazine, the Pall Mall Magazine, and the Times of India. The contents run from bills of birds, tails, noses, and ears to the barn owl and domestic animals. Snakes take three chapters: snakes themselves, the Indian snake-charmer, and cures for snake-bite.

The cobra bungalow and the panther the author did not shoot keep the Indian setting. Coconut tree, betel nut, a Hindu festival, Indian poverty, and borrowed Indian words widen the book beyond zoology. Its illustration captions joke in the same voice: the rat, a near relation of the squirrel, is personally a gutter-snipe, known by the tail he drags like a dirty rope.
concerning-cats-my-own-and-some-others:
Concerning Cats: My Own and Some Others, by Helen M. Winslow, is a cat book in fourteen chapters, all titled with its own word. It begins with Concerning the Pretty Lady. She is the author's cat: gentle, dignified, and reserved as a duchess. She followed her mistress from boarding house to seashore cottage, to the mountains, and back. She was contented wherever her person went.

Other chapters take up her other cats, other people's cats, and historic cats. Cats in England, cat clubs and shows, and high-bred cats in America widen the survey; the Hon. Mrs. McLaren Morrison's cattery at Kepwick Park is visited with delight. Cats in poetry, cat artists, cat hospitals and refuges, the origin of cats, their varieties, and cat language close the circle.
creative-impulse-in-industry-a-propositi:
A plea to join schooling with the creative side of work fills Helen Marot's 1918 book, issued by the Bureau of Educational Experiments in New York. She calls it a proposition for educators. The book is inscribed to Caroline Pratt, who worked on play in child learning.

Four chapters make the case. First comes work and the creative impulse, then the American way of fitting people to industry, then the German way. Marot doubts the German system would thrive here, and says it is not the schooling America wants. The last chapter urges forms of industry that teach as they produce. The book speaks to the old fight over what job training should do to the worker.
days-of-the-discoverers:
Tales of the early voyages to America fill Louise Lamprey's book for young readers, issued by Frederick A. Stokes Company of New York under copyright of 1921. It stands in the Great Days in American History line. Florence Choate and Elizabeth Curtis drew the pictures.

Cortes in Mexico fills the sampled middle of the book. Envoys draw the strange beasts and the thunder birds, whose mouths breathed destruction, for the Emperor to see. The governor pledges goods till orders come, then takes his leave, and a game of diplomacy begins. Other chapters treat other discoverers in the same story form. Lamprey writes history as narrative, with speech and scene, for school-age readers.
de-quincey-s-revolt-of-the-tartars:
The flight of the Kalmuck Tartars fills De Quincey's essay, in a school edition made by William Edward Simonds of Knox College. Ginn and Company of Boston issued it in 1899 at the Athenæum Press. Simonds thanks the earlier editors, and Masson above all, in his preface.

De Quincey tells how the Kalmucks fled Russian rule for China. A strong Russian force hung on their rear, slowed only by its guns. New motives pressed the worn people on each day, he writes, while they were exhausted already. The Khan's advance reached its mark only on the second day of February. Notes and an introduction fit the tale for school use. The prose is De Quincey at his most rolling and grand.
deep-waters:
Short sea tales by W. W. Jacobs fill Deep Waters, dated 1919 on its title page. Twelve stories stand in the contents, among them Shareholders, Paying Off, Sam's Ghost, and The Winter Offensive. A night-watchman tells most of them in his own broad speech.

A sailorman, says the watchman, is like a fish: safest at sea. Ashore, one poor chap kept getting married, till six women stood in court at once to take away his character. Money, wives, ghosts, and skippers fill the rest of the set. One tale turns on a woman who thought the watchman was her lost husband. Jacobs writes dry, sly comedy of the docks, in tales short enough for one sitting.
dewey-and-other-naval-commanders:
Sea captains of the United States fill Edward S. Ellis's book for boys, issued by Hurst and Company of New York under a copyright of 1899. A portrait of Admiral George Dewey stands at the front. Ellis had written histories of the world, of the United States, and of New York.

Three chapters give Dewey's birth, boyhood, Civil War service, and war with Spain. Then the book runs back to the birth of the navy: privateers, Paul Jones, and the Ranger's fight with the Drake. The Barbary wars and Tripoli follow. Privateers of 1814, among them the Reindeer, Avon, and Blakely built near Boston, close the sampled text. Ellis writes stirring naval history for the young.
dickinson-life-and-letters:
Martha Dickinson Bianchi, Emily Dickinson's niece, published The Life and Letters of Emily Dickinson in 1924. Bianchi had known her aunt and guarded the family papers. Her book mixes biography with letters not printed before.

She describes the Amherst household, the poet's white dress, and her rare meetings with visitors. Family quarrels over the poems' editing hum in the background of the story. The letters show Dickinson's humor and devotion across her whole life. Though later scholars corrected some details, Bianchi's portrait fixed the myth of the recluse poet for a generation of readers. Photographs of the house and family accompany her text in this edition.
doe-osti-17133600-corrosion-tests-with-d:
E. Schneiderlochner, Ana Maria Popa, Yifeng Liao, and William Ebert of Argonne ran standard corrosion tests on eight TARS waste form materials from Pacific Northwest, in report ANL/CFCT-26/20 dated 30 September 2026. TARS materials are alkali borosilicate glass ceramics meant to lock up dehalogenated waste salt from fuel treatment. Locking cesium and strontium in a durable solid is the point.

Tests followed ASTM methods at 90 degrees Celsius and below, varying pH, temperature, and solution saturation. Crystal content rose from almost none in TARS-1 to dominant in TARS-8, and most crystals outlasted the glass phase, which carried the dose giving elements. Overall response looked like normal borosilicate glass. TARS-1 came out most durable and most promising, though its rate did not rise smoothly with temperature.
doe-osti-2589590-randomized-algorithms-f:
Faster ways to solve large linear systems close out a laboratory research project by Andrew Higgins, in Sandia report SAND2025-11831R. The method family is randomized sketching: shrinking a huge problem with a random map before solving it. Theory promised big savings, but how to sketch well in practice, and what sketching does to accuracy, had been little studied.

The team built fast graphics processor versions of three sketches: a dense Gaussian sketch, a sparse CountSketch, and a Hadamard-based method. Combining sketches captured the strengths of each. Their combined least squares solver beat the classic normal equations route by up to 77 percent on speed, while also improving stability. Code and results give solver writers hardware-tested options instead of paper promises.
doe-osti-2996972-water-sorption-study-of:
Emily Chavez and Dali Yang measure how polymers and their composites drink water from humid air, in Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-29643, issued 29 September 2025. Polymer binders hold many composites together, including Estane in the explosive PBX 9501 and a vinyl elastomer in filled composites. Both binders can break down with water, so uptake rates govern shelf life.

An automated vapor sorption instrument generated large data sets across humidity and temperature settings, replacing slow manual weighing. Python scripts processed the data and extracted the temperature laws for diffusion and sorption. Film samples of two Estane grades were run one-sided for short exposures as part of the set. The framework gives aging studies a faster, repeatable way to rank binder stability.
doe-osti-2998342-maintenance-of-advanced:
Argonne National Laboratory final report on the MARS project, led by Alexander Heifetz and covering October 2020 to March 2025, develops sensors that let advanced reactors maintain themselves. High-temperature reactors should undercut today's plants on cost, but upkeep is projected to be their largest operating expense. The test case is Kairos Power's fluoride salt-cooled reactor, a sealed design meant to run on its own with online refueling.
