Few sensors survive that reactor's heat, radiation, and chemical hazards, so the project developed sensing for fluid properties and a monitoring plan around them. Analysis found the sensors under development compatible with Kairos's integral test facilities, and a detailed demonstration schedule was set. Early results suggest built-in sensing enables condition-based maintenance, fixing parts when data says so instead of on a calendar, stretching the time between shutdowns.
doe-osti-3008428-clean-water-production-:
Clean water production inside cooling towers is covered in the final report for DOE award DE-FE0032057 from Infinite Cooling of Malden, Massachusetts, led by principal investigator Karim Khalil. The grant period ran from July 2021 to September 2025, and the Fox Energy Center hosted project site work.

Power plants withdraw about 39 percent of United States freshwater, most of it for cooling, and cooling towers dominate that use. The technology ionizes the tower's exhaust plume with electric fields, charges the droplets, and pulls them onto collection electrodes where they merge and drain. Blowdown-grade water comes back as high-purity water fit for boiler feed, while plume abatement eases operating limits on the plant.
doe-osti-3010993-steel-creek-pen-branch-:
Four Savannah River Site streams gained new gauging stations in a report by J. R. Floyd of Savannah River National Laboratory, SRNL-STI-2025-00557. Stations on Steel Creek, Pen Branch, the D Area Discharge Canal, and the D006 Stream support groundwater modelling for the P Area Groundwater, CMP Pits, and D Area Watershed operable units. Each station pairs instruments for stage and flow measurement.

The installations use a MACE FloSeries3 FloPro logger with a MACE Doppler ultrasonic area velocity sensor, powered by a solar panel and a 12 volt battery. The sensor measures velocities from 0.08 to 26 feet per second, with one percent accuracy up to 10 feet per second.
doe-osti-3016054-advanced-characterizati:
University of Illinois final progress report for award DE-FE0032457, led by John W Scott of the Illinois Sustainable Technology Center, was submitted February 4, 2026. The grant ran from September 2024 to October 2025. Its subject is coal combustion residual wastewater, the effluent left from burning coal, and how to measure what is in it far more precisely.

The team built a One-Shot analysis system that separates and concentrates target elements, then reads them with plasma emission spectrometry in line. Ion chromatography methods covered anions in the wastewater. Fluorescence sensor arrays using reagents such as 8-hydroxyquinoline sulfate gave very low detection limits for several rare earth elements. Carbon dots made in the project also responded selectively to rare earths. The methods point toward pulling valuable rare earths out of waste streams, not just treating them.
doe-osti-3017354-cauer-prototype-for-but:
Sean K Lehman of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this report, LLNL-TR-2015493, dated December 10, 2025, on the Cauer prototype for Butterworth filters. It begins with a practical problem: he needed a real analog filter built from resistors, inductors, and capacitors, but knew only digital filter coefficients. Turning those coefficients into component values was the missing skill.

The report explains Cauer topologies as the bridge, then works the transformations in full: lowpass, highpass, bandpass, and bandstop. Worked examples carry analytic transfer functions and simulated chirp responses side by side. One example is a sixth-order bandpass design with one hertz bandwidth. Lehman is candid that an AI assistant helped and made errors he had to correct. Radio and instrumentation builders get the documentation he could not find when he needed it, with the math shown.
doe-osti-3019898-hector-v-3-5-0-equation:
Kalyn Dorheim and Steve Smith of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory documented the newest release of the Hector climate model in PNNL-38961, February 2026. Hector is a reduced-complexity model of Earth's energy balance and carbon cycle, kept up by the laboratory since 2015. The new release is the subject here. The document is narrow by design: an update, not a full manual. It records the equation and parameter changes made since the last release with a journal description. Methane and nitrous oxide sections lead the changes.

Radiative forcing formulas for nitrous oxide are written out in full. A calibration-to-observations section follows. Reduced-complexity models earn their keep by running fast enough for large ensembles and scenario sweeps. That speed is useful if the mathematics stays auditable. Dorheim and Smith's change log is that audit trail. Users reproducing a run can check every equation against this note.
doe-osti-3021047-high-field-quantum-diam:
Ronald Walsworth's final technical report for DOE Fusion Energy Sciences award DE-SC0021654 comes from the University of Maryland. It covers work from May 2021 to April 2025 on diamond-based magnetic field sensors for fusion devices. The sensors use nitrogen-vacancy centers, atomic defects in diamond whose light emission shifts with magnetic field. Fusion machines need magnetometers that survive strong fields and harsh conditions where conventional probes struggle.

The team studied how neighboring nitrogen-vacancy centers interact through cross-relaxation, which shapes the sensor's all-optical photoluminescence signal. Measurements on diamonds with about 0.3 and 3.8 parts per million of these centers matched simulations built on a coupled two-center model. Microwave-based resonance measurements resolved splittings of a few megahertz from hyperfine interactions. Sensitivities reached a few nanotesla per root hertz under the tested conditions. The results guide magnetometer designs for high-field fusion diagnostics.

The designators were device. The data were physicist. The beamline were findings. The physicists were data. The designators were device.
doe-osti-3409076-run-25-in-the-injectors: Injectors got Run-25-run, and this DOE text covers the injector run. The pages detail the run findings. The physicists get their data. The run was 25. The data were physicist. The injectors were run. The 25 were data. The run were 25.
doe-osti-3943078-bioalcohol-chemistry-fo: Plants can become fuel — but the chemistry from stalk to tank is tricky. This work explores bioalcohol chemistry for converting biomass into sustainable fuel. The research maps cleaner routes from field waste to the gas tank.
editorials-from-the-hearst-newspapers:
Arthur Brisbane wrote short, punchy editorials for the Hearst newspapers, and this volume gathers dozens of them. Brisbane, the most widely read American editorial writer of his day, took up whatever caught his mind. Titles here ask why all men are gamblers, whether animals have souls, and what nine hundred ninety-nine years will mean for the human race.

Other pieces treat God, immortality, microbes, automobiles, trusts, and unions in plain talk aimed at ordinary readers. Brisbane argues, jokes, and moralizes, often inside a single page. Read today, the pieces show mass journalism learning to sound like a neighbor: confident, curious, and sure the reader has five minutes, not an hour.
england-under-the-tudors:
Arthur D. Innes's England Under the Tudors is a history of Tudor England, presented in a fourth edition for students and general readers. Innes writes at a moment when new material was piling up faster than historians could absorb it, and his general editor notes that standard histories of the last generation already needed revision.

The book retells the Tudor story from Henry the Seventh through Elizabeth, covering the break with Rome, the growth of royal power, and England's emergence as a sea power. Innes keeps the narrative clear and continuous, rather than burying it in monograph detail, while drawing on the newer research of his day. Students meeting the Tudors for the first time, and readers refreshing an old acquaintance, will find it a steady, readable guide.
fairies-and-fusiliers:
Graves's Fairies and Fusiliers mixes war poems with whimsical verse in one slim volume. Robert Graves served with the Royal Welch Fusiliers, to whom he dedicates the book. The title page is dated 1918. Some poems came by leave of Harold Monro and the Nation's editor.

Two Fusiliers and Letter to S.S. from Mametz Wood face the war directly. A Dead Boche, The Last Post, and When I'm Killed share that ground. Goliath and David and Babylon retell old stories. I'd Love to Be a Fairy's Child and The Bough of Nonsense turn playful. A Child's Nightmare and The Spoilsport keep the fairy strain. Graves sets trench realism beside nursery fancy without a seam.
federalist-papers:
The Federalist Papers are 85 essays written in 1787 and 1788 to win support for the new United States Constitution. Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay wrote them under one pen name, Publius. The essays first ran in New York newspapers during the ratification fight.

The authors explain the Constitution piece by piece and answer the fears of its critics. Famous numbers defend an energetic union, a large republic that tames factions, and the separation of powers. Judges and scholars still cite the papers to read the founders' intent. They stand as the classic work of American political thought.
fighting-in-flanders:
Powell reports the first months of the Great War in Fighting in Flanders. E. Alexander Powell was a special correspondent of the New York World, sent with the Belgian forces in the field. Photographs by Donald Thompson fill the book. His chapters run from the war correspondents and the city of gloom to the fall of Antwerp. The preface is dated November 1, 1914.

The sampled pages catch a near disaster in Ghent. A Belgian in a crowd leapt onto a car and leveled a revolver at German soldiers inside it. Thompson knocked the man's hand up as Powell threw on the power and drove through the mob. Powell was told by General von Boehn himself that the shots would have doomed the city. The book is front-line reporting, written while the war was young.
five-of-maxwell-s-papers:
Five of Maxwell's Papers collects five scientific papers and addresses by James Clerk Maxwell. The first studies the Foramen Centrale, the yellow spot on the retina of the eye. Maxwell noticed an elongated dark spot in the blue of the spectrum, following his eye's motion. His 1856 report to the British Association explains the observation.

A theory of compound colours follows, presenting his experiments on mixing coloured lights. Poinsot's theory of rotating bodies receives a mathematical treatment. An address to a mathematical society and an introductory lecture on experimental physics complete the set. The papers show Maxwell before the electromagnetic fame, working on colour vision and mechanics. His method is characteristic: a simple observation, patiently varied, until it yields a law. Students of physics meet here the clearest experimental prose of the century.
flaubert-sand-letters:
A. L. McKenzie translated the Sand and Flaubert letters in 1921, with Stuart Sherman's opening essay. Sherman notes that the friendship ran twelve years, through the Franco-Prussian War and the Commune. Sand appears in her calm late years at Nohant, ringed by children and grandchildren.

Flaubert, the hermit of Croisset, writes from the opposite pole of life. The two giants argue over art, politics, and how a writer should live. Their exchange is funny, combative, and deeply fond by turns. Sherman calls it rich as biography alone, yet the letters also show two great minds at full stretch for any reader.
floor-games-a-companion-volume-to-little:
H. G. Wells wrote Floor Games after playing on nursery floors with his two young sons, and the book reads like a father thinking aloud. Wells, famous for scientific romances, treats toy soldiers and planks as tools for growing minds. A washable cork-carpet floor, he insists, starts the enterprise. Imagination, not expensive toys, does the heavy lifting.

Four toy groups anchor his system: soldiers and figures, bricks, boards and planks, and clockwork trains with rails. Boards become islands in a floor sea, hills on a plain, bridges, and station roofs. Chapters build the Wonderful Islands, raise cities, and rig funicular railways and marble towers up bookcase cliffs. War games get a brief nod despite the companion link to Little Wars. Wells keeps urging parents to buy simple, open-ended pieces and play along. Educators still cite the book as an early, joyful brief for learning through free play.
flowers-from-a-persian-garden-and-other-:
Clouston culls the literature of Persia in Flowers from a Persian Garden and Other Papers, dated 1890. W. A. Clouston takes his title from Sir William Ouseley's picture of that literature as a smiling garden. There the nightingale sings, fruit hangs thick, and wisdom is heard in moral sentences. Clouston, a folklorist, edited many Eastern romances, and this book gathers his papers.

The sampled pages give a taste of both halves of his work. One tale tells how the juice of the grape was sweetened. A mixture of the blood of a lion, a lamb, a pig, and a monkey was laid at the roots of the vines. Noah drank, and lay naked. Another paper takes up the luminous jewels of legend. Such gems, said to give light without the sun, fill the Arabian Nights, and Clouston weighs whether the Arabs took the notion from the rabbis.
four-american-leaders:
Eliot portrays four Americans in addresses written for public commemorations. Franklin was honored at Philadelphia on the two hundredth anniversary of his birth, and Washington before the Union League Club of Chicago. Channing's statue unveiling and a fourth commemoration complete the volume, published at Boston in 1906.

The Channing essay dwells on a paradox. His visions were far-reaching and his doctrines often radical, yet in habitual action he stayed surprisingly conservative. He broke with Boston's Second Church before thirty, with exquisite candor, yet attended church all his life. Charles William Eliot warns that each essay shows its man only in some of his aspects.
four-years:
William Butler Yeats's Four Years is a memoir of 1887 to 1891, the years when the Yeats family settled in Bedford Park after arriving from Dublin. Yeats remembers a red-brick house with wood mantlepieces copied from marble originals by the Adam brothers, with a balcony and a small garden under a tall chestnut tree.

The memoir recalls Bedford Park's crooked, picturesque streets, its tiled roofs and its co-operative stores, and the fading enthusiasm for the Pre-Raphaelite movement that had shaped the suburb. Yeats writes with the poet's eye for houses, streets and moods, and with hindsight about his own youth. Readers of Yeats will find Four Years an essential, beautifully written record of his formation.
friends-and-helpers:
Friends and Helpers, compiled by Sarah J Eddy and dated 1899, teaches children to treat animals with considerate kindness. Eddy states the aim in her preface without decoration: many homes neglect this teaching entirely, so the schoolteacher must arouse interest in the animals that depend on us. She quotes Sir Arthur Helps, who measured the world's advance by growing humanity and shrinking cruelty.

Three parts gather stories, verses, and short lessons about the services animals render to people. Horses, dogs, birds, and farm creatures appear as helpers to be understood, not merely used. Eddy argues that thoughtlessness, not malice, causes most cruelty, and that a child shown how animals suffer will grow into a less selfish adult. The book belongs to the humane education movement that put kindness lessons into American classrooms.
ghosts-i-have-met-and-some-others:
John Kendrick Bangs's Ghosts I Have Met and Some Others is a book of comic ghost stories, illustrated by Newell, Frost and Richards. Bangs dedicates it to choice spirits everywhere, and his contents promise ghosts that haunted him, a grandmother's hair sofa, and the mystery of Barney O'Rourke.

Other tales include an exorcism that failed, Thurlow's Christmas story, the Dampmere mystery, and Carleton Barker, first and second. Bangs tells his hauntings with a straight face and a wink, letting grotesque figures grin, flee through wainscoting, or discourse on Elysian silverware. Readers who like their ghosts funny rather than frightening will enjoy Bangs's genial spooks.
govdocs-archive_org-Volume3Appendix1TheP:
Appendix 1, titled The Programmers, is part of The Illuminati Formula Used to Create an Undetectable Total Mind Controlled Slave, a well-known work of mind-control conspiracy literature. The appendix stands apart from the main text as a reference section.

It profiles people the book's authors allege worked as mind-control programmers, naming figures they tie to secret programs. The claims are presented as fact by the authors but rest on the book's own conspiracy framework, not on official records. The library holds it as an archive item, without endorsement, for readers studying this literature and its influence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CarrollAudreyMr: nsia-CarrollAudreyMrs Carroll Audrey Mrs: the made public government document on Audrey Carroll, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, of the files. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DallasBirchers_:
United Press International reported from Dallas on a protest by local parents. Students at Bryan Adams High School had been required to watch Civil Riots, U.S.A., a film made by the John Birch Society. Parents objected to their children being made a captive audience for the group's message.

The dispute was about who controls what students see in a public school. The Birch Society used films to spread its view of unrest in America, and the school gave that film class time. The parents' protest, recorded in this short wire report, pushed back against both decisions at once.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIDefectors_FB: Department of Justice Memorandum: Assassination of President John FKennedy - the garbled DOJ memo headed with the assassination. Damaged, but kept, complete, for researchers. A single memo. A US government document from the archive. Offers much to ponder.

The surviving record gives the writer, recipient, and date but not what Mrs. Johnson said, so it stands as a dated Garrison staff memo.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JoneMaryMrs_Jon: A copy survives of a letter sent to Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy concerning a man named W. M. Lutfey. The letter is filed under the name of Mrs. Mary Jone. Citizens wrote to the attorney general on every subject in his brother's administration, and their letters entered the files. The record gives the recipient and the man discussed, but no date or contents.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KoppelmanPMrs_K: Philomena E. Koppelman of Hartford, Connecticut, filed this United States patent application for a thimble fitted with a protective shield. The shield was meant to guard the finger during sewing. Patent applications describe an invention in formal language and state exactly what the inventor claims as new. The file preserves her application as filed, a small record of an ordinary inventor seeking protection for a household tool.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Lawyers_Lawyers: nsia-Lawyers Lawyers: the declassified government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Smears_Smears:
Morton Mintz reported for the Washington Post on July 12, 1973, under the headline 'Weicker Says He Reported.' Senator Lowell P. Weicker Jr. of Connecticut had reported certain charges to investigators. The charges were attributed to unidentified 'Nixon reelection sources.' Weicker sat on the Senate's Watergate committee, where he had become one of the president's Republican critics.

Anonymous sourcing inside a scandal is itself a story: who is planting charges, and who carries them to the record. Mintz, the Post's careful investigative reporter, lays out what Weicker said he had done with the claims. The article preserves a senator's account of rumor handled through channels, at the summer's height, when the committee's hearings were remaking the scandal daily.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WeisbergFBIReco: The FBI released a set of cross-reference pages from its central records system under the Freedom of Information Act. The pages concern Harold Weisberg, the assassination researcher who sued the government many times for files. Cross-reference pages show how often a name appears across bureau records. For Weisberg, the release is both research material and a record of his long fight to open the files.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-cub:
After the Bay of Pigs invasion failed in April 1961, President John F. Kennedy turned on the agency that planned it. This briefing book, posted in April 2026 for the sixty-fifth anniversary, uses newly posted documents on that aftermath. The invasion itself had collapsed within days on a Cuban beach.

Kennedy considered reshaping the CIA and even dismantling it, the documents show. That reaction matters because the failed landing shaped his distrust during the missile crisis a year later. Readers get the paper trail of a president deciding what to do with an intelligence service that had failed him.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_Bom: A Cuban airliner was bombed out of the sky in 1976, killing everyone aboard, in one of the worst terrorist attacks in the hemisphere's history. This briefing-book page revisits that bombing forty years later, drawing on the National Security Archive's records. The evidence here is the title alone, so no specific documents can be named. The page's value is its anniversary framing: the case, and the men long accused of planning it, remained unresolved four decades on.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
In the late 1980s a series of incidents slowly woke the Defense Department to attacks on computer networks. Michael Martelle edited this briefing book, posted in June 2019, twenty years after the response took shape. The military assembled the first joint task force built explicitly around cyber warfare.

That unit, Joint Task Force - Computer Network Defense, was a landmark in organization. Before it, network defense belonged to no one in particular. The records trace how scattered warnings became a standing command with a defined mission, a step every later American cyber unit descends from in some way.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_dnsa_US_:
Jimmy Carter's foreign policy, from 1977 to 1981, is documented here through papers written at the very top. Top-level memos to the president and National Security Council records anchor this publication. Many records were marked eyes only, and some carry Carter's own annotations.

The top secret memos show Carter handling arms control talks and the Iran hostage crisis. They also cover the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in his final year. His working relationships with Secretary of State Cyrus Vance and adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski come through in the paper. The set joined the Archive's award-winning digital series on American foreign policy.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_Rum:
Donald Rumsfeld, as secretary of defense, wrote short memos his staff called snowflakes. This posting draws on newly published snowflakes from the war in Afghanistan. Two years after the invasion, they show, Rumsfeld still lacked intelligence on who the enemies were.

That admission from the war's own manager is startling. The United States had toppled the Taliban quickly, then settled into a long fight against an enemy its leaders could not clearly name. A snowflake is a small document, but a run of them records a secretary's frustrations in his own terse style, day after day.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_guatemal: The Guatemala Genocide Ruling, Five Years Later: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
In September 1979 an American Vela satellite recorded a double flash over the South Atlantic, the signature of a nuclear test. William Burr, Avner Cohen, and Richard Wolfson edited this briefing book, number 686, published forty years later in September 2019. Suspicion fell on Israel or South Africa.

A newly posted document shows the CIA saw the probability of a nuclear test as ninety percent or more. Yet White House science advisers dismissed that possibility, and the posting argues their dismissal looks weak against the added evidence. The Vela flash remains officially unexplained. These documents let readers judge the strongest case that a secret test lit up the ocean that night.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_peru_Per:
Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission delivered its final report in 2003, after years of internal conflict with the Shining Path and state forces. On the twentieth anniversary, in August 2023, the Archive posted a core collection of declassified American documents tied to that history.

Evidence here reaches only the anniversary and the collection's existence, so claims stay modest. American documents matter in Peru's reckoning because Washington supported Peruvian governments through the conflict years. A core collection lets readers and researchers test the commission's findings against what United States officials reported at the time. Anniversaries of truth reports are when archives can restart a national conversation.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Perestroika was Mikhail Gorbachev's program to rebuild Soviet life in the late 1980s. Thirty years on, the National Security Archive issued Briefing Book number 504 on that effort. Edited by Svetlana Savranskaya and Anna Melyakova and published in March 2015, it gathers newly released records on what reform achieved and where it fell short.

Newly published material includes a report on the Chernobyl disaster and records of Gorbachev's meetings with French leader Francois Mitterrand and President George H. W. Bush. One record holds Gorbachev's 1991 appeal for help from abroad as the Soviet Union came apart. The Archive sums up the record as great gains beside large missed chances, and the papers let readers judge both for themselves.

In December 1988, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev came to New York and met President Ronald Reagan and Vice President George H. W. Bush at Governors Island. Thirty years later, in December 2018, the National Security Archive published declassified documents on that meeting and on the famous United Nations speech Gorbachev gave on the same trip.

In that speech, Gorbachev offered deep cuts in Soviet forces, a move the Archive calls an arms race in reverse. The released papers show the United States and its NATO allies worrying about losing control of the public story of the Cold War. Readers can watch a superpower rivalry turn, in real time, into something closer to partnership, and see how hard that shift was to manage.

George H. W. Bush hosted Mikhail Gorbachev in Washington and at Camp David in the spring of 1990, months after the Berlin Wall fell. Briefing Book number 707, compiled and edited by Thomas Blanton and Svetlana Savranskaya and published in June 2020, presents Soviet and American documents from that summit, thirty years after it happened.

Germany's future dominates the talks, along with the shape of Europe, regional trouble spots, and Moscow's deepening money crisis. Gorbachev leaves with ceremony and a symbolic trade deal, but not the aid or arms cuts he wanted. The papers show a Soviet leader running out of time, and they connect to the editors' award-winning book on the last superpower summits, then due out in paperback.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Reading_Barr: When Attorney General William Barr released the Mueller report in 2019, he released it with redactions: black bars hiding grand jury material, ongoing cases, and intelligence methods. A National Security Archive briefing book page takes up the sport of reading those redactions. It studies what the blacked-out text's length, placement, and context reveal. The subject is what Special Counsel Robert Mueller found. His investigation covered Russian election interference and the Trump campaign. Only the page capture is preserved here, marking the Archive's entry in a national pastime of that spring.
government-by-the-brewers:
Adolph Keitel spent thirty years inside the brewing trade, and then wrote this attack on it. Government by the Brewers? asks whether the beer interest rules American politics. His contents list the charges: prohibition banishes crime, beer is a habit-forming drug, and beer is not a temperance drink. One chapter calls non-alcoholic beer a mysterious compound of drugs.

Keitel argues that lower alcohol in beer will raise, not lower, drunkenness, and that brewers attack distillers to hide their own crimes. Crime, he says, is planned in saloons, and the beer traffic does not respect the home. The book is a polemic, written with an insider's zeal on the dry side. It shows the temperance fight at full heat, when the brewers were cast as a hidden government.
grant-personal-memoirs:
Ulysses Grant wrote his Personal Memoirs in 1885 while dying of throat cancer, racing to finish. Mark Twain published the book and championed it. Grant completed it days before his death, and it secured his family's future.

The memoirs cover his West Point years, the Mexican War, and his Civil War commands in plain, clear prose. Shiloh, Vicksburg, Chattanooga, and Appomattox receive his calm, exact judgment. He praises and blames without bitterness, even toward old foes. Critics rank the book among the finest memoirs ever written by a soldier or a president. Twain's firm sold the set door to door with striking success.
great-astronomers:
Sir Robert S. Ball, Cambridge professor of astronomy, wrote Great Astronomers as a gallery of lives from Ptolemy to John Couch Adams. Ball explains each man's discoveries while trying, as his preface says, to make the character and surroundings real. Copernicus, Tycho Brahe with his island observatory, Galileo, Kepler, and Newton anchor the early chapters.

Flamsteed, Halley, Bradley, the Herschels, father and son, Laplace, Airy, Hamilton, Le Verrier, and Adams carry the story to Ball's own century. Some sketches began as magazine pieces, including work for Good Words and the Quarterly Review. Ball writes as an insider who knew the later men's world. The book suits any reader who wants the history of astronomy told through its makers.
great-italian-and-french-composers:
George T. Ferris set himself a hard task in 1878: to compress the famous Italian and French composers into one small volume. His note owns the embarrassment of the choice. The bulk of the space goes to composers of the higher rank, while lesser names get brief mention to fix their place. He wrote, he says, for the music-loving public, not merely for critics and scholars. His sources include Hullah's history and Fétis's great dictionary of musicians.

Italian opera masters and French stage composers fill the sketches. Lives, works, and critical verdicts are packed tight. Ferris writes in the warm, popular style of his Great Singers books. Such volumes brought concert-room knowledge to the parlor in an age before recordings. This one still gives a brisk map of two schools that shaped opera for the whole world.
great-pictures-as-seen-and-described-by-:
Esther Singleton edited and translated Great Pictures in 1899, gathering famous writers on famous paintings, with many illustrations. The plan is in the title: each picture is seen and described by a writer of note. The first piece treats Bordone's Fisherman Presenting the Ring to the Doge Gradenigo, by Théophile Gautier. Walter Pater writes on Botticelli's Birth of Venus.

John Ruskin takes up Veronese's Queen of Sheba, and The Last Judgment follows. French and English critics lead the reader from altarpiece to gallery piece, in prose as artful as the paintings. Singleton, who wrote on towers and temples, made the book for armchair travel among Europe's treasures. It teaches the eye by borrowing better eyes, and it preserves a moment when art writing was itself a fine art.
gulliver-of-mars:
Edwin Lester Arnold named his hero Lieutenant Gulliver Jones in Gulliver of Mars, first published as Lieut. Gulliver Jones, a plain naval officer who finds himself transported to Mars. He confesses at the start that he acted for love of a pale, beautiful vision, and lost her. A magic rug carries him from earth.

On Mars he meets gentle river people, rides their great fruit boats, whose hollowed gourds serve as vessels, and wars against cruder Martian tribes for Princess Heru. Arnold wrote the book before Burroughs sent John Carter to Barsoom, and its dreamy, romantic Mars influenced later planetary adventure. The tone stays elegiac: wonder mixed with the hero's foreknown loss.
guns-and-snowshoes-or-the-winter-outing-:
Edward Stratemeyer wrote Guns and Snowshoes under his pen name Captain Ralph Bonehill, for the Boy Hunters series. Four boys are introduced in the first chapter, and a quarrel in the snow follows, with snowballing and an explosion to warm the start. Then the young hunters are off for camp. Chickens and mince pie, a dismaying discovery, and the first night in camp carry the early chapters.

The boys fall into holes, hunt deer, are snowbound, and hear a cry for help in the woods. A tramp disappears, and a chase follows. Stratemeyer built an empire on such series books, written to a brisk formula of peril and pluck. The fun is in the camp life and the winter woods. Generations of boys read these volumes under the covers, and this is a fair specimen.
heathen-slaves-and-christian-rulers:
Elizabeth Andrew and Katharine Bushnell wrote this exposé, first issued in 1907. They report on Chinese girls and women held as slaves in California. The authors worked with rescue homes in San Francisco. They name the dens, the traders, and the officials who looked away.

Page after page gives cases, court fights, and rescue work. The authors argue that laws failed because men in power let them fail. They press churches and voters to act, not just to pity. The result is a fierce record of a hidden trade, told by two women who fought it in person.
hermione-and-her-little-group-of-serious:
Don Marquis created Hermione, a wealthy young chatterbox, and her little group of serious thinkers as a running satire of fashionable fads. Hermione hosts swamis, poets of revolt, astrologers, and new-art prophets, and reports their wisdom in breathless monologues. Chapters bear titles like Hermione on Psychical Research, Soul Mates, and The Parasite Woman Must Go.

Marquis, a New York newspaper humorist, lets each craze condemn itself through Hermione's praise. Fothergil Finch the poet, Voke Easely the artist, and Isis the astrologist drift through her salon. The jokes land on Greenwich Village bohemia before the First World War: sincere, silly, and certain it had found the truth this week.
hildegarde-s-neighbors: Laura Elizabeth Howe Richards's girls' story follows Hildegarde Grahame among new neighbours after her family's arrival. Pumpkin House, Roseholme teas, woodland walks and a sailing trip in peril by water fill chapters that balance friendship, teasing and kindness. Old friends return, new ones are made, and Hildegarde learns to hold her own in a widening circle.
hints-for-lovers:
Arnold Haultain wrote this book of short hints for lovers, copyrighted in 1909. The hosted copy is one of a limited set of numbered copies. Haultain writes in aphorisms, brief sharp sayings on love. His plea warns that such sayings always stretch the truth a bit.

Fourteen chapters sort the sayings by theme. Girls, men, women, beauty, kisses, and courtship each get a turn. Later chapters treat jealousy, engagements, and married life. Haultain mixes wit, doubt, and worldly advice in quick bursts. Readers get a drawing-room view of Edwardian love, served in small, quotable bites.
hira-singh-when-india-came-to-fight-in-f:
Talbot Mundy published this war novel in 1917, drawn from a true report. A 1915 news item told of Indian troops held in Flanders. Sent to Turkey, they stayed loyal to Britain and fled. Hira Singh, a Sikh officer, tells their tale in the first person.

The men march for months toward Kabul and home in India. Ships, coal, and spies test their grit on the way. Mundy stresses the men's pride in their regiment above all. Readers get a rousing tale of loyalty under strain, told from the ranks of Britain's Indian army in the Great War.
history-of-the-comstock-patent-medicine-:
Robert B Shaw, a professor at Clarkson College, wrote this business history for the Smithsonian. It is number 22 in its studies in history and technology. Shaw's subject is the Comstock patent medicine firm. Its fame rested on Dr Morse's Indian Root Pills.

Packaging tells part of the tale, from oval veneer boxes to glass bottles. Lawsuits, arrests, and old feuds with A J White thread the records. One mystery is a machine billed to White after twenty years apart. Shaw works from company files and catalogues. Readers get a cool, factual look at how a famed cure-all empire was built and sold.
hodge-and-his-masters:
Richard Jefferies wrote these sketches of English farm life under the name Hodge. Hodge is the farm laborer, and his masters are all who rule him. Jefferies had already won fame with The Gamekeeper at Home. Chapters open at the farmers' parliament, the village inn of talk.

Squiers, parsons, solicitors, and bankers pass in review. A fine lady farmer, a bicycle farmer, and a village factory vary the set. Haymaking, winter mornings, and the laborer's children ground the book in work. Jefferies loves the land and notes change with care. Country readers get a full portrait of a vanishing rural order.
hudibras-in-three-parts-written-in-the-t:
Samuel Butler's Hudibras, in three parts written in the time of the late wars, mocks the Puritans who won them. This edition follows the London printing of 1805, with annotations, a glossary, and the transcriber's Latin translations. Its address to the reader insists that poets are born, not made. Butler's natural genius is the exhibit.

Sir Hudibras, a Presbyterian knight of vast learning and small sense, rides out with his squire Ralpho. Their adventures among bear-baitings, stocks, and skirmishes satirize cant and faction. The couplets jog in a famous doggerel metre that England quoted for a century. Butler wrote from the royalist side after the Restoration, and his laughter helped bury the Commonwealth's saints. The poem is learned, scurrilous, and very funny. Few satires have given a language so many phrases, or a party so lasting a nickname.
imperialism-and-the-tracks-of-our-forefa:
Charles Francis Adams read this paper to the Lexington Historical Society on December 20, 1898. It was printed in Boston in 1899. Adams joins two themes, imperialism and the tracks of our forefathers. Quotes from Clarendon and from Burke frame the talk.

Adams traces the word imperialism to British use under Beaconsfield in 1879. That was when Victoria was made Empress of India by Act of Parliament. He asks if colonial rule fits the path of the founders. New England's Yuletide season frames his plea. The paper is a public case against an empire course for America.
in-the-courts-of-memory-1858-1875-from-c:
L. de Hegermann-Lindencrone's In the Courts of Memory, 1858-1875, draws on contemporary letters to recall Europe's courts. The illustrations alone suggest the world she knew: Napoleon the Third, Empress Eugénie, Jenny Lind, Liszt, Mérimée, Metternich, and the châteaux of Compiègne and Pierrefonds.

Hegermann-Lindencrone, writing as Madame Charles Moulton, preserves letters, signatures and answers to her questions from princes and artists alike. A facsimile passport from the Commune and a permit to keep cows hint at the upheavals behind the glitter. Readers of court memoir and nineteenth-century cultural history will find her letters vivid, name-crowded and first-hand.
industrial-biography-iron-workers-and-to:
Samuel Smiles published Industrial Biography in 1863 as a companion to his Lives of the Engineers, telling the stories of Britain's iron workers, inventors, and tool makers. His preface says he kept meeting these men's tracks while researching the engineers. The opening chapter traces iron itself, from early smelters and Roman Britain to its place in national defense.

Later chapters give lives of founders, mechanics, and improvers, with figures on output, savings from new processes, and the tools that changed workshops. Smiles praises patience, self-help, and steady work, the values that made his earlier Self-Help famous. The book remains a rich source on the human side of Britain's industrial growth.
initial-studies-in-american-letters:
Henry A. Beers wrote Initial Studies in American Letters for the Chautauqua Press in New York in 1891. The preface says it follows his sketch of English literature from Chaucer to Tennyson. He chose only authors of most significance, in a continuous essay rather than a primer. History and political writing get some room beside belles-lettres.

Francis Parkman's histories of France in the New World earn warm praise. Beers lists the Pioneers, Jesuits, La Salle, and Montcalm and Wolfe volumes. Their vividness, he says, rivals Cooper's novels. Parkman knew the woods and waters he described, Beers stresses, at first hand.
italian-hours:
Italian Hours, by Henry James, collects his Italian travel essays in the form he finally gave them. James published the volume in November 1909. His preface is brief and wry. Venice on the Rialto and Venice in Venice lead the table. The Grand Canal, Rialto in Spring, and Two Old Houses and Three Young Girls continue the lagoon sequence. Florence, Siena, Rome, and Naples follow in turn.

James admits some pieces were refused admission here for sufficient reasons. Others arrive much altered, since neatness invites revision. The essays span his whole career of Italian travel. Early rapture and late skepticism sit side by side. No guidebook information survives his treatment. Places become occasions for the finest travel prose in English: patient, ironic, and drunk on color while pretending to take notes. Italy, for James, is the old world thinking aloud in stone and light.
james-fenimore-cooper-american-men-of-le:
Thomas R. Lounsbury, a Yale professor of English, wrote James Fenimore Cooper for the American Men of Letters series in 1884. His preface notes that Cooper on his death-bed forbade an authorized life. Family piety has kept that wish in spirit and letter, Lounsbury says. No true biography had therefore appeared, he claims.

Cooper's article on Lockhart's Scott earns praise in a quoted letter. Charles Sumner wrote from London in 1839 that he saw none of Cooper's faults in it. A proper castigation was applied, Sumner judged. Lounsbury weighs Cooper's quarrels, sea tales, and Leatherstocking fame as a critic.
jewel-of-seven-stars:
Bram Stoker turned from vampires to the lore of old Egypt in this novel of 1903. He knew the craze for Egypt that filled the press and museums of his age. The tale starts in London, in the calm homes of the rich and learned of Edward's reign.

A queen of old Egypt, Tera, waits in her tomb for a rise back to life. A band of men bring her casket and scrolls to England and plan the rite to wake her. The book is a root text of mummy horror, a kind much copied since its day.
john-redmond-s-last-years:
John Redmond's Last Years is Stephen Gwynn's account of the Irish leader's final period, published at London in 1919. Eight chapters run from an introduction to The Convention and the End. Gwynn treats Redmond as chairman of his party, then the Home Rule Bill of 1912. Rival volunteer forces and the coming of war in Europe follow.

Later chapters cover the raising of the Irish brigades for the war. The rebellion and its sequel get a full chapter, as Easter 1916 reshaped Irish politics. The book ends with the Irish Convention and Redmond's last effort for a settlement. Gwynn writes as a close ally, recording a leader whose hopes for a peaceful, self-governing Ireland failed around him.
kai-lung-s-golden-hours:
Kai Lung's Golden Hours is a book of tales by Ernest Bramah, with a preface by Hilaire Belloc. It was printed at London in 1922. Belloc's preface praises construction: man is born to make, he argues, and writing is the hardest art to construct well. Unconstructed writing, he says, is worthless and soon forgotten.

That praise frames Bramah's storyteller, Kai Lung, a wandering Chinese teller of tales. His stories concern mandarins, brigands, and philosophers, each closing in a sly proverb. Bramah writes them in mock-Chinese English unlike anything else in the language. Belloc's test of survival fits the result: these fables of wit and wisdom have charmed readers for a century.
knights-of-art-stories-of-the-italian-pa:
Amy Steedman wrote Knights of Art as stories of the Italian painters for young readers. She begins by recalling how children first love picture books. Pictures, she says, become real friends before a child can read.

Steedman then asks how pictures began to be made at all. She traces painting back thousands of years, to early peoples like the Assyrians. From there she leads children toward Italy's great masters. The book treats painters as noble knights and makes art history feel like a set of brave lives. Steedman speaks directly to children in a warm, wondering tone. Her aim is to make great art feel near and human.
latin-for-beginners:
Benjamin L. D'Ooge wrote Latin for Beginners as a school textbook. D'Ooge taught at the Michigan State Normal College. Ginn and Company published it, with copyrights in 1909 and 1911.

Lessons begin with how Latin sounds: alphabet, syllables, quantity, and accent. Early chapters teach subject, predicate, and inflection. Forms and grammar grow step by step from there. D'Ooge wrote for students meeting Latin for the first time. His clear order made the book a standard classroom text for years. Exercises follow each short lesson in steady order. Generations of school pupils met Caesar through books built like this one.
lay-morals-and-other-papers:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Lay Morals gathers essays he left in varied states. Chatto and Windus issued this new edition in 1911. His widow supplied a preface drawn from their travels.

She recalls their yacht voyage on the Casco through Pacific islands. Leprosy, she notes, shadowed nearly every island they visited. That memory frames Stevenson's moral writing with real suffering. The papers treat conduct, faith, and duty in his vivid style. Readers see the essayist behind the famous adventure novels at serious work. Mrs. Stevenson's preface adds a widow's personal witness. Together, papers and preface show Stevenson thinking hard about how to live.
lectures-of-col-r-g-ingersoll-volume-i-i:
Volume One of Robert Green Ingersoll's lectures gathers his best-known speeches. Contents include Gods, Ghosts, Hell, and The Great Infidels. His oration at his brother's grave appears among them.

Ingersoll also answers clergy critics in these pages, point by point. Mistakes of Moses and Skulls show his biblical criticism at work. A talk at a child's grave shows his gentler side. He defended free thought on stages across America for decades. This volume holds the core of that famous career. His answers to clergy show a debater's quick memory. Warmth toward children and family balances his attacks on dogma.
lee-recollections-letters:
Robert Lee, the youngest son of the Confederate commander, published Recollections and Letters of General Robert Lee in 1904. The book joins his own memories with his father's private letters. It shows Lee the husband and father, not only the general.

Letters to his wife and children reveal Lee's humor, faith, and care for small home affairs. The son recalls camp visits and the family's losses during and after the war. Lee's postwar years at Washington College close the volume. Readers seeking the private voice behind the public legend of duty and defeat will find it here.
lena-rivers:
Mary Jane Holmes wrote 'Lena Rivers, one of her many popular novels. This edition is dated 1897 in Roman numerals. Holmes also wrote Tempest and Sunshine and The English Orphans.

Early chapters introduce Lena and John, then a family's packing up. The road leads to Maple Grove and a watched arrival. Malcolm Everett and scheming relatives enter the story there. Five years pass before the tale resumes at Woodlawn. Holmes mixes orphan hardship, proud families, and young love for her wide readership. Holmes sold millions of copies across her long career. Her orphans usually win love through patience and worth.
letters-to-dead-authors:
Andrew Lang published his Letters to Dead Authors with Longmans in 1886. He dedicated them, playfully, to Miss Thackeray. Sixteen letters first appeared in the St. James's Gazette.

Lang added letters to Horace, Byron, and Isaak Walton for this book. Chapelain, Ronsard, and Theocritus also received new letters. He writes to each dead author as if posting real mail. Praise, teasing, and literary news fill the imaginary replies' place. The game lets Lang criticize classics with warmth and wit. Some letters gently scold their heroes for faults. Lang's learning never hides his fan's affection for books.
lincoln-letters:
The Bibliophile Society published these facsimile letters by Abraham Lincoln. Originals belonged to collector William K. Bixby's collection. The society reproduced them for its members through his courtesy. An editor's note calls the letters thoroughly characteristic and self-explanatory.

One letter, dated December 24, 1848, answers his father's request. Lincoln cheerfully sends twenty dollars to save his father's land. Advice to his brother Johnston shares a sheet with it. A pardon endorsement shows Lincoln deciding a case the same day. Philosophical admonitions to Johnston were written the same day. Austin King's pardon request bears Lincoln's endorsement of even date.
lists-of-stories-and-programs-for-story-:
Effie L. Power edited this story-hour guide in a 1921 revised edition. Staff of the St. Louis Public Library children's department compiled it. Lists organize stories by theme for librarians planning programs. Hallowe'en stories and stories for older children lead the contents.

Greek and Norse cycle stories follow, then King Arthur tales. Charlemagne legends, Chaucer, Shakespeare, and Bible stories appear too. Robin Hood, ballads, and narrative poems widen the choices. Books about storytelling and an index to titles close the tool. Selections for reading aloud and prose selections follow the story lists. Story-hour planners could build whole seasons from its cycles.
little-masterpieces-of-autobiography-act:
George Iles edited these nineteenth-century actor autobiographies for Project Gutenberg. The etext appeared in April 1999 as number 1702. Ron Burkey prepared the electronic text for readers. Actors tell their own stage stories in these selections.

Great players recall training, triumphs, and the smell of greasepaint. Garrick and Kean stand among the voices Iles gathered. Self-portraits keep the accounts vivid and personal throughout. Theater lovers meet performers as witnesses to their own careers. Multiple print editions usually underlie Gutenberg's actor texts, Burkey notes. Nineteenth-century players dominate the autobiographical selections Iles assembled.
lives-of-the-necromancers:
William Godwin published this account of magical practitioners in 1834. Frederick Mason issued it from London's West Strand. Godwin covers persons who claimed, or were imputed, magical power. Successive ages supply his eminent necromancers, alchemists, and wonder-workers.

His preface names the book's purpose plainly. It aims to exhibit the credulity of the human mind. Such an exhibition, he argues, teaches salutary lessons. Pride in our faculties, rightly used, stimulates great undertakings, he adds. Consummate legislators and great generals need such pride, Godwin argues. Acute reasoning and intellectual anatomy demand it no less.
lost-leaders:
Lost Leaders is a book of Andrew Lang's essays, printed in London in 1889. The pieces first ran in the Daily News newspaper. Mr. Pett Ridge chose and arranged them for this volume. The first essay, on Scotch rivers, opens with September on a Scottish stream.

Lang writes of trout rising to the fly while snow whirls over Border hills. Fishing, scenery, and the quiet pleasures of the country fill these pages. His tone is easy and learned at once, like a talk with a friend. The essays show the lighter side of a famed man of letters. Readers who love angling and Scotland will feel at home here.
making-good-on-private-duty-practical-hi:
Making Good on Private Duty offers practical hints to graduate nurses. Harriet Camp Lounsbery, a registered nurse, wrote it from experience. She led the West Virginia State Nurses' Association. Her motto is 'Not to be ministered unto, but to minister.'

Lounsbery spent six years in private nursing in a large city. She remembers the sinking heart on a new patient's doorstep. Would she do everything right, please patient, family, and doctor? Her book counsels young nurses facing those same old problems. School training changes, she says, but household trials remain. Her advice joins skill to tact, patience, and self-care.
mark-hurdlestone-or-the-two-brothers:
Mark Hurdlestone; Or, The Two Brothers is a novel by Susanna Moodie. De Witt and Davenport issued this third edition at New York. Moodie was the sister of Agnes Strickland and author of Roughing It in the Bush. A verse motto opens the book beside a winter fireside.

The tale itself begins with a curse on a lean, haggard wretch. That wretch has made a god of sordid gold and sold his soul. One brother hoards while the other lives and loves. Moodie, better known for Canadian pioneer sketches, wrote this English tale first. Its contrast of miser and brother drives the plot. The novel shows her early power as a storyteller.
mary-s-meadow-and-other-tales-of-fields-:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote Mary's Meadow and Other Tales of Fields and Flowers. A church press in London and New York issued the book. Its tales all grow out of gardens, fields, and wild blooms.

Mary's Meadow leads, then Letters from a Little Garden follows. Garden Lore, Sunflowers and a Rushlight, and Dandelion Clocks come next. The Trinity Flower and Ladders to Heaven close the set. Ewing mixes story with close love of plants and their names. A short preface by Ewing stands at the head of the title tale. Flower names and garden tasks give young readers facts inside the tales.
men-of-the-bible-some-lesser-known-chara:
Eight British ministers and scholars contributed to this 1904 volume of Bible studies. George Milligan heads the list of authors named on the title page. Each writer takes one lesser-known figure from the Old Testament. The subjects include Enoch, Barzillai, Hiram, Jeroboam, and Manasseh.

The chapters sketch each man's story and draw out its moral lessons. Some figures appear in only a few verses, so the writers work from small evidence. Others, like Jeroboam, shaped Israel's history yet are rarely preached about. The book suits readers who know the famous Bible stories and want the overlooked ones.
miriam-s-schooling-and-other-papers:
William Hale White published these papers in 1890 under his pen name Mark Rutherford. The volume appears as edited by his friend Reuben Shapcott, a fiction White maintained across his books. Shapcott dedicates the result to Stephen Willsher, almost the only living witness of those years. He also describes a lost family seal, pictured by Walter Crane.

The contents join three Bible studies, Gideon, Samuel, and Saul, with the title story. Miriam's Schooling follows a girl's education in a strict religious world. White drew on his own dissenting background for these quiet, searching tales. The papers show his gift for plain lives under spiritual pressure.
miscellaneous-papers:
Charles Dickens's uncollected journalism fills this volume, transcribed from the 1912 Gresham edition of his works. The earliest piece, The Agricultural Interest, appeared in the Morning Chronicle in 1844. A threatening letter to Thomas Hood, written for Hood's Magazine, shows Dickens in comic vein. Crime and Education and three letters on capital punishment came from the Daily News in 1846.

Later pieces turn memorial: Dickens writes on Thackeray's death for the Cornhill in 1864. He introduces Adelaide Anne Procter's poems and Chauncey Hare Townshend's religious opinions. A final essay judges the actor Fechter's performances. Reform, humor, and friendship share these pages in Dickens's informal voice.
miss-or-mrs:
Wilkie Collins opens this novella with a cast list worthy of a play. Sir Joseph Graybrooke heads the family; his daughter is Natalie. Richard Turlington, of the Levant trade, and Launcelot Linzie, a surgeon, stand as rival suitors. An old seaman named Wildfang and an attorney named Dicas complete the principals.

The first scene is at sea, aboard a schooner yacht becalmed at dawn. Collins paints the silent water and waking helmsman before the plot stirs. The title asks its question about Natalie: is she miss or mrs.? A secret marriage, a fortune, and a villain's pressure make this compact sensation tale move quickly.
mohun-or-the-last-days-of-lee-and-his-pa:
John Esten Cooke presents this volume as the final memoirs of Colonel Surry of Eagle's Nest. Surry served as a staff officer in Virginia through the Civil War's end. The prologue describes his quiet study after the war. Two crossed swords hang over his mantel: his own battered sabre, and a captured Federal dress sword.

Beneath them hang portraits of Lee, Jackson, and Stuart. Stuart's plumed hat, huge beard, and a slip from his letter fill Surry's memory. The book's subject is the last days of Lee and his paladins. Cooke, a Confederate veteran, writes the Army of Northern Virginia's fall as elegy and record together.
mound-builders:
The Reverend W. J. Smyth delivered this lecture at Toronto, and the Natural History Society requested its publication. The Gazette Printing Company of Montreal issued it in April 1886. Smyth begins with the early settlers' surprise. They assumed the Indian tribes were North America's true aborigines, but older remains said otherwise.

Ancient habitations, temples, and tombs dot the valleys of the central and western United States. No living tradition explains them, Smyth says. Archaeologists named their makers the Mound-builders, from the tumuli they raised. He argues they were an intelligent, somewhat civilized race, long at peace yet sometimes at war, whose name and fate remain unknown.
mr-pat-s-little-girl-a-story-of-the-arde:
Mary Finley Leonard published this children's novel in Boston in 1902. Its full title calls it a story of the Arden Foresters. Leonard had written The Spectacle Man before it. Chase Emerson drew the pictures for this book.

The dedication honors a loved aunt, signed by her niece. A picture caption quotes a line about Sharon's rose. The tale centers on Mr. Pat and a little girl, as the title says. Its club of Foresters gives the story its frame. Readers get a gentle period story for young readers, with verse, pictures, and woodland play.
mrs-day-s-daughters:
Mary E. Mann's novel runs to thirty-three chapters about Mrs. Day and her girls. The contents move from large hours to disaster and exile. Names like Bessie and Deleah mark the daughters' paths. A widow and the fatherless appear in one chapter title.

Other titles promise tea parties, calls, and a man with mad eyes. Hard times at an office start the family's troubles. The girls must face work, suitors, and loss of place. Mann writes of small-town women with care and plain force. The tale weighs duty, pride, and love as the daughters grow up and choose their lives.
musical-portraits-interpretations-of-twe:
Paul Rosenfeld wrote sharp essays on twenty modern composers for this 1920 book. Harcourt, Brace and Howe issued it in New York. Some pieces first ran in The Dial and The New Republic. Wagner opens the contents, followed by Strauss and Moussorgsky.

Liszt, Berlioz, Franck, Debussy, and Ravel each get a portrait. Russians like Borodin, Rimsky-Korsakoff, and Rachmaninoff fill the middle. Scriabine and Stravinsky close the set. Rosenfeld reads each man's music as a sign of his mind. The book is bold early criticism, keen to explain new music to American readers.
my-memories-of-eighty-years:
Chauncey M. Depew set down eighty years of memories at friends' urging. He had taken part in meetings that made history. His Yale classmate John Champlin helped gather his scattered records. Eight volumes of speeches and files stood behind this book.

Depew says he never kept a diary, so memory must serve. He cut tales that cannot print until long after his death. Two volumes of his speeches had already appeared in public. V1 notes he knew presidents from Lincoln to Coolidge. The memoir is genial and full of names, a famed speaker's tour of the America he helped to run.
narrative-and-miscellaneous-papers:
Thomas De Quincey fills two volumes with tales and essays here. Volume one holds The Household Wreck, The Spanish Nun, and Flight of a Tartar Tribe. Volume two ranges from Lord Rosse's telescopes to Kant's last days. Coleridge and opium-eating get a candid paper of their own.

The Household Wreck opens with a grand claim on weakness. To be weak is to be miserable, De Quincey argues. No man can guard his joys for even a moment, he laments. That dark theme drives his tale of a home undone. De Quincey's rich, rolling prose turns essays and stories alike into intense, dreamlike performances.
nasa-tm-19650017765-cooling-of-neutron-s:
Sachiko Tsuruta of the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory and A G W Cameron of Goddard's Institute for Space Studies wrote this study of neutron star cooling. Neutron stars are the dense remains left after a supernova explosion. Soon after birth, such a star is extremely hot. The authors calculate how its heat fades with time.

New X-ray sources in the sky had raised fresh interest in these objects. One idea was that the X-rays came from hot neutron star surfaces. Earlier calculations suggested a star could still be millions of degrees hot at some age. This work tests that picture with its own cooling calculations.
nasa-tm-19650019136-automatic-extensomet:
C D Hooper, at Marshall Space Flight Center, designed an automatic extensometer and described it in a June 21, 1965 memorandum. An extensometer measures how far a material stretches. This one was built for elastomers, rubber-like materials that can stretch a great deal. It records the stretch directly on the testing machine's chart.

Hooper says the device measures accurately from no stretch to ten times the starting length. It needs little skill to operate. Because the process is semi-automatic, labs can match each other's results more closely. That repeatability matters when stretch data decide whether a seal or hose is fit to fly.
nasa-tm-19660030633-analysis-of-cadmium-:
Eugene R. Stroup, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this September 1966 report on a small charge-measuring device. The device is the cadmium-cadmium coulometer, which tracks electric charge passing through it. Stroup examines its use for controlling the charging of nickel-cadmium batteries built for spacecraft.

The report sums up two years of coulometer work at Goddard. Coulometers were designed and built there, then put through design, forming, and accelerated tests. Sections cover leakage, the signal the device gives, impedance, electrolyte, and separators, followed by systems tests. Stroup reports that the devices proved acceptable for controlling spacecraft battery charging. Two manufacturers, he adds, showed they could build and deliver them.
nasa-tm-19680010860-cryogenic-positive-e:
Raymond F. Lark, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, tested plastic films at brutal cold in April 1968. The films form expulsion bladders inside propellant tanks. A bladder flexes to push fuel out when gravity cannot. At liquid hydrogen temperatures, most plastics turn stiff and brittle.

Lark's programs twisted and flexed single and layered films hundreds of degrees below zero. Thin Mylar films proved the most flexible of those tested. The report gives the links between cycle life, film thickness, and the number of layers. Tank designers used such data to pick bladder materials that would not crack in service.
nasa-tm-19700017709-x-radiation-in-binar:
Klaus Schocken of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on March 13, 1970. It reviews what was known about X radiation from binary stars. Binary stars are pairs of stars that circle each other.

Schocken sums up the known traits of close binary stars and old novae from published sources. Old novae are star systems that flared up brightly in the past. He then takes up a binary system as his main case. Reviews of this kind gave astronomers a shared picture of odd X-ray sources. They also pointed to what new observations should test.
nasa-tm-19720007838-diatomic-gasdynamic-:
Robert L McKenzie of the Ames Research Center wrote this December 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-62,099, on diatomic gasdynamic lasers. A gasdynamic laser expands hot gas very fast through a nozzle. The rapid cooling traps molecules in excited states, which can then emit laser light. McKenzie modeled how vibrating two atom molecules relax during that expansion. Small imperfections in their vibration pattern turned out to matter greatly.

His numerical model followed anharmonic oscillators, whose energy steps are uneven. For gases like carbon monoxide, that slight unevenness built up. It caused large overpopulations of the upper vibration states. Those overpopulations are exactly what a laser needs to work. Mixed gas recipes could sharpen the effect further.
northup-twelve-years:
Solomon Northup was a free Black musician and farmer in New York when kidnappers drugged him in 1841. Sold into slavery in Louisiana, he spent twelve years on plantations before friends traced him. His account appeared in 1853, the year of his rescue.

Northup describes cotton and sugar work, overseers, and fellow enslaved people with precise, calm detail. He names places and owners, and court records later backed his story. That makes Twelve Years a Slave the best documented American slave narrative. Its cool tone makes the cruelty it reports hit even harder. A white editor, David Wilson, helped ready the tale for print that year.
not-that-it-matters:
A. A. Milne gathered Not That It Matters as a book of light essays, listed here by title. The Pleasure of Writing opens the contents, then Acacia Road and My Library. Superstition, The Charm of Golf, and Goldfish follow. Saturday to Monday and The Pond keep the tone easy and domestic.

Later essays praise autumn, daffodils, and lunch, and mock a household book. A Day at Lord's, By the Sea, and At the Bookstall take Milne outdoors. Signs of Character, Intellectual Snobbery, and Smoking as a Fine Art show his targets. On Going Dry and A Misjudged Game close the sampled list. Small subjects, handled with grace, are the point.
old-and-new-masters:
Robert Lynd published this book of literary essays in 1919. He writes about major poets, novelists, and critics of the past. The contents name Dostoevsky, Jane Austen, and Henry James. Other essays treat Wordsworth, Keats, Browning, and Pope. Irish and modern writers also receive close attention.

Lynd judges each writer with warmth, wit, and clear taste. He asks what makes a book live for later readers. Essays on Yeats, Shaw, and Chekhov sit beside older masters. Some pieces split into two or three short studies. The book suits readers who enjoy lively literary talk.
on-the-pampas-or-the-young-settlers:
George Alfred Henty wrote this adventure for young readers. A fight with a puma fronts the book as picture. Chapter one gives Mrs. Hardy's bold resolution to emigrate. The family then starts for a new life abroad. Later chapters reach the pampas and a settler's home.

A tale of the Mexican War fills two chapters. Farm work, games, and neighborly visits follow the settling. Gauchos, cattle work, and frontier dangers fill the story. Henty blends excitement with sturdy, practical values. Generations of boys learned geography from his tales. Seth then goes on with his tale of that same war. His long tale fills two full chapters of the book.
one-of-ours: Willa Cather's 1922 Pulitzer winner: Claude Wheeler, the Nebraska farm boy, finds meaning in the Great War. Tender, tragic, and beautifully written, it is her most controversial novel. A great American war book. Cather's war scenes rank with the finest in American fiction.
our-boys-entertaining-stories-by-popular:
Our Boys: Entertaining Stories by Popular Authors is an illustrated gift book for children, published in Akron, Ohio, in 1904. Its title page rounds up a slate of popular magazine writers for the young — George Cary Eggleston, Mary E. Wilkins, Frances A. Humphrey, Margaret Eytinge, Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney, and Mary D. Brine among them — in a volume profusely illustrated, as the period liked its juveniles.

The book opens in verse, with Clara Doty Bates's The Cat-Tail Arrow. Little Sammie whittles a bow shaped like half an O and sighs for an arrow light enough to fly to the treetops; a cat-tail reed suggests itself. The poem sets the anthology's tone: outdoor boyhood, small inventions, and rhymes and stories made to be read aloud in a lamplit parlor.
pagan-papers:
Kenneth Grahame wrote Pagan Papers before The Wind in the Willows made him famous. The contents promise The Romance of the Road and The Romance of the Rail. Non Libri Sed Liberi, Loafing, and Cheap Knowledge follow. The Rural Pan, Marginalia, and Of Smoking close the range. These are essays for a countryman stranded in the city.

The Romance of the Road opens with Rabelais. Pantagruel visited an island whose roads literally went to places. Grahame's real-life answer is the Ridgeway of the North Berkshire Downs. Join it at Streatley, where it crosses the Thames. It strikes away from the habitable world at once. A broad green ribbon of turf, it keeps the highest ridge. No village tempts it aside for a yard.
pages-from-a-journal-with-other-papers: Pages from a Journal with Other Papers is by Mark Rutherford. That was the pen name of William Hale White. T. Fisher Unwin published this second impression in London in 1901. The hosted sample shows the title page and contents only. A Visit to Carlyle in 1868 leads the contents. Journal entries for January, March, June, and August follow. Pieces on Spinoza, Injustice, Faith, and talking about our troubles complete it. No essay text appears in the sample.
pardners:
Rex Beach's Pardners collects tales of the Alaskan gold country. Beach had written The Spoilers and The Barrier. Ten stories fill the contents. The Mule Driver and the Garrulous Mute appears. So do The Colonel and the Horse-Thief and The Thaw at Slisco's. Bitter Root Billings and North of Fifty-Three close the range. The title story opens the book in a tent.

Joyce, its narrator, announces that most quotations need fixing. Marriages, the old saying claims, are made in heaven. Joyce insists the saying meant pardnerships. A true pardnership is the sanctifiedest relation that grows. Just then the camp dogs erupt outside. Joyce dives through the tent flap to arbitrate. Beach's Alaska runs on that mixture: philosophy, profanity, and dogfights.
parish-papers: Norman Macleod's Parish Papers appeared in 1863. Macleod was a Doctor of Divinity and one of Queen Victoria's chaplains for Scotland. He dedicated the papers to his parishioners of Loudoun, Dalkeith, and the Barony. The hosted sample shows the title page, dedication, and contents only. Thoughts on Christianity leads, asking what Christianity is and who Jesus was. Thoughts on the Final Judgment and on Future Life follow. Future Punishment and What After Death? close the range. No essay text appears in the sample.
patty-s-suitors: In the hosted sample, only the front matter of Patty's Suitors, the title page and table of contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Carolyn Wells and E. C. Caswell as illustrator. The contents open with a Valentine party and move through a house party, a quarantine, May-Day, and moonlight, with chapters named Eddie Bell, Kenneth, and Belle Harcourt. Those chapters mark the social round in which Patty's suitors appear.
phaethon-loose-thoughts-for-loose-thinke:
Charles Kingsley's Phaethon, dated 1852, is subtitled Loose Thoughts for Loose Thinkers. Two friends lounge by a clear limestone stream in a park, fishing badly on a lovely morning. Templeton confesses he has been dreaming instead of fishing; the narrator has sat up all night writing after a talkative evening.

The talk of that evening runs on, in dialogue, while the flies rise and the keeper despairs of them. Kingsley uses the fishing idyll to carry arguments about faith, doubt, and the Church. The book is a conversation piece: theology in waders, with the Severn hills in view.
piano-mastery-talks-with-master-pianists: In the hosted sample, only the front matter of Piano Mastery, the title page and the start of the contents, with no talk text visible. The title page names Harriette Brower and promises talks with master pianists and teachers, an account of a Von Bülow class, hints on interpretation by William Mason and William H. Sherwood, and sixteen portraits. The contents open with a prelude and Paderewski, then Ernest Schelling on the hand of a pianist and Sigismond Stojowski on mind in piano study.
pindar-odes-myers:
Pindar of Thebes was the greatest lyric poet of ancient Greece. Ernest Myers translated his surviving victory odes into English. The odes celebrate winners at the Olympic, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian games.

Each ode weaves the victor's praise together with myth and moral warning. Pindar warns athletes that glory is brief and pride draws divine anger. His language is dense, soaring, and famously hard to follow. Chariot owners, wrestlers, and boy boxers all receive the same lofty treatment. Myers helps modern readers through the thickets of allusion. These poems defined how Greece praised excellence in public.
pirke-avot-the-sayings-of-the-jewish-fat: Joseph Isaac Gorfinkle's edition presents Pirke Avot, the Sayings of the Jewish Fathers. It is the third volume in a Library of Jewish Classics series, after works by Zunz and Hyman Hurwitz. The sample held for this entry holds the transcriber's comments, not the sayings themselves. Those notes say the source book printed all of Pirkei Avot in Hebrew with vowels. That Hebrew text is left out of this e-text, and Hebrew words appear in brackets in transliterated form. Footnotes were moved to follow the passages they belong to.
podcast-joerogan-Xr0jaqT8eRs:
Jay Anderson joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2430 for a full-length conversation. The entry keeps the show's standard shape: one guest across hours of open talk with Rogan, with the transcript holding the whole session as it aired.

The value of such entries is the record itself, the guest's views and stories in his own words rather than in clips cut by others. Readers can follow the exchange from start to finish and judge the ideas whole. The episode stands in the library as a complete sitting with the day's guest, filed for listeners who want nothing trimmed away.
podcast-joerogan-nMBFf1SIBRs:
Benjamin Franklin is the unlikely star of this Joe Rogan Experience segment about skeletons found in a London basement. Franklin lived in the house for years while serving as a colonial agent. When workers dug into the cellar, they found human bones buried under the floor.

Rogan and his guest sort through why the bones were there. The leading account points to an anatomy school run by Franklin's friend, who used bodies for study and buried the remains in secret. They weigh that sober story against darker rumors. It is a short, strange detour into the hidden side of a founding father.
ponkapog-papers:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich gathered his miscellaneous notes and essays as Ponkapog Papers, explaining the odd title in a note from Redman Farm, Ponkapog, in 1903. Ponkapog, a little Massachusetts settlement under the Blue Hills on an old Indian reservation, has no illusions about rivalling great centers. Aldrich claims the same modesty for his papers, with alluring alliteration as a further excuse. The book is dedicated to Francis Bartlett.

Contents promise a notebook's variety: leaves from a notebook, asides, an essay on Tom Folio, queer surnames, a note on Rostand's L'Aiglon. Plot and character, the cruelty of science, Leigh Hunt and Barry Cornwall, Decoration Day, writers and talkers, and the case against early rising. Aldrich, poet, editor of the Atlantic, and author of the Story of a Bad Boy. Writes here as a gentleman at leisure, and the slightness he apologizes for is exactly the charm his readers bought.
primavera-poems-by-four-authors:
Thomas B. Mosher of Portland, Maine, published Primavera in 1900 from his press at 45 Exchange Street. A volume of poems by four authors, issued with the care for type and paper that made Mosher's books collectible on sight. An epigraph from Guarini's Pastor Fido gives the book its name and season: spring, youth of the year. Beautiful mother of flowers and new loves, returns, but the serene days of the speaker's joys do not return with her.

The opening poem refuses the Muse outright: no Muse will I invoke, for she is fled. Sitting breathing yet all but dead, she who dreamed of gods in Tempe's golden air and deemed heroic Greece could never die. The four poets of the volume, young men of the 1890s little magazine world, mourn and celebrate that fled muse between them. Primavera is the American aesthetic movement in one small garland.
quiet-talks-with-world-winners: Quiet Talks with World Winners, by S. D. Gordon, is shown here by its contents alone. Part one, World-winning, treats the master passion, the Master's plan, the need, the present opportunity, the pressing emergency, the past failure, and the coming victory. Part two, Winning Forces, names the church, each single believer, Jesus, the Holy Spirit, prayer, money, and sacrifice. The opening talk, The Master Passion, breaks into heads that run from the earliest Calvary picture to Jesus' world-passion.
quotations-from-georg-ebers: Quotations from Georg Ebers is one of David Widger's quotation volumes, drawn from the Project Gutenberg edition of Ebers's collected historical novels. The pages shown give Widger's editor's note and the start of his contents. He invites readers who know the novels to check whether their favorite passages are listed and to send additions. The contents begin with the ten volumes of Uarda and the volumes of An Egyptian Princess, each tied to its source file.
quotes-and-images-from-the-novels-of-geo:
